author: Decemviri
source_text: Si in ius vocat, ito. Ni it, antestamino. Igitur em capito.
question: Quid facere debet qui in ius vocat, antequam vocatum ire nolentem capiat, ex lege duodecim tabularum?
question_en: Under the Law of the Twelve Tables, what must the summoner do before he seizes a man who, summoned to court, refuses to go?
derivation: Procedure of tab. I: ni it, antestamino; igitur em capito — first call witnesses, only then lay hold of him. The antestatio was ambient legal culture (cf. Horace, Sermones 1.9.76 'licet antestari?'). Anchored to the named law; single supported answer.

author: Decemviri
source_text: Si calvitur pedemve struit, manum endo iacito.
question: Quid ei licet qui in ius vocat, si vocatus calvitur pedemve struit, ex lege duodecim tabularum?
question_en: What may the summoner do under the Law of the Twelve Tables if the man summoned shirks or takes to flight?
derivation: Tab. I on the evasive defendant: si calvitur pedemve struit, manum endo iacito — the archaic clause glossed by Festus. The permitted act (laying on of the hand) is the single supported answer; anchored to the named law and the defined situation.

author: Decemviri
source_text: Si morbus aevitasve vitium escit, iumentum dato.
question: Quid dari lex duodecim tabularum iubet, si morbus aevitasve eum qui in ius vocatur impedit?
question_en: What does the Law of the Twelve Tables order to be provided if sickness or age hinders the man summoned to court?
derivation: The humane transport clause of tab. I, discussed at length by Gellius 20.1.25-29: if illness or age is the impediment, the summoner must supply a iumentum. Single named-object answer supported verbatim.

author: Decemviri
source_text: Si morbus aevitasve vitium escit, iumentum dato. Si nolet, arceram ne sternito.
question: Quale vehiculum aegro vocato sternere non cogitur is qui in ius vocat, ex lege duodecim tabularum?
question_en: What kind of vehicle is the summoner not obliged to furnish for a sick man he has summoned, under the Law of the Twelve Tables?
derivation: Counterpart of the iumentum clause: si nolet, arceram ne sternito — he need not spread the cushioned covered cart. The arcera is glossed from this very clause by Gellius 20.1.29-30. Single named-object answer supported verbatim.

author: Decemviri
source_text: Assiduo vindex assiduus esto. Proletario iam civi quis volet vindex esto.
question: Qualis vindex assiduo esse debet ex lege duodecim tabularum?
question_en: What sort of surety (vindex) must a landholder have under the Law of the Twelve Tables?
answer_en: A landholder (an assiduus, one of his own class).
derivation: The class rule on the vindex, quoted by Gellius 16.10.5: for an assiduus the surety must be an assiduus. Anchored to the named law and the named class; single supported answer.

author: Decemviri
source_text: Assiduo vindex assiduus esto. Proletario iam civi quis volet vindex esto.
question: Quis proletario civi vindex esse potest ex lege duodecim tabularum?
question_en: Who may act as surety (vindex) for a proletarian citizen under the Law of the Twelve Tables?
derivation: Second half of the vindex rule: for the proletarius, quis volet — any volunteer suffices. The assiduus/proletarius contrast made this clause a standard citation (Gellius 16.10). Single supported answer.

author: Decemviri
source_text: Ni pacunt, in comitio aut in foro ante meridiem caussam coiciunto.
question: Quo tempore diei litigantes causam coicere iubentur ex lege duodecim tabularum?
question_en: At what time of day are the litigants ordered to state their case under the Law of the Twelve Tables?
derivation: Time rule of the same clause: the pleading happens ante meridiem. Single time answer supported verbatim; pairs with the post-meridiem default judgment that follows.

author: Decemviri
source_text: Com peroranto ambo praesentes. Post meridiem praesenti litem addicito.
question: Cui litem post meridiem addici lex duodecim tabularum iubet, si alter litigantium abest?
question_en: To whom does the Law of the Twelve Tables order the suit to be awarded after midday, if one of the litigants is absent?
derivation: The default-judgment rule: post meridiem praesenti litem addicito — after noon, judgment goes to whichever party showed up. Anchored to the named law; single supported answer.

author: Decemviri
source_text: Si ambo praesentes, solis occasus suprema tempestas esto.
question: Quae est, ex lege duodecim tabularum, suprema tempestas qua iudicium finiri debet?
question_en: Under the Law of the Twelve Tables, what is the latest hour (suprema tempestas) by which court proceedings must end?
derivation: The celebrated court deadline: solis occasus suprema tempestas esto — sunset closes the day's proceedings. Quoted by Gellius 17.2.10 and proverbial in legal culture. Single supported answer.

author: Decemviri
source_text: Actor dicito: ex sponsione te mihi . . . dare oportere aio. Quando tu negas, te praetor iudicem sive arbitrum postulo uti des.
question: A quo actor, ex lege duodecim tabularum, iudicem sive arbitrum dari postulat, quando reus negat?
question_en: From whom, under the Law of the Twelve Tables, does the plaintiff demand that a judge or arbiter be given, when the defendant denies the claim?
derivation: The formula of the legis actio per iudicis arbitrive postulationem (cf. Gaius, Inst. 4.17a): the plaintiff addresses the praetor — te praetor iudicem sive arbitrum postulo uti des. The named magistracy is the single supported answer.

author: Decemviri
source_text: . . . morbus sonticus . . . aut status dies cum hoste . . . quid horum fuit unum iudici arbitrove reove, eo dies diffissus esto.
question: Quid fit de die iudicii, si morbus sonticus aut status dies cum hoste iudici arbitrove reove fuit, ex lege duodecim tabularum?
question_en: What happens to the trial day under the Law of the Twelve Tables if a grave illness, or a day appointed with a foreigner, has befallen the judge, the arbiter, or the defendant?
answer_en: The day is broken off (the hearing is postponed).
derivation: Adjournment clause of tab. II: morbus sonticus or a status dies cum hoste splits the trial day (dies diffissus esto). Cicero, De officiis 1.37 quotes status dies cum hoste to show hostis anciently meant the foreigner. Single supported outcome.

author: Decemviri
source_text: Cui testimonium defuerit, is tertiis diebus ob portum obvagulatum ito.
question: Quibus diebus is, cui testimonium defuerit, ob portum testis obvagulatum ire iubetur ex lege duodecim tabularum?
question_en: On which days is the man whose witness has failed him ordered to go wail before that witness's doorway, under the Law of the Twelve Tables?
derivation: The obvagulatio: the party let down by his witness goes every third day to howl before the defaulter's door (portus = house door, Festus). The interval tertiis diebus is the single supported answer; the picturesque rite made the clause memorable.

author: Decemviri
source_text: Aeris confessi rebusque iure iudicatis XXX dies iusti sunto.
question: Quot dies iusti debitori aeris confessi rebusque iure iudicatis lege duodecim tabularum dantur?
question_en: How many days of grace does the Law of the Twelve Tables give a debtor after admission of the debt or lawful judgment?
derivation: The famous thirty iusti dies of grace before execution on a confessed or adjudged debt (Gellius 20.1.42-43 explains them). Anchored to the named law; single number answer supported verbatim (XXX).

author: Decemviri
source_text: Post deinde manus iniectio esto. In ius ducito.
question: Quid debitori imminet ex lege duodecim tabularum, cum triginta dies iusti praeterierunt nec iudicatum fecit?
question_en: What awaits the debtor under the Law of the Twelve Tables once the thirty days of grace have passed and he has not satisfied the judgment?
answer_en: The laying-on of hands (manus iniectio — personal seizure).
derivation: Sequence of tab. III: after the thirty days, post deinde manus iniectio esto — the creditor seizes the debtor and hales him in ius. The named institution is the single supported answer.

author: Decemviri
source_text: Si volet suo vivito, ni suo vivit, qui eum vinctum habebit, libras faris endo dies dato.
question: Quantum farris in dies debitori vincto, qui suo non vivit, dare debet qui eum vinctum habet?
question_en: How much spelt per day must the creditor who holds a debtor in bonds give him, if the debtor does not live at his own expense?
answer_en: A pound of spelt (far) a day.
derivation: The maintenance clause of tab. III: the creditor must give libras faris endo dies — a pound of far daily — to the imprisoned debtor who has no means of his own (Gellius 20.1.45). Single measure answer supported verbatim.

author: Decemviri
source_text: Erat autem ius interea paciscendi ac nisi pacti forent habebantur in vinculis dies LX.
question: Quot dies debitores addicti, nisi pacti erant, in vinculis habebantur, ut Gellius de lege duodecim tabularum tradit?
question_en: For how many days were bound-over debtors kept in chains if no settlement was reached, as Gellius reports of the Law of the Twelve Tables?
derivation: Gellius 20.1.46 (quoted in the text) on the debt procedure: sixty days in chains with the right to settle meanwhile. Attributed to Gellius since the number comes from his account of the law; single number answer supported verbatim (dies LX).

author: Decemviri
source_text: Tertiis nundinis partis secanto.
question: Quibus nundinis creditoribus partes debitoris secare licet ex lege duodecim tabularum?
question_en: On which market-day may the creditors cut their portions of the debtor, under the Law of the Twelve Tables?
derivation: The most notorious clause of the Tables: tertiis nundinis partis secanto — on the third nundinae the creditors may cut their shares. Gellius 20.1.48-52 discusses it with horror and notes no case was recorded. Single supported answer.

author: Decemviri
source_text: Si pater filium ter venum duit, filius a patre liber esto.
question: Quotiens pater filium venum dare debet, ut filius a patre liber sit, ex lege duodecim tabularum?
question_en: How many times must a father sell his son for the son to be free of the father, under the Law of the Twelve Tables?
derivation: The celebrated thrice-sold-son rule, the foundation of Roman emancipatio and adoption procedure (Gaius, Inst. 1.132 builds on it). Anchored to the named law; single number answer supported verbatim (ter).

author: Decemviri
source_text: Si iurgant . . . tres arbitri . . .
question: Quot arbitri dantur ex lege duodecim tabularum, si vicini de finibus iurgant?
question_en: How many arbiters are appointed under the Law of the Twelve Tables when neighbors quarrel over their boundaries?
derivation: The boundary-dispute clause: si iurgant — Cicero, De legibus 1.55 attests that iurgium in the Tables is precisely the neighbors' quarrel over fines — three arbiters are given to settle it. Single number answer supported by the fragment.

author: Decemviri
source_text: Si membrum rupsit, ni cum eo pacit, talio esto.
question: Quae poena est ex lege duodecim tabularum, si quis membrum alteri rupit nec cum eo pacit?
question_en: What is the penalty under the Law of the Twelve Tables if a man has maimed another's limb and does not come to terms with him?
derivation: The talion clause — si membrum rupsit, ni cum eo pacit, talio esto — the most famous penal provision of the Tables, quoted by Festus and discussed by Gellius 20.1.14-38. Anchored to the named law; single supported answer.

author: Decemviri
source_text: si iniuriam faxsit, viginti quinque poenae asses sunto.
question: Quot asses poenae sunt ex lege duodecim tabularum, si quis iniuriam alteri fecit?
question_en: How many asses is the penalty under the Law of the Twelve Tables if a man has committed a simple outrage (iniuria) against another?
derivation: The 25-as fine for iniuria, made famous by Gellius 20.1.13: L. Veratius strolled about slapping free men while a slave paid out the twenty-five asses on the spot — the anecdote that showed the tariff obsolete. Single number answer supported verbatim.

author: Decemviri
source_text: Patronus si clienti fraudem fecerit, sacer esto.
question: Quid fit patronus ex lege duodecim tabularum, si clienti fraudem fecerit?
question_en: What does a patron become under the Law of the Twelve Tables if he has wronged his client?
answer_en: Accursed (sacer — forfeited to the gods, an outlaw).
derivation: The patronage clause: patronus si clienti fraudem fecerit, sacer esto — the faithless patron becomes sacer, killable without penalty. Quoted by Servius (ad Aen. 6.609); the sanctity of the patron-client bond is core Roman social knowledge. Single supported answer.

author: Decemviri
source_text: Hominem mortuum in urbe ne sepelito neve urito.
question: Ubi hominem mortuum sepeliri urive lex duodecim tabularum vetat?
question_en: Where does the Law of the Twelve Tables forbid a dead man to be buried or burned?
derivation: The most famous funerary provision of Roman law: hominem mortuum in urbe ne sepelito neve urito (quoted by Cicero, De legibus 2.58) — the reason Roman tombs line the roads outside the gates. Anchored to the named law; single place answer supported verbatim.

author: Decemviri
source_text: hoc plus ne facito: rogum ascea ne polito.
question: Qua re rogum poliri lex duodecim tabularum vetat?
question_en: With what tool does the Law of the Twelve Tables forbid the funeral pyre to be smoothed?
answer_en: With the adze (ascia) — the pyre wood was to be left rough.
derivation: The funeral-expense limits of tab. X: rogum ascea ne polito — no dressed timber for the pyre, a curb on funerary display quoted by Cicero, De legibus 2.59. Single named-tool answer supported verbatim.

author: Decemviri
source_text: Homine mortuo ne ossa legito, quo post funus faciat.
question: Quid homine mortuo legi vetat lex duodecim tabularum, quo post funus alterum fiat?
question_en: What does the Law of the Twelve Tables forbid to be gathered from the dead, for the purpose of holding a second funeral later?
derivation: The one-funeral rule: ne ossa legito, quo post funus faciat — the bones may not be collected to stage a later funeral (Cicero, De legibus 2.60 notes the exception for death in war or abroad). Single supported answer (ossa).

author: Decemviri
source_text: Neve aurum addito.
question: Quod metallum cum mortuo poni lex duodecim tabularum vetat?
question_en: Which metal does the Law of the Twelve Tables forbid to be placed with the dead?
derivation: The grave-goods restriction: neve aurum addito — no gold in the burial, part of the sumptuary program of tab. X quoted by Cicero, De legibus 2.60. Single named-metal answer supported verbatim.

author: Decemviri
locus: Lex XII Tabularum, tab. XI 1 (Cicero, De re publica 2.36-37)
source_text: qui duabus tabulis iniquarum legum additis...conubia haec illi ut ne plebei cum patribus essent, inhumanissima lege sanxerunt.
question: Quorum inter se conubia duae postremae tabulae legum duodecim vetuerunt?
question_en: Marriages between which two orders did the last two of the Twelve Tables forbid?
derivation: The notorious conubium ban of the eleventh table, branded inhumanissima lex by Cicero (De re publica 2.63, quoted in the text) and repealed by the lex Canuleia of 445 BC — a hinge of the Struggle of the Orders and standard Roman historical knowledge. Two-order supported answer.

author: Vinidarius (ex Apicio)
provenance: Bibliotheca Augustana (www.hs-augsburg.de/~harsch), text after the Teubner edition (M. E. Milham)
source_text: OFELLAS GARATON: Lasar, zingiber, cardamomum et uno acetabulo liquaminis misces cum his omnibus tritis et ibi ofellas coques.
question: Quae duo aromata cum lasare in ofellas garaton in excerptis Vinidarii teruntur?
question_en: What two aromatics are ground with laser for the ofellae 'garaton' in the excerpts of Vinidarius?
derivation: The garum-sauced ofellae of the excerpts cook in a pounding of laser, ginger and cardamom in a measure of liquamen — the eastern spice trade in a pork dish. Two-name answer verbatim (zingiber, cardamomum).

author: Vinidarius (ex Apicio)
provenance: Bibliotheca Augustana (www.hs-augsburg.de/~harsch), text after the Teubner edition (M. E. Milham)
source_text: PISCES SCORPIONES RAPVLATOS: Coquis in liquamen et oleo et cum mediaverit coctura, tolles. rapas elixas madidas et minutissime concisas manibus depressabis, ut humorem non habeant, et cum pisce obligas, et bulliat cum oleo abunde. et, iam bullivit, teres cuminum, lauri bacam dimidiam, addes propter colorem crocum. amulabis de oryza propter spissitudinem. superfundes et tunc inferes. addes modicum acetum.
question: Quid piscibus scorpionibus rapulatis propter colorem in excerptis Vinidarii additur?
question_en: What is added for the sake of color to the scorpion fish with turnips in the excerpts of Vinidarius?
derivation: The scorpion fish with turnips (pisces scorpiones rapulati) is colored with saffron, the text stating the reason itself (propter colorem). Named dish with a single-word answer; verbatim (addes propter colorem crocum).

author: Vinidarius (ex Apicio)
provenance: Bibliotheca Augustana (www.hs-augsburg.de/~harsch), text after the Teubner edition (M. E. Milham)
source_text: PISCES SCORPIONES RAPVLATOS: Coquis in liquamen et oleo et cum mediaverit coctura, tolles. rapas elixas madidas et minutissime concisas manibus depressabis, ut humorem non habeant, et cum pisce obligas, et bulliat cum oleo abunde. et, iam bullivit, teres cuminum, lauri bacam dimidiam, addes propter colorem crocum. amulabis de oryza propter spissitudinem. superfundes et tunc inferes. addes modicum acetum.
question: Ex quo grano fit amulum, quo pisces scorpiones rapulati in excerptis Vinidarii propter spissitudinem obligantur?
question_en: From what grain is the starch made with which the scorpion fish with turnips is thickened in the excerpts of Vinidarius?
derivation: The dish is thickened with rice starch (amulum de oryza) — rice, an exotic import, appearing in the late Roman kitchen as a thickener, with the purpose stated (propter spissitudinem). Verbatim (amulabis de oryza).

author: Vinidarius (ex Apicio)
provenance: Bibliotheca Augustana (www.hs-augsburg.de/~harsch), text after the Teubner edition (M. E. Milham)
source_text: PORCELLVM THYMO SPARSVM: Porcellum lactentem pridie occisum elixas sale et anethum et in aqua frigida adsidue intingis, ut candorem habeat.
question: Quo consilio porcellus thymo sparsus in aqua frigida adsidue in excerptis Vinidarii intingitur?
question_en: For what purpose is the thyme-sprinkled suckling pig repeatedly dipped in cold water in the excerpts of Vinidarius?
answer_en: So that it may have whiteness.
derivation: The thyme-strewn suckling pig, killed the day before, is boiled with salt and dill and plunged again and again into cold water to whiten the flesh — the aesthetic of the pale-boiled pig, purpose stated verbatim (ut candorem habeat).

author: Vinidarius (ex Apicio)
provenance: Bibliotheca Augustana (www.hs-augsburg.de/~harsch), text after the Teubner edition (M. E. Milham)
source_text: HAEDVM LASARATVM: Haedi intestinas bene purgatas imples piper, liquamen, lasar, oleum et intra haedum mittes et bene consues et cum haedo simul coquuntur.
question: Quae pars haedi lasarati impleta intra haedum in excerptis Vinidarii remittitur?
question_en: What part of the laser-seasoned kid is stuffed and put back inside the kid in the excerpts of Vinidarius?
derivation: The haedus lasaratus: the kid's cleaned intestines are filled with pepper, liquamen, laser and oil, returned inside the animal, sewn in and cooked with it. Named dish; verbatim (intestinas... imples... et intra haedum mittes).

author: Apicius
source_text: ABSINTHIUM ROMANUM SIC FACIES. Conditi Camerini praeceptis, utique pro absinthio cessante; in cuius vicem absinthi Pontici purgati terendique unciam, Thebaicam dabis, masticis, folii scripulos III, vini eius modi sextarios XVIII.
question: Quod absinthium in absinthium Romanum conficiendum apud Apicium mittitur?
question_en: Which wormwood goes into the making of absinthium Romanum (Roman wormwood wine) in Apicius?
derivation: Absinthium Romanum, the Roman wormwood aperitif, is made with an ounce of cleaned Pontic wormwood (absinthi Pontici purgati... unciam). Named drink plus named regional variety; one checkable answer, verbatim.

author: Apicius
source_text: Folias rosarum, albo sublato, lino inseris ut sutilis facias, et vino quam plurimas infundes, ut septem diebus in vino sint. Post septem dies rosam de vino tollis et alias sutiles recentes similiter mittis, ut per dies septem in vino requiescant, et rosam eximis.
question: Per quot dies folia rosarum singulis vicibus in vino manent, cum rosatum apud Apicium paratur?
question_en: For how many days at each steeping do the rose petals stay in the wine when rosatum is prepared in Apicius?
derivation: Rosatum, the Roman rose wine, is made by steeping stitched garlands of rose petals in wine seven days at a time, three times over. Number fact tied to a named wine; septem diebus verbatim.

author: Apicius
source_text: Similiter et tertio facies et rosam eximis et vinum colas et, cum ad bibendum voles uti, addito melle rosatum conficies, sane custodito ut rosam a rore siccam et optimam mittas.
question: Quid rosato, cum ad bibendum uti voles, additur apud Apicium?
question_en: What is added to rosatum in Apicius when you wish to use it for drinking?
derivation: The rose-steeped wine only becomes rosatum for drinking with the addition of honey (addito melle rosatum conficies). Named drink; single-ingredient answer, verbatim.

author: Apicius
source_text: ROSATUM SINE ROSA SIC FACIES. Folia citri viridia in sportella palmea in dolium musti mittes antequam ferveat, et post quadraginta dies exime.
question: Ex quibus foliis rosatum sine rosa apud Apicium fit?
question_en: From what leaves is 'rosatum without roses' made in Apicius?
derivation: A celebrated kitchen substitution: rose wine counterfeited with green citron leaves steeped in must for forty days. Named preparation (rosatum sine rosa); answer verbatim (folia citri viridia).

author: Apicius
source_text: In oleo Spano mittes hellenium et cyperi et folia lauri non vetusta, tunsa omnia et cribellata, ad levissimum pulverem redacta, et sales frictos et tritos, et per triduum vel plus promisce diligenter. Post haec aliquanto tempore patere requiescere, et Liburnicum omnes putabunt.
question: Ex quo oleo Apicius oleum Liburnicum imitatur?
question_en: From what oil does Apicius counterfeit Liburnian oil?
derivation: Oleum Liburnium, a prized branded oil, is imitated by seasoning Spanish oil with elecampane, cyperus and fresh bay leaves until 'everyone will think it Liburnian' (Liburnicum omnes putabunt). Geographic-brand fact of Roman food commerce; base oil verbatim (in oleo Spano).

author: Apicius
source_text: Lomentum ex faba factum vel ovorum trium alborem in lagonam mittis et diutissime agitas: alia die erit candidum.
question: Ex quo legumine lomentum fit, quo vinum atrum apud Apicium candidum redditur?
question_en: From what legume is the meal made with which dark wine is turned white in Apicius?
derivation: Wine-fining as household practice: bean meal (lomentum ex faba) shaken in the flask leaves dark wine white by the next day. Named technique with a single-ingredient answer, verbatim.

author: Apicius
source_text: Liquamen si odorem malum fecerit, val inan inversum fumiga lauro et cupresso, et in hoc liquamen infunde ante ventilatum.
question: Quibus lignis vas inversum fumigatur, si liquamen odorem malum fecerit, ut apud Apicium emendetur?
question_en: With what woods is the upturned vessel fumigated, according to Apicius, when liquamen has developed a bad smell?
derivation: How to rescue spoiled liquamen, the universal Roman fish sauce: fumigate a vessel with laurel and cypress smoke and pour the aired sauce into it. Staple-sauce repair is insider kitchen knowledge; both woods verbatim.

author: Apicius
source_text: UT CARNES SINE SALE QUOVIS TEMPORE RECENTES SINT. Carnes recentes quales volueris melle tegantur, sed vas pendeat et, quando volueris, utere.
question: Quo teguntur carnes, ut sine sale quovis tempore recentes sint, apud Apicium?
question_en: With what are meats covered, according to Apicius, so that they stay fresh at any time without salt?
derivation: Keeping meat fresh without salting: cover it in honey in a hanging vessel. Honey as the Roman kitchen's preservative constant; verbatim (melle tegantur), anchored by the rubric sine sale.

author: Apicius
source_text: Carnem salsam dulcem facies, si prius in lacte coquas et postea in aquam.
question: In quo liquore carnem salsam prius coqui oportet, ut apud Apicium dulcis fiat?
question_en: In what liquid must salted meat first be boiled, according to Apicius, to make it sweet again?
derivation: Desalting carnes salsae, the standard preserved meat of the Roman larder: boil first in milk, then in water. Single-answer technique fact, verbatim (prius in lacte coquas).

author: Apicius
source_text: UT PISCES FRICTI DIU DURENT. Eodem momento quo friguntur et levantur ab aceto calido perfunduntur.
question: Quo perfunduntur pisces fricti statim ubi levantur, ut apud Apicium diu durent?
question_en: With what are fried fish doused the moment they are taken up, according to Apicius, so that they keep long?
derivation: Preserving fried fish by dousing them with hot vinegar straight from the pan - vinegar as the Roman escabeche-style preservative. Verbatim (ab aceto calido perfunduntur).

author: Apicius
source_text: OSTREA, UT DIU DURENT. Lavas ab aceto, aut ex aceto vasculum picitum lava, et ostrea compone.
question: Quo liquore ostrea lavantur, ut apud Apicium diu durent?
question_en: With what liquid are oysters washed in Apicius so that they keep long?
derivation: Keeping oysters - a Roman luxury shipped far inland - by washing them, or a pitched jar for them, with vinegar. Named delicacy; single-answer verbatim.

author: Apicius
source_text: Laser in spatiosum doliolum vitreum mittis et nucleos pineos et puta viginti, cumque utendum fuerit lasere, nucleos contere, et in cibis miraberis sapores; et tantum numero nucleorum doliolo reserentur.
question: Cum quibus nucleis uncia laseris apud Apicium conditur, ut toto tempore duret?
question_en: With what nuts is an ounce of laser stored in Apicius so that it lasts indefinitely?
derivation: Laser (silphium juice), famously scarce and costly, is stretched by keeping it with about twenty pine nuts in a glass jar; the nuts, crushed into dishes, carry its flavor. Iconic luxury-ingredient economy; nucleos pineos verbatim.

author: Apicius
source_text: MEL CORRUPTUM UT PROBES. Inlunium infundes in melle et incende. Si incorruptum est, lucet.
question: Quid facit mel incorruptum apud Apicium, cum ellychnium eo infusum incenditur?
question_en: What does unspoiled honey do in Apicius when a lamp-wick dipped in it is set alight?
derivation: The honey test: a wick dipped in honey and lit burns clear if the honey is unspoiled. Verifiable single-word answer, verbatim (si incorruptum est, lucet).

author: Apicius
source_text: Accipies uvas de vite inlaesas, et aquam pluvialem ad tertias decoques, et mittis in vas in quo et uvas mittis. Vas picari et gipsari facies, et in locum frigidum ubi soli accesusum non habet reponi facies et, quando volueris, uvas virides invenies.
question: In qua aqua uvae inlaesae apud Apicium conduntur, ut virides serventur?
answer: In aqua pluviali ad tertias decocta.
question_en: In what water are unblemished grapes stored in Apicius so that they keep green?
answer_en: In rainwater boiled down to a third.
derivation: Keeping grapes fresh through the year: sealed in rainwater reduced to a third, in a pitched and plastered jar in a cold place. Named preservation practice; aqua pluvialis ad tertias verbatim.

author: Apicius
source_text: UT MALA CIDONIA DIU SERVENTUR. Eligis mala sine vitio cum ramulis et foliis et condes in vas et suffundes mel et defritum et diu servabis.
question: Quibus liquoribus mala cydonia apud Apicium suffunduntur, ut diu serventur?
question_en: With what liquids are quinces covered in Apicius so that they keep long?
derivation: Quinces keep under honey and defrutum - two staples of the Roman larder in one practice. Two-item answer verbatim (suffundes mel et defritum).

author: Apicius
source_text: FICUM RECENTEM, MALA, PRUNA, PIRA, CERASIA UT DIU SERVES. Omnia cum peciolis diligenter legito et in melle ponito ne se contingant.
question: In quo ficus recentes, pruna, pira, cerasia apud Apicium ponuntur, ut diu serventur?
question_en: In what are fresh figs, plums, pears, and cherries placed in Apicius so that they keep long?
derivation: Fresh fruit is kept by laying it, stalks on, in honey so that the pieces do not touch. Honey as the all-purpose Roman preservative; in melle ponito verbatim.

author: Apicius
source_text: CUMINATUM IN OSTREA ET CONCHICLA. Piper, ligusticum, petroselinum, mentam siccam, folium, malabatrum, cuminum plusculum, mel, acetum et liquamen.
question: In quae edulia cuminatum apud Apicium paratur?
question_en: For what foods is the cumin sauce (cuminatum) prepared in Apicius?
derivation: The rubric ties the named sauce to its foods: cuminatum is the dressing for oysters and shellfish. Named preparation plus named foodstuffs, verbatim in the heading.

author: Apicius
source_text: OENOGARUM IN TUBERA. Piper, ligusticum, coriandrum, rutam, liquamen, mel, vinum et oleum modice.
question: Quod condimentum apud Apicium in tubera paratur?
question_en: What sauce is prepared for truffles in Apicius?
derivation: Oenogarum - the ubiquitous wine plus fish-sauce blend - is the dressing Apicius assigns to truffles. Named sauce, named delicacy; rubric verbatim.

author: Apicius
source_text: Piperis semunciam, silis Gallici scripulos II, cardamomi scripulos VI, cumini scripulos VI, folii scripulum I, mentae siccae scripulos VI, tunsa cribrataque melle colligis. Cum opus fuerit, liquamen et acetum addis.
question: Qui duo liquores oxygaro digestibili apud Apicium, cum opus fuerit, adduntur?
question_en: Which two liquids are added to the digestive oxygarum in Apicius when required?
derivation: Oxygarum, the vinegar-sharpened garum digestive, is finished with liquamen and vinegar - the pair that gives it its name (oxy- plus garum). Verbatim (liquamen et acetum addis).

author: Apicius
provenance: Bibliotheca Augustana (www.hs-augsburg.de/~harsch), text after the Teubner edition (M. E. Milham)
source_text: Ius in murena assa: piper, ligusticum, satureiam, crocomagma, cepa, pruna damascena enucleata, vinum, mulsum, acetum, liquamen, defritum, oleum, et coques.
question: Quod condimentum ex croco factum in ius in murenam assam apud Apicium mittitur?
question_en: What saffron preparation goes into the sauce for roasted moray in Apicius?
derivation: The moray eel, the most storied fish of Roman luxury (kept in the piscinae of the rich), gets a sauce containing crocomagma, the pressed cake of saffron unguent — an exotic pharmacological luxury in the kitchen. Verbatim.

author: Apicius
provenance: Bibliotheca Augustana (www.hs-augsburg.de/~harsch), text after the Teubner edition (M. E. Milham)
source_text: Ius in anguilla: piper, ligusticum, apii semen, anethum, rhus Syriacum, caryotam, mel, acetum, liquamen, oleum, sinape et defritum.
question: Quod condimentum Syriacum in ius in anguillam apud Apicium mittitur?
question_en: What Syrian seasoning goes into the sauce for eel in Apicius?
derivation: The eel chapter's sauce features rhus Syriacum, the imported sumac of Syria — a geographically branded spice on a named fish. Verbatim; the same spice recurs in the boiled moray sauce.

author: Apicius
provenance: Bibliotheca Augustana (www.hs-augsburg.de/~harsch), text after the Teubner edition (M. E. Milham)
source_text: Ius in dentice asso: piper, ligusticum, coriandrum, mentam, rutam aridam, malum cydonium coctum, mel, vinum, liquamen, oleum. calefacies, amulo obligabis.
question: Quod pomum coctum in ius in denticem assum apud Apicium mittitur?
question_en: What cooked fruit goes into the sauce for roasted dentex in Apicius?
derivation: The sauce for roast dentex is anchored by a cooked quince (malum cydonium) — the one whole fruit among the seasonings, the sweet-sour fish dressing of the Roman table. Verbatim (malum cydonium coctum).

author: Apicius
source_text: Assas iecur porcinum et eum enervas. Ante tamen teres piper, rutam, liquamen, et sic superinmittis iecur et teres et misces, sicut pulpa omentata, et singula involvuntur folia lauri et ad fumum suspenduntur quamdiu voles.
question: Ex cuius animalis iecore omentata apud Apicium fiunt?
question_en: From the liver of what animal are the omentata made in Apicius?
derivation: The omentata, caul-wrapped forcemeats, are built on roasted pork liver. Named preparation, single-ingredient answer, verbatim (assas iecur porcinum).

author: Apicius
source_text: Assas iecur porcinum et eum enervas. Ante tamen teres piper, rutam, liquamen, et sic superinmittis iecur et teres et misces, sicut pulpa omentata, et singula involvuntur folia lauri et ad fumum suspenduntur quamdiu voles.
question: Quibus foliis involuta omentata ad fumum apud Apicium suspenduntur?
question_en: Wrapped in what leaves are the omentata hung in the smoke in Apicius?
derivation: The omentata are wrapped one by one in bay leaves and hung in the smoke to cure. Distinctive named practice; folia lauri and ad fumum verbatim.

author: Apicius
source_text: Pusilla esicia formabis, intus nucleis et pipere positis. Involuta omento subassabis cum careno.
question: Quo involuta isicia omentata apud Apicium subassantur?
question_en: Wrapped in what are the isicia omentata browned in Apicius?
derivation: The name-defining fact of the isicia omentata: they are wrapped in omentum (caul fat) and browned with caroenum. Named dish; involuta omento verbatim.

author: Apicius
source_text: Accipies adipes fasiani recentes, praeduras et facis ex eo tessellas, cum pipere, liquamine, careno in isicio includes, ex idrogaro coques et inferes.
question: Cuius avis adipes recentes in isiciis plenis apud Apicium includuntur?
question_en: The fresh fat of what bird is enclosed inside the 'stuffed' isicia (isicia plena) in Apicius?
derivation: Isicia plena are forcemeats hiding cubes of fresh pheasant fat inside - a luxury-bird fact. Named dish; adipes fasiani recentes verbatim.

author: Apicius
source_text: Ad unum liquaminis acetabulum aquae septem mittes, modicum apii viridis, triti piperis cocleare.
question: Quot acetabula aquae ad unum liquaminis acetabulum in isicio simplici apud Apicium mittuntur?
question_en: How many measures of water go to one measure of liquamen in the isicium simplex of Apicius?
derivation: The dilution of the staple sauce for the plain isicium: one acetabulum of liquamen to seven of water. Clean number fact, verbatim (aquae septem).

author: Apicius
source_text: Isiciola incoques et sic ad ventrem solvendum dabis. Idrogaro feces conditi addes.
question: Ad quem usum isiciola in hydrogaro cocta apud Apicium dantur?
question_en: For what use are the little forcemeats boiled in hydrogarum given in Apicius?
derivation: Food as medicine: the light isiciola in hydrogarum are prescribed as a laxative (ad ventrem solvendum). Purpose fact with a short verbatim answer.

author: Apicius
source_text: Isicia de pavo primum locum habent ita si fricta fuerint ut callum vincant. Item secundum locum habent de fasianis, tem tertium locum habent de cunicuis, tiem quartum locum habent de pullis, item quintum locum habent de porcello tenero.
question: Cuius avis isicia primum locum apud Apicium habent?
question_en: The forcemeats of which bird hold first place in Apicius?
derivation: The celebrated ranking of isicia: peacock first, then pheasant, rabbit, chicken, and tender suckling pig. Peacock as the prestige bird of the Roman table; primum locum de pavo verbatim.

author: Apicius
source_text: Quod si non fuerit, vel caricarum defritum mittes quod Romani colorem vocant, ac deineps amulum infusum adicies vel orizae sucum et lento igni fervere facias.
question: Cuius grani sucus pro amulo ad ius obligandum apud Apicium adhiberi potest?
question_en: The juice of what grain can serve in place of starch for thickening a sauce in Apicius?
derivation: Rice water as the substitute for amulum (starch) in binding sauces - rice as an exotic thickener in the Roman kitchen. Single-ingredient answer, verbatim (vel orizae sucum).

author: Apicius
source_text: Alicam elixa cum nucleis et amigdalis depilatis et in aqua infusis et lotis ex creta argentaria ut ad candorem pariter perducantur. Cui ammiscebis uvam passam, carenum vel passum. Desuper piper confractum asparges et in boletari inferes.
question: Ex quo frumento apothermum apud Apicium elixatur?
question_en: From what grain preparation is the apothermum boiled in Apicius?
derivation: Apothermum, the sweet spoon-dish of grits with pine nuts, skinned almonds, raisins and caroenum or passum, is built on alica - the Roman staple emmer grits. Named dish, base grain verbatim (alicam elixa).

author: Apicius
source_text: Cum liquamine admixto, pipere integro et abundanti pinguedine et nucleis inicies in intestinum perquam tenuatim perductum, et sic ad fumum suspenditur.
question: Quo lucanicae confectae apud Apicium suspenduntur?
question_en: Where are the finished lucanicae (Lucanian sausages) hung in Apicius?
derivation: Lucanicae - the famous sausage named for Lucania - are stuffed into a casing drawn very thin and hung in the smoke to cure. The defining process fact of a celebrated regional food; ad fumum suspenditur verbatim.

author: Apicius
source_text: Lucanicarum confectio teritur piper, cuminum, satureia, ruta, petroselinum, condimentum, bacae lauri, liquamen, et admiscetur pulpa bene tunsa ita ut denuo bene cum ipso subtrito fricetur.
question: Quae bacae in confectionem lucanicarum apud Apicium teruntur?
question_en: What berries are ground into the mixture for the lucanicae in Apicius?
derivation: Bay berries are the distinctive aromatic pounded into the lucanica mix alongside the pantry staples. Component fact of a famous named sausage; bacae lauri verbatim.

author: Apicius
source_text: Farcies intestinum et elixabis, deide cum sale assabis et cum senapi inferes, vel sic concisum in disco.
question: Cum quo condimento farcimen ex alica et pulpa apud Apicium infertur?
question_en: With what condiment is the sausage of grits and minced meat served in Apicius?
derivation: The boiled-then-roasted farcimen is brought to table with mustard - sausage and mustard already paired on the Roman table. Single-condiment answer, verbatim (cum senapi inferes).

author: Apicius
source_text: Reples intestinum inpensam esicii et circellum facies rotundum; fumas. Cum miniaverit, subassas, exornas, oenogaruo fasiani profundas, sed cuminum addes.
question: Quo iure circelli isiciati apud Apicium profunduntur?
question_en: With what sauce are the ring sausages (circelli isiciati) doused in Apicius?
derivation: The circelli - sausage bent into a round ring and smoked - are finished under pheasant oenogarum with added cumin. Named dish plus named sauce; oenogaro fasiani verbatim.

author: Apicius
source_text: Omne holus smaragdinum fit, si cum nitro coquatur.
question: Quo cum cocto omne holus apud Apicium smaragdinum fit?
question_en: Cooked with what does every green vegetable turn emerald in Apicius?
derivation: The famous opening trick of the vegetable book: any vegetable boiled with nitrum keeps an emerald color. Kitchen chemistry every Roman cook carried; the whole sentence is the fact, verbatim.

author: Apicius
source_text: Betas minutas et porros requietos elixabis, in patina compones. Teres piper, cuminum, suffundes liquamen, passum, ut quaedam dulcedo sit. Facias ut ferveat. Cum ferbuerit, inferes.
question: Ex quibus holeribus pulmentarium ad ventrem apud Apicium componitur?
question_en: From what vegetables is the bowel-easing dish (pulmentarium ad ventrem) composed in Apicius?
derivation: The pulmentarium ad ventrem - the digestive vegetable dish opening the chapter - is small beets and rested leeks, boiled and sweetened with passum. Named preparation; both vegetables verbatim.

author: Apicius
source_text: Varro: Betacios, sed nigros, quorum detersas radices et mulso decoctas cum sale modico et holeo vel sale, aqua et oleo in se coctas iusculum facere et potari, melius etiam si in eo pullus sit decoctus.
question: Cuius coloris betacios Varro apud Apicium commendat?
question_en: Beets of what color does Varro recommend, as quoted in Apicius?
derivation: The one recipe in Apicius quoted under Varro's name - a dish carried on a famous author's authority. Varro specifies black beets (betacios, sed nigros); person-anchored, single-word verbatim answer.

author: Apicius
source_text: Varro: Betacios, sed nigros, quorum detersas radices et mulso decoctas cum sale modico et holeo vel sale, aqua et oleo in se coctas iusculum facere et potari, melius etiam si in eo pullus sit decoctus.
question: Quo liquore decoctae radices betaciorum iusculum faciunt secundum Varronem apud Apicium?
question_en: Boiled down in what liquid do the beet roots make a broth, according to Varro as quoted in Apicius?
derivation: Varro's beet broth is made by boiling the cleaned roots in mulsum, the honey-wine staple. Person-anchored named preparation; mulso decoctas verbatim.

author: Apicius
source_text: Varro: Betacios, sed nigros, quorum detersas radices et mulso decoctas cum sale modico et holeo vel sale, aqua et oleo in se coctas iusculum facere et potari, melius etiam si in eo pullus sit decoctus.
question: Quo addito iusculum betaciorum Varronis etiam melius fit apud Apicium?
question_en: With what addition does Varro's beet broth become even better, according to Apicius?
answer_en: With a chicken boiled in it.
derivation: The closing touch of Varro's prescription: the beet broth is better still if a chicken has been boiled in it. Person-anchored, single short answer verbatim (si in eo pullus sit decoctus).

author: Apicius
source_text: Pepones, melones. Piper, puleium, mel vel passum, liquamen, acetum. Interdum et silfi accedit.
question: Quod condimentum interdum peponibus et melonibus apud Apicium accedit?
question_en: What seasoning is sometimes added to melons and gourds-melons in Apicius?
derivation: Melons at the Roman table take pepper, pennyroyal, honey and vinegar - and sometimes silphium, the celebrated luxury resin. Named foodstuff plus named seasoning; interdum et silfi accedit verbatim.

author: Apicius
source_text: ALITER BETAS ELIXAS. Ex sinapi, oleo modico et aceto bene inferuntur.
question: Ex quo condimento betae elixae apud Apicium bene inferuntur?
answer: Ex sinapi, oleo modico et aceto.
question_en: With what dressing are boiled beets best served in Apicius?
answer_en: With mustard, a little oil, and vinegar.
derivation: Boiled beets under a mustard vinaigrette - a table constant stated in one clause. Brief verbatim dressing as the whole answer.

author: Apicius
source_text: Rafanos cum piperato, ita ut piper cum liquamine teras.
question: Cum quo condimento rafani apud Apicium eduntur?
question_en: With what sauce are radishes eaten in Apicius?
derivation: Radishes take piperatum - pepper ground up with liquamen. Named vegetable plus named sauce, both verbatim; the definition of the piperatum is given in the same clause.

author: Apicius
source_text: HOLUS MOLLE EX HOLISATRO. Coctum ex aqua nitrata expressum concides minutum et teres piper, ligusticum, satureiam siccam cum cepa sicca, liquamen, oleum et vinum.
question: In quali aqua holus molle ex holisatro apud Apicium coquitur?
question_en: In what kind of water is the 'soft vegetable' of alexanders cooked in Apicius?
derivation: Holus molle, the pureed vegetable dish, is boiled in aqua nitrata - the same nitrum trick that keeps greens green, applied to a named preparation. Verbatim (coctum ex aqua nitrata).

author: Apicius
source_text: Urticam feminam, sole in ariete positio, adversus aedritudinem sumes, si voles.
question: Quo in signo sole posito urtica femina adversus aegritudinem apud Apicium sumitur?
question_en: With the sun standing in what sign is the female nettle taken against sickness in Apicius?
derivation: Food-medicine with an astrological clock: the female nettle is taken against illness when the sun is in Aries. Roman dietetic lore; sole in ariete verbatim, single named answer.

author: Apicius
source_text: intubae ex liquamine, oleo modico medere cepa concisa. Pro lactucis vero hieme intubae ex embammate vel melle et aceto acri.
question: Quae holera hieme pro lactucis apud Apicium adhibentur?
question_en: What vegetable stands in for lettuce in winter, according to Apicius?
derivation: The seasonal substitution of the Roman salad table: in winter endives take the place of lettuce, dressed with sauce or with honey and sharp vinegar. Verbatim (pro lactucis vero hieme intubae).

author: Apicius
source_text: LACTUCAS. Cum oxyporio et aceto modico liquamine.
question: Cum quo condimento digestorio lactucae apud Apicium dantur?
question_en: With what digestive condiment are lettuces served in Apicius?
derivation: Lettuce - reputed hard on the stomach - is served with oxyporium, the spiced digestive of cumin, ginger and honey, plus vinegar and a little liquamen. Named preparation, verbatim (cum oxyporio).

author: Apicius
source_text: Carotae frictae oenogaro inferuntar.
question: Quo iure carotae frictae apud Apicium inferuntur?
question_en: With what sauce are fried carrots served in Apicius?
derivation: Fried carrots under oenogarum, the wine-and-garum staple sauce. One-sentence fact, wholly verbatim; named vegetable plus named sauce.

author: Apicius
source_text: Panem ex posca maceratum exprimes, caseum bubulum, cucumeres in caccabulo compones, interpositis nucleis.
question: Ex quo liquore panis in sala cattabia apud Apicium maceratur?
question_en: In what liquid is the bread soaked for the sala cattabia in Apicius?
derivation: Sala cattabia, the cold bread salad, starts from bread soaked in posca - the everyday vinegar-water of soldiers and travelers. Named dish plus named drink; ex posca maceratum verbatim.

author: Apicius
source_text: Adicies in caccabulo panis Picentini frusta, interpones pulpas pulli, glandulas haedinas, caseum Vestinum, nucleos pinos, cucumeres, cepas aridas minute concisas.
question: Qui caseus in salam cattabiam Apicianam apud Apicium interponitur?
question_en: What cheese is layered into the Apician sala cattabia?
derivation: Vestine cheese - the celebrated cheese of the Vestini - is the cheese of the sala cattabia Apiciana. Second place-named product in the same dish; caseum Vestinum verbatim.

author: Apicius
source_text: Accipies asparagos purgatos, in moratrio fricabis, aqua suffundes, perfricabis, per colum colabis. Et mittes ficetulas curatas, teres in mortario piperis scripulos sex, adicies liquamen, fricabis, vini ciatum I, passi ciatum I, mittes in caccabus olei uncias III.
question: Quae aviculae in patinam de asparagis frigidam apud Apicium mittuntur?
question_en: What little birds go into the cold asparagus patina in Apicius?
derivation: The cold asparagus patina hides figpeckers - the tiny songbirds that were a byword for Roman luxury dining. Named dish plus named delicacy; ficetulas curatas verbatim.

author: Apicius
source_text: Accipies rosas et exfoliabis, album tolles, mittes in mortarium, suffundes liquamen, fricabis. Postea mittes liquaminis ciatum unum semis et sucum por colum colabis. Accipies cerebella IV, enervabis et teres piperis scripulos VIII, suffunes ex suco, fricabis.
question: Quae membra animalium cum suco rosarum in patina de rosis apud Apicium coquuntur?
question_en: What animal parts are cooked with the rose juice in the rose patina of Apicius?
derivation: The patina de rosis, the rose-petal custard, is bound on four brains with eggs - flowers and offal in one celebrated composite. Named dish; cerebella IV verbatim.

author: Apicius
source_text: Desuper leviter compones urticas marinas ut non cum ovis misceantur.
question: Quae animalia marina patinae de apua sine apua desuper apud Apicium componuntur?
question_en: What sea creatures are laid on top of the 'anchovy patina without anchovy' in Apicius?
derivation: The illusion dish patina de apua sine apua is finished with sea nettles laid lightly on top so they do not sink into the eggs. Named mock dish; urticas marinas verbatim.

author: Apicius
source_text: PATINAM APICIANAM SIC FACIES. Frustra suminis cocti, pulpas piscium, pulpas pulli, ficetulas vel pectora turdorum cocta et quaecumque optima fuerint, haec omnia concides diligenter praeter ficetulas.
question: Cuius partis suillae frustra in patinam Apicianam apud Apicium mittuntur?
question_en: Pieces of what part of the pig go into the patina Apiciana in Apicius?
derivation: The patina bearing Apicius' own name opens with cooked sumen - sow's udder, the byword pork delicacy - alongside fish, chicken, figpeckers or thrush breasts 'and whatever is finest', layered with lagana. Named dish; frustra suminis cocti verbatim.

author: Apicius
source_text: PATINA DE PIRIS. Pira elixa et purgata e medio teres cum pipere, cumino, melle, passo, liquamine, oleo modico. Ovis missis patinam facies, piper super aspargis et inferes.
question: Quibus missis pira trita in patinam apud Apicium coguntur?
question_en: With what added is the ground pear mixture set into a patina in Apicius?
derivation: The pear patina - the celebrated Roman pear custard: boiled cored pears ground with honey, passum and spices, set with eggs. Named dish; ovis missis patinam facies verbatim.

author: Apicius
source_text: Persica duriora purgabis, frustratim concides, elixas in patinia compones, olei modicum superstillabis et cum cuminato inferes.
question: Cum quo condimento patina de persicis apud Apicium infertur?
question_en: With what sauce is the peach patina served in Apicius?
derivation: The peach patina goes to table with cuminatum, the named cumin sauce of book I - fruit under a savory dressing, a very Roman pairing. Verbatim (cum cuminato inferes).

author: Apicius
source_text: Mala cydonia cum porris, melle, liquamine, oleo, defricto coques et inferes, vel elixata ex melle.
question: Cum quo holere mala cydonia in patina apud Apicium coquuntur?
question_en: With what vegetable are quinces cooked in their patina in Apicius?
derivation: The quince patina pairs the fruit with leeks under honey, liquamen and defrutum - a checkable, surprising pairing of named foodstuffs. Verbatim (mala cydonia cum porris).

author: Apicius
source_text: Cum cocta fuerit, addes echinos recentiores, piper asparges et inferes.
question: Quae animalia marina patinae ex lacte postremo apud Apicium adduntur?
question_en: What sea creatures are added last to the milk patina in Apicius?
derivation: The great patina ex lacte - the milk-and-egg composite of vegetables, chicken, sausages and shellfish - is crowned at the end with fresh sea urchins, a luxury of the Roman table. Verbatim (addes echinos recentiores).

author: Apicius
source_text: Oleum, liquamen, vinum, porrum capitatum, mentam, pisciculos, esiciola minuta, testiculos caponum, glandulas porcellinas, haecomnia in se coquantur.
question: Cuius avis testiculi in minutal Apicianum apud Apicium coquuntur?
question_en: The testicles of what bird are cooked into the minutal Apicianum?
derivation: The minutal Apicianum - the fricassee under Apicius' own name - includes capon testicles and piglet sweetbreads among its meats. Named dish; testiculos caponum verbatim, single answer.

author: Apicius
source_text: Adicies in caccabo oleum, liquamen, vinum, concides cepam Ascaloniam aridam, spatulam porcinam coctam tessellatim concides.
question: Quae cepa arida in minutal ex praecoquis apud Apicium conciditur?
question_en: What dried onion is chopped into the apricot minutal in Apicius?
derivation: The apricot stew (minutal ex praecoquis) starts from the Ascalonian onion - the shallot, named for Ascalon in Judaea; a place-named staple of the Roman kitchen. Verbatim (cepam Ascaloniam aridam).

author: Apicius
source_text: MINUTAL TERENTINUM. Concides in caccabum albanem de porris minutatim, adicies oleum, liquamen, cocturam, isiciola valde minuta, et sic temperas ut tenerum sit.
question: Cuius holeris albamen in minutal Terentinum apud Apicium minutatim conciditur?
question_en: The white of what vegetable is chopped fine into the minutal Terentinum?
derivation: The minutal Terentinum - another name-bearing stew - is built on the white of leeks with very fine forcemeat balls. Named dish; albamen de porris verbatim.

author: Apicius
source_text: Cum ferbuerit, tractam confringes, obligas, agitas, piper aspargis et inferes.
question: Qua re minutal marinum apud Apicium obligatur?
question_en: With what is the seafood minutal thickened in Apicius?
derivation: The signature binding of the minutal dishes: a sheet of tracta pastry crumbled in to thicken the pot - the same tracta that names the pultes tractogalatae. Anchored to the minutal marinum; tractam confringes, obligas verbatim.

author: Apicius
source_text: Tisanam lavando fricas, quam ante diem infundes. Impones supra ignem calidum.
question: Quando tisana apud Apicium aqua infunditur, antequam coquatur?
question_en: When is the barley for tisana put to soak in Apicius, before it is cooked?
derivation: Tisana, the barley gruel of ancient dietetics, is rubbed clean and soaked a day ahead. Named staple preparation; quam ante diem infundes verbatim.

author: Apicius
source_text: TISANAM BARRICAM. Infundes cicer, lenticulam, pisam. Defricas tisanam cum leguminibus elixas.
question: Quae legumina cum tisana barrica apud Apicium elixantur?
question_en: What legumes are boiled with the barley in the tisana barrica of Apicius?
derivation: The tisana barrica joins barley to the three staple legumes of the Roman diet - chickpea, lentil, pea - plus a garden of greens. Brief verbatim list as the whole answer.

author: Apicius
source_text: GUSTUM DE HOLERIBUS. Condies bulbos liquamine, oleo et vino. Cum cocti fuerint, iecinera porcelli et gallinarum et ungellas et ascellas divisas, haec omnia cum bulbis ferveant.
question: Quod holus in gusto de holeribus apud Apicium primum liquamine, oleo et vino conditur?
question_en: What vegetable is first seasoned with liquamen, oil, and wine in the vegetable starter (gustum de holeribus) of Apicius?
derivation: The gustum de holeribus, the vegetable appetizer course, is built on bulbi - the edible bulbs prized by Romans - simmered with piglet and chicken livers. Named course; condies bulbos verbatim.

author: Apicius
source_text: Alligas fasciculos rutae et origani, el subinde fasciculos apobaptidiabis. Cum cocta fuerit, proicies fasciculos, et piper asperges et inferes.
question: Quarum herbarum fasciculi in patina de apua apud Apicium alligantur et post cocturam proiciuntur?
question_en: Bundles of what herbs are tied for the anchovy patina in Apicius and thrown away after cooking?
derivation: The Roman bouquet garni: tied bundles of rue and oregano dipped into the anchovy patina and discarded once it is cooked. Named dish plus named technique; fasciculos rutae et origani verbatim.

author: Apicius
source_text: PATINA VERSATILIS VICE DULCI. Nucleos pinos, nuces fractas et purgatas, attorebis eas, teres cum melle, pipere, liquamine, lacte, ovis, modico mero et oleo.
question: Quo loco cenae patina versatilis ex nucleis et nucibus apud Apicium infertur?
question_en: In what place in the meal is the turned-out nut patina served in Apicius?
answer_en: In place of the sweet course.
derivation: The patina versatilis of toasted pine nuts and walnuts in a honey-milk-egg custard is served vice dulci - as the dessert. A fact about the courses of the Roman meal; rubric verbatim.

author: Apicius
source_text: PULTES IULIANAE SIC COQUUNTUR. Alicam purgatam infundis, coques, facies ut ferveat. cum ferbuerit, oleum mittis.
question: Ex quo frumento pultes Iulianae apud Apicium coquuntur?
question_en: From what grain are the pultes Iulianae (Julian porridge) cooked in Apicius?
derivation: The pultes Iulianae - the name-bearing version of puls, the ancestral Roman porridge - are built on cleaned alica. Named dish plus staple grain; alicam purgatam infundis verbatim.

author: Apicius
source_text: PULTES CUM IURE OENOCOCTI. Pultes oenococti iure condies, copadia, similam sive alicam coctam hoc iure condies, et cum copadiis porcinis adponis oenococti iure conditis.
question: Cum quibus copadiis pultes iure oenococti conditae apud Apicium adponuntur?
question_en: With what pieces of meat is the porridge dressed in wine-cooked sauce served in Apicius?
derivation: Pultes with oenococtum sauce come to table with pork copadia dressed in the same sauce. Named preparation; cum copadiis porcinis verbatim.

author: Apicius
source_text: PULTES TRACTOGALATAE. Lactis sextarium et aquae modicum mittes in caccabo novo et lento igni ferveat. tres orbiculos tractae siccas et confringis et partibus in lac summittis.
question: In quo liquore pultes tractogalatae apud Apicium coquuntur?
question_en: In what liquid are the pultes tractogalatae cooked in Apicius?
derivation: The pultes tractogalatae - pastry-and-milk porridge, as the Greek name (tracta + gala) says - simmer broken tracta in a sextarius of milk, finished with honey. Named dish; lactis sextarium verbatim.

author: Apicius
source_text: LENTICULAM DE CASTANEIS. Accipies caccabum novum, et castaneas purgatas diligenter mittis. Adicies aquam et nitrum modice, facies ut coquatur.
question: Quod legumen castaneae apud Apicium imitantur?
question_en: What legume do chestnuts stand in for in Apicius?
derivation: The rubric lenticula de castaneis names a mock dish: chestnuts cooked and dressed as 'lentils'. A celebrated Apician substitution, closed-book from the dish's name and nature; castaneas purgatas verbatim.

author: Apicius
source_text: PISUM INDICUM. Pisum coques. cum despumaverit, porrum et coriandrum concidis et mittis in caccabum ut ferveat. et accipies sepias minutas, sic quomodo sunt cum atramento suo, ut simul coquantur.
question: Quae animalia marina cum atramento suo in pisum Indicum apud Apicium coquuntur?
question_en: What sea creatures are cooked with their own ink into the 'Indian peas' of Apicius?
derivation: Pisum Indicum, the place-named pea dish, gets its dark exotic look from little cuttlefish cooked whole with their ink (cum atramento suo). Named dish; sepias minutas verbatim.

author: Apicius
source_text: PISAM VITELLIANAM SIVE FABAM. Pisam coques lias. teres piper, ligusticum, gingiber, et super condimenta mittis vitella ovorum, quae dura coxeris, mellis uncias III, liquamen, vinum et acetum.
question: Quae pars ovorum durorum in pisam Vitellianam apud Apicium teritur?
question_en: What part of the hard-boiled eggs is ground into the pisa Vitelliana in Apicius?
derivation: Pisa Vitelliana - peas in the style of Vitellius - is dressed with the yolks of hard-boiled eggs, three ounces of honey and spices. An emperor-named dish, exactly the hunted insider fact; vitella ovorum verbatim.

author: Apicius
source_text: PISAM SIVE FABAM VITELLIANAM. pisam sive fabam coques. cum despumaverit, mittis porrum, coriandrum et flores malvarum.
question: Cuius herbae flores in pisam sive fabam Vitellianam apud Apicium mittuntur?
question_en: The flowers of what plant go into the Vitellian peas or beans in Apicius?
derivation: The second Vitellian recipe adds mallow flowers to the pot with leek and coriander - flowers as a checkable, distinctive ingredient of an emperor-named dish. Verbatim (flores malvarum).

author: Apicius
source_text: ALITER. Fabaciae frictae ex liquamine inferuntur.
question: Quo iure fabaciae frictae apud Apicium inferuntur?
question_en: With what sauce are fried green beans served in Apicius?
derivation: Fried fabaciae come to table with liquamen alone - the staple fish sauce as the whole dressing. One-sentence fact, wholly verbatim.

author: Apicius
source_text: Baianas elixas minutatim concidis. ruta, apio viridi, porro, aceto, oleo, liquamine, caroeno vel passo modico inferes.
question: Quibus herbis fabae Baianae elixae apud Apicium inferuntur?
question_en: With what herbs are boiled Baian beans served in Apicius?
answer_en: With rue, green celery, and leek.
derivation: The fabae Baianae - the beans named for Baiae, the luxury resort - are boiled, chopped fine, and dressed with rue, green celery and leek. Place-named foodstuff; the three herbs verbatim.

author: Apicius
source_text: Faenum Graecum ex liquamine, oleo et vino.
question: Quibus rebus faenum Graecum apud Apicium infertur?
question_en: With what is fenugreek served in Apicius?
derivation: Fenugreek's entire chapter is one clause: dressed with liquamen, oil and wine. Named legume of the Roman diet; the brief verbatim list is the complete answer.

author: Apicius
source_text: Faseoli virides et cicer ex sale, cumino, oleo et mero modico inferuntur.
question: Quibus rebus faseoli virides et cicer apud Apicium inferuntur?
answer: Sale, cumino, oleo et mero modico.
question_en: With what are green beans and chickpeas served in Apicius?
answer_en: With salt, cumin, oil, and a little unmixed wine.
derivation: The everyday dressing of the plebeian staples faseoli and cicer: salt, cumin, oil, a little merum. One-sentence fact, wholly verbatim.

author: Apicius
source_text: et elixati, sumpto semine, cum ovis in patella, feniculo viridi, piper et liquamine et caroeno modico pro salso inferuntur, vel simpliciter, ut solet.
question: Pro quo cibo faseoli sive cicer elixati cum ovis et feniculo viridi apud Apicium inferuntur?
question_en: In place of what food are boiled beans or chickpeas with eggs and green fennel served in Apicius?
derivation: A substitution fact of the Roman table: legumes dressed with eggs, fennel, pepper, liquamen and caroenum stand in for salsum, the salt-fish course. Verbatim (pro salso inferuntur).

author: Apicius
provenance: Bibliotheca Augustana (www.hs-augsburg.de/~harsch), text after the Teubner edition (M. E. Milham)
source_text: In struthione elixo: piper, mentam, cuminum assum, apii semen, dactilos vel caryotas, mel, acetum, passum, liquamen et oleum modice. et in caccabo facies ut bulliat. amulo obligas, et sic partes struthionis in lance perfundis, et desuper piper aspargis. si autem in condituram coquere volueris, alicam addis.
question: Quid apud Apicium struthioni additur, si eum in condituram coquere velis?
question_en: What is added in Apicius for the ostrich, if you wish to cook it in its sauce?
derivation: Book VI (Aeropetes) opens with boiled ostrich (in struthione elixo), the most spectacular bird of the Roman table; the recipe's one marked variant is that alica goes in when the bird is cooked in the sauce itself. Anchored to Apicius + the ostrich; one-word answer verbatim (alicam addis).

author: Apicius
provenance: Bibliotheca Augustana (www.hs-augsburg.de/~harsch), text after the Teubner edition (M. E. Milham)
source_text: gruem cum coquis, caput eius aqua quam non contingat, sed sit foris ab aqua.
question: Quae pars gruis, dum apud Apicium coquitur, aquam contingere non debet?
question_en: Which part of the crane, while it cooks in Apicius, must not touch the water?
derivation: The famous crane-cooking trick: the bird is boiled with its head held out of the water. Anchored to the crane in Apicius; single named part, verbatim (caput eius aqua quam non contingat).

author: Apicius
provenance: Bibliotheca Augustana (www.hs-augsburg.de/~harsch), text after the Teubner edition (M. E. Milham)
source_text: cum cocta fuerit, de sabano calido involves gruem et caput eius trahe. cum nervis sequetur, ut pulpae vel ossa remaneant, cum nervis enim manducare non potest.
question: Quid e grue cocta, cum caput eius tractum est, una sequitur?
question_en: What comes out of the cooked crane along with the head when the head is pulled?
derivation: The second half of the crane trick: wrap the cooked bird in a warm cloth and pull the head, and the inedible sinews follow it out, leaving meat and bones — 'for with the sinews it cannot be eaten.' Verbatim (cum nervis sequetur).

author: Apicius
provenance: Bibliotheca Augustana (www.hs-augsburg.de/~harsch), text after the Teubner edition (M. E. Milham)
source_text: avem sapidiorem et altiliorem facies et ei pinguedinem servabis, si eam farina oleo subacta contextam in furnum miseris.
question: Qua re contecta avis in furnum mittitur, ut apud Apicium sapidior et altilior fiat?
question_en: Covered in what is a bird sent into the oven so that, in Apicius, it comes out tastier and plumper?
answer_en: In flour dough worked with oil.
derivation: Baking a bird in a dough crust to keep its fat and flavor — an ancestor of cooking en croute, offered as the way to make any bird sapidior et altilior. Answer verbatim (farina oleo subacta contextam).

author: Apicius
provenance: Bibliotheca Augustana (www.hs-augsburg.de/~harsch), text after the Teubner edition (M. E. Milham)
source_text: Aliter avem: in ventrem eius fractas olivas novas mittis et consutam sic elixabis. deinde coctas olivas eximes.
question: Quid in ventrem avis missum et post cocturam exemptum avem apud Apicium condit?
question_en: What is put into a bird's belly and taken out again after cooking, to season the bird in Apicius?
derivation: A whole recipe in two sentences: the bird is sewn up around cracked fresh olives, boiled, and the olives are removed — flavoring by insertion. Verbatim (fractas olivas novas... coctas olivas eximes).

author: Apicius
provenance: Bibliotheca Augustana (www.hs-augsburg.de/~harsch), text after the Teubner edition (M. E. Milham)
source_text: Phoenicopterum eliberas, lavas, ornas, includis in caccabum, adicies aquam, salem, anethum et aceti modicum. dimidia coctura alligas fasciculum porri et coriandri, ut coquatur. prope cocturam defritum mittis, coloras. adicies in mortarium piper, cuminum, coriandrum, laseris radicem, mentam, rutam, fricabis, suffundis acetum, adicies caryotam, ius de suo sibi perfundis. reexinanies in eundem caccabum, amulo obligas, ius perfundis et inferes. idem facies et in psittaco.
question: Cui alii avi idem ius quod phoenicoptero Apicius parari iubet?
question_en: For what other bird does Apicius direct the same sauce to be made as for the flamingo?
derivation: The most celebrated line of book VI: the flamingo recipe closes 'idem facies et in psittaco' — the same preparation serves for parrot. Two exotic table birds in one sentence; single-word answer verbatim.

author: Apicius
provenance: Bibliotheca Augustana (www.hs-augsburg.de/~harsch), text after the Teubner edition (M. E. Milham)
source_text: Aves omnes ne liquescant: cum plumis elixare omnibus melius erit.
question: Quomodo aves apud Apicium elixantur, ne liquescant?
question_en: How are birds boiled in Apicius so that they do not fall apart?
derivation: General rule of the bird book: boiling any bird in its plumage keeps it from disintegrating. Counterintuitive, memorable kitchen doctrine; verbatim (cum plumis elixare omnibus melius erit).

author: Apicius
provenance: Bibliotheca Augustana (www.hs-augsburg.de/~harsch), text after the Teubner edition (M. E. Milham)
source_text: Anserem elixum calidum ex iure frigido Apiciano: teres piper, ligusticum, coriandri semen, mentam, rutam, refundis liquamen et oleum modice, temperas. anserem elixum ferventem sabano mundo exsiccabis, ius perfundis et inferes.
question: Quo iure anser elixus calidus apud Apicium infertur?
question_en: With what sauce is hot boiled goose served in Apicius?
derivation: The goose chapter is a single dish: hot boiled goose under a cold sauce bearing Apicius' own name (ius frigidum Apicianum). Dish named for the author himself; verbatim in the rubric.

author: Apicius
provenance: Bibliotheca Augustana (www.hs-augsburg.de/~harsch), text after the Teubner edition (M. E. Milham)
source_text: Pullum Parthicum: pullum aperies a navi et in quadrato ornas. teres piper, ligusticum, carei modicum. suffunde liquamen. vino temperas. componis in cumana pullum et condituram super pullum facies. laser et vivum in tepida dissolvis, et in pullum mittis simul, et coques.
question: Quod condimentum, in aqua tepida dissolutum, in pullum Parthicum apud Apicium mittitur?
question_en: What seasoning, dissolved in warm water, is poured onto the Parthian chicken in Apicius?
derivation: Pullus Parthicus, the chicken named for Parthia, is defined by its dose of laser vivum dissolved in warm water. Place-named dish plus the celebrated Eastern resin; verbatim (laser et vivum in tepida dissolvis).

author: Apicius
provenance: Bibliotheca Augustana (www.hs-augsburg.de/~harsch), text after the Teubner edition (M. E. Milham)
source_text: Pullum Numidicum: pullum curas, elixas, levas, laser ac piper aspergis et assas.
question: Quibus pullus Numidicus apud Apicium aspergitur, priusquam assatur?
question_en: With what is the Numidian chicken sprinkled in Apicius before it is roasted?
derivation: Pullus Numidicus, chicken named for Numidia: parboiled, then dusted with laser and pepper and roasted. Place-named dish; answer verbatim (laser ac piper aspergis).

author: Apicius
provenance: Bibliotheca Augustana (www.hs-augsburg.de/~harsch), text after the Teubner edition (M. E. Milham)
source_text: Pullus Vardanus: pullum coques iure hoc: liquamine, oleo, vino, cui mittis fasciculum porri, coriandri, satureiae. cum coctus fuerit, teres piper, nucleos cyathos duos et ius de suo sibi suffundis et fasciculos proicies. lac temperas, et reexinanies in mortarium supra pullum, ut ferveat. obligas eundem albamentis ovorum tritis, ponis in lance et iure supra scripto perfundis. hoc ius candidum appellatur.
question: Quo nomine ius pulli Vardani, lacte et albamentis ovorum confectum, apud Apicium appellatur?
question_en: By what name is the sauce of the pullus Vardanus, made with milk and egg whites, called in Apicius?
derivation: Pullus Vardanus ends with a naming sentence: its milk-and-egg-white sauce 'is called ius candidum.' A named dish plus a named sauce; verbatim (hoc ius candidum appellatur).

author: Apicius
provenance: Bibliotheca Augustana (www.hs-augsburg.de/~harsch), text after the Teubner edition (M. E. Milham)
source_text: Pullum Frontonianum: pullum praedura, condies liquamine, oleo mixto, cui mittis fasciculum anethi, porri, satureiae et coriandri viridis, et coques. ubi coctus fuerit, levabis eum, in lance defrito perungues, piper aspargis et inferes.
question: Quo pullus Frontonianus, ubi coctus in lance positus est, perungitur apud Apicium?
question_en: With what is pullus Frontonianus (Fronto's chicken), once cooked and placed on its platter, glazed in Apicius?
derivation: Pullus Frontonianus, the chicken bearing the name of Fronto, is finished by anointing with defrutum on the serving dish. Person-named dish; verbatim (in lance defrito perungues).

author: Apicius
provenance: Bibliotheca Augustana (www.hs-augsburg.de/~harsch), text after the Teubner edition (M. E. Milham)
source_text: Pullus tractogalatus: pullum coques liquamine, oleo, vino, cui mittis fasciculum coriandri, cepam. deinde, cum coctus fuerit, levabis eum de iure suo et mittis in caccabum novum lac et salem modicum, mel et aquae minimum id est tertiam partem. ponis ad ignem lentum ut tepescat, tractum confringis et mittis paulatim, assidue agitas, ne uratur.
question: Quid in lac confractum paulatim mittitur, cum pullus tractogalatus apud Apicium paratur?
question_en: What is crumbled and added little by little to the milk when the pullus tractogalatus is prepared in Apicius?
derivation: Pullus tractogalatus — 'pastry-and-milk chicken' — is finished in sweetened milk thickened with crumbled tracta. Named dish; verbatim (tractum confringis et mittis paulatim).

author: Apicius
provenance: Bibliotheca Augustana (www.hs-augsburg.de/~harsch), text after the Teubner edition (M. E. Milham)
source_text: pullus leucozomus accipiat aquam et oleum Spanum abundans.
question: Quod oleum pullus leucozomus apud Apicium abundans accipit?
question_en: What oil does the pullus leucozomus ('white-broth chicken') receive in abundance in Apicius?
derivation: Pullus leucozomus cooks in nothing but water and abundant Spanish oil, agitated so the bird makes its own thickening. Named dish plus a named provincial product (oleum Spanum); verbatim.

author: Apicius
provenance: Bibliotheca Augustana (www.hs-augsburg.de/~harsch), text after the Teubner edition (M. E. Milham)
source_text: Pullum anethatum: mellis modice, liquamine temperabis. levas pullum coctum et sabano mundo siccas, caraxas et ius scissuris infundis, ut combibat, et cum combiberit, assabis et suo sibi iure pinnis tangis.
question: Quibus pullus anethatus, dum assatur, suo iure apud Apicium tangitur?
question_en: With what is the dill chicken (pullus anethatus) basted with its own juice while it roasts, in Apicius?
derivation: The Roman basting brush: the scored, honey-glazed dill chicken is touched with its own juice using feathers as it roasts. Vivid, characteristic kitchen practice; verbatim (suo sibi iure pinnis tangis).

author: Apicius
provenance: Bibliotheca Augustana (www.hs-augsburg.de/~harsch), text after the Teubner edition (M. E. Milham)
source_text: Vulvam ut tostam facias, in cantabro involve et postea in muriam mitte et sic coque.
question: Quo involvitur vulva apud Apicium, ut tosta fiat?
question_en: In what is the sow's womb wrapped in Apicius, to make it come out 'toasted'?
derivation: The trick for vulva tosta: wrap the womb in bran (cantabrum), then cook it in brine. Single-word answer verbatim (in cantabro involve), tied to the famous delicacy.

author: Apicius
provenance: Bibliotheca Augustana (www.hs-augsburg.de/~harsch), text after the Teubner edition (M. E. Milham)
source_text: Sumen plenum: teritur piper, careum, echinus salsus, consuitur et sic coquitur. manducatur cum allece, sinapi.
question: Quod animal marinum salsum in sumen plenum apud Apicium teritur?
question_en: What salted sea creature is ground into the stuffed sow's udder (sumen plenum) in Apicius?
derivation: Sumen, the sow's udder, was a proverbial Roman luxury; the stuffed version (sumen plenum) is filled with pepper, caraway and salted sea urchin and sewn up. Surprising surf-and-turf pairing; verbatim (echinus salsus).

author: Apicius
provenance: Bibliotheca Augustana (www.hs-augsburg.de/~harsch), text after the Teubner edition (M. E. Milham)
source_text: In ficato oenogarum: piper, thymum, ligusticum, liquamen, vinum modice, oleum.
question: Quod ius in ficato apud Apicium paratur?
question_en: What sauce is prepared for ficatum (fig-fattened liver) in Apicius?
derivation: Ficatum — liver of an animal fattened on figs — is the luxury whose name became the Romance word for liver itself (fegato, foie, higado); Apicius dresses it with oenogarum. Named delicacy plus named sauce, verbatim in the rubric.

author: Apicius
provenance: Bibliotheca Augustana (www.hs-augsburg.de/~harsch), text after the Teubner edition (M. E. Milham)
source_text: Assaturam: assam a furno simplicem salis plurimo conspersam cum melle inferes.
question: Cum quo assatura simplex, sale plurimo conspersa, apud Apicium infertur?
question_en: With what is the plain roast, sprinkled with plenty of salt, served in Apicius?
derivation: The simplest roast of the luxury book: straight from the oven, heavily salted, served with honey. The Roman sweet-salt taste in one sentence; verbatim (cum melle inferes).

author: Apicius
provenance: Bibliotheca Augustana (www.hs-augsburg.de/~harsch), text after the Teubner edition (M. E. Milham)
source_text: Pernam, ubi eam cum caricis plurimis elixaveris et tribus lauri foliis, detracta cute tessellatim incidis et melle complebis.
question: Cum quibus fructibus siccis perna apud Apicium elixatur?
question_en: With what dried fruit is the ham boiled in Apicius?
derivation: The celebrated Apician ham: boiled with plenty of dried figs and three bay leaves, then skinned, scored in squares and filled with honey. Anchored to perna; answer verbatim (cum caricis plurimis).

author: Apicius
provenance: Bibliotheca Augustana (www.hs-augsburg.de/~harsch), text after the Teubner edition (M. E. Milham)
source_text: Pernam, ubi eam cum caricis plurimis elixaveris et tribus lauri foliis, detracta cute tessellatim incidis et melle complebis. deinde farinam oleo subactam contexes et ei corium reddis ut, cum farina cocta fuerit, eximas furno est et inferes.
question: Qua re perna melle completa apud Apicium contegitur, priusquam in furnum mittitur?
question_en: With what is the honey-filled ham covered in Apicius before it goes into the oven?
answer_en: With flour dough worked with oil.
derivation: The second act of the fig-boiled ham: a dough of flour and oil is laid over it to 'give it back its skin,' and it bakes until the crust is done — ham baked in pastry. Answer verbatim (farinam oleo subactam contexes).

author: Apicius
provenance: Bibliotheca Augustana (www.hs-augsburg.de/~harsch), text after the Teubner edition (M. E. Milham)
source_text: Laridi coctura: tectum aqua cum multo anetho coques, oleum modicum distillabis et modicum salis.
question: Cum quo condimento multo laridum apud Apicium coquitur?
question_en: With plenty of what herb is bacon (laridum) boiled in Apicius?
derivation: The standard treatment of laridum, the cured pork fat of the Roman larder: boiled covered in water with much dill, a little oil and salt. Staple food, one-herb answer verbatim (cum multo anetho).

author: Apicius
provenance: Bibliotheca Augustana (www.hs-augsburg.de/~harsch), text after the Teubner edition (M. E. Milham)
source_text: Aliter dulcia: siligineos rasos frangis, et buccellas maiores facies. in lacte infundis, frigis et in oleo, mel superfundis et inferes.
question: Quo buccellae siligineae, in lacte infusae et in oleo frictae, apud Apicium perfunduntur?
question_en: With what are pieces of fine wheat bread, soaked in milk and fried in oil, doused in Apicius?
derivation: The famous Apician fried-bread dessert — wheat bread soaked in milk, fried in oil, drowned in honey — the ancestor of French toast. Verbatim (in lacte infundis, frigis et in oleo, mel superfundis).

author: Apicius
provenance: Bibliotheca Augustana (www.hs-augsburg.de/~harsch), text after the Teubner edition (M. E. Milham)
source_text: Boletos fungos: caroenum, fasciculum coriandri viridis. ubi ferbuerint, exempto fasciculo inferes.
question: In quo liquore boleti apud Apicium cum fasciculo coriandri viridis coquuntur?
question_en: In what liquid are boletus mushrooms cooked with a bundle of green coriander in Apicius?
derivation: Boleti, the most prized mushrooms of the Roman table (the mushroom of the Claudius story), are simmered in caroenum with a coriander bundle that is discarded at serving. Named luxury food; verbatim.

author: Apicius
provenance: Bibliotheca Augustana (www.hs-augsburg.de/~harsch), text after the Teubner edition (M. E. Milham)
source_text: Tubera radis, elixas, sale aspergis, et surculo infiges. subassas, et mittes in caccabum oleum, liquamen, caroenum, vinum, piper et mel.
question: Quo tubera apud Apicium infiguntur, priusquam subassantur?
question_en: On what are truffles stuck in Apicius before they are lightly roasted?
derivation: The truffle chapter's master method: scraped, boiled, salted truffles are spitted on a twig and part-roasted before saucing. Truffles were a celebrated Roman luxury; verbatim (surculo infiges).

author: Apicius
