provenance: Bibliotheca Augustana (www.hs-augsburg.de/~harsch), text after the Teubner edition (M. E. Milham)
source_text: Cochleas lacte pastas: accipies cochleas, spongizabis, membranam tolles, ut possint prodire. adicies in vas lac et salem uno die, ceteris diebus in lac per se, et omni hora mundabis stercus. cum pastae fuerint, ut non possint se retrahere . . . et ex oleo friges.
question: Quo cibo cochleae apud Apicium pascuntur, donec se retrahere non possint?
question_en: On what food are snails fattened in Apicius until they can no longer draw themselves back into their shells?
derivation: The famous milk-fed snails (cochleae lacte pastae): kept in milk until too fat to withdraw into the shell, then fried in oil. One of the best-known excesses of Roman gastronomy; verbatim in the rubric and recipe.

author: Apicius
provenance: Bibliotheca Augustana (www.hs-augsburg.de/~harsch), text after the Teubner edition (M. E. Milham)
source_text: Ova frixa: oenogarata.
question: Quo iure ova frixa apud Apicium apponuntur?
question_en: With what sauce are fried eggs served in Apicius?
derivation: The shortest recipe in Apicius: fried eggs are 'oenogarata' — dressed with oenogarum. Fried eggs under fish sauce is a hallmark of Roman taste; the whole recipe is the answer.

author: Apicius
provenance: Bibliotheca Augustana (www.hs-augsburg.de/~harsch), text after the Teubner edition (M. E. Milham)
source_text: In ovis hapalis: piper, ligusticum, nucleos infusos. suffundes mel, acetum, liquamine temperabis.
question: Quod dulce in ius ovorum hapalorum apud Apicium suffunditur?
question_en: What sweetener is poured into the sauce for soft-boiled eggs in Apicius?
derivation: The celebrated sauce for ova hapala (soft-boiled eggs): pepper, lovage and soaked pine nuts, with honey and vinegar tempered with liquamen — sweet-sour-salt on eggs. Verbatim (suffundes mel).

author: Apicius
provenance: Bibliotheca Augustana (www.hs-augsburg.de/~harsch), text after the Teubner edition (M. E. Milham)
source_text: Porcellum Flaccianum: porcellum ornas in modum apri, sale asperges et in furnum mittes. dum coquitur, adicies in mortarium piper, ligusticum, careum, apii semen, laseris radicem, rutam viridem, fricabis, suffundes liquamen, vino et passo temperabis. in caccabo cum olei modico ferveat. amulo obligas. porcellum coctum ab ossibus tanges, apii semen teres ita ut fiat pulvis, asperges et inferes.
question: Cuius seminis pulvis porcello Flacciano cocto apud Apicium aspergitur?
question_en: The powder of what seed is sprinkled over the cooked Flaccian suckling pig in Apicius?
derivation: Porcellus Flaccianus, named for a Flaccus: boar-style roast pig finished with celery seed ground to powder. Person-named dish with a single-seed answer; verbatim (apii semen teres ita ut fiat pulvis).

author: Apicius
provenance: Bibliotheca Augustana (www.hs-augsburg.de/~harsch), text after the Teubner edition (M. E. Milham)
source_text: Porcellum hortulanum: porcellus hortulanus exossatur per gulam in modum utris. mittitur in eo pullus isiciatus particulatim concisus, turdi, ficetulae, isicia de pulpa sua, lucanicae, dactili exossati, fabriles bulbi, cochleae exemptae, malvae, betae, porri, apium, cauliculi elixi, coriandrum, piper integrum, nuclei, ova XV superinfunduntur, liquamen piperatum ova mittantur tria.
question: Quae aves parvae in porcellum hortulanum apud Apicium mittuntur?
question_en: What small birds go into the 'gardener's' suckling pig in Apicius?
derivation: Inside the porcellus hortulanus go whole thrushes and fig-peckers — the two prized small birds of the Roman table — along with chopped chicken forcemeat and Lucanian sausages. Two-name answer verbatim (turdi, ficetulae).

author: Apicius
provenance: Bibliotheca Augustana (www.hs-augsburg.de/~harsch), text after the Teubner edition (M. E. Milham)
source_text: Leporem Passenianum: leporem curas, exossas, extensum ornas, suspendes ad fumum. cum coloraverit, facies ut dimidia coctura coquatur.
question: Quo lepus Passenianus exossatus apud Apicium suspenditur, ut coloretur?
question_en: Where is the boned Passenian hare hung in Apicius, so that it takes color?
derivation: Lepus Passenianus, the hare named for a Passenus/Passienus: boned, stretched, and hung in the smoke until colored, then half-cooked and roasted. Person-named dish; verbatim (suspendes ad fumum).

author: Apicius
provenance: Bibliotheca Augustana (www.hs-augsburg.de/~harsch), text after the Teubner edition (M. E. Milham)
source_text: Leporis conditura: teritur piper, ruta, cepula et iecur leporis, liquamen, caroenum, passum, olei modicum. amulum, cum bullit.
question: Quod viscus leporis in leporis condituram apud Apicium teritur?
question_en: What organ of the hare is ground into the hare's own sauce in Apicius?
derivation: The leporis conditura thickens and flavors the hare with its own pounded liver — the liver-bound game sauce that outlived antiquity (cf. civet). One-word answer verbatim (iecur leporis).

author: Apicius
provenance: Bibliotheca Augustana (www.hs-augsburg.de/~harsch), text after the Teubner edition (M. E. Milham)
source_text: Aliter locusta: isicia de cauda eius sic facies: folium nocivum prius demes et elixas, deinde pulpam concides, cum liquamine, pipere et ovis isicia formabis.
question: Ex qua parte locustae isicia apud Apicium formantur?
question_en: From what part of the lobster are rissoles formed in Apicius?
derivation: Lobster rissoles (isicia) are made from the tail meat, after the harmful gut-strip is removed, bound with liquamen, pepper and eggs. Named preparation from a named part; verbatim (isicia de cauda eius).

author: Apicius
provenance: Bibliotheca Augustana (www.hs-augsburg.de/~harsch), text after the Teubner edition (M. E. Milham)
source_text: In torpedine elixa: piper, ligusticum, petroselinum, mentam, origanum, ovi medium, mel, liquamen, passum, vinum, oleum. si voles, addes sinape, acetum. si calidum volueris, uvam passam addes.
question: Quid iuri in torpedinem elixam apud Apicium additur, si calidum volueris?
question_en: What is added to the sauce for boiled torpedo ray in Apicius, if you want it served hot?
derivation: The torpedo (electric ray) was a delicacy of the Roman fish market; its boiled dressing takes raisins when the dish is to be served hot. The one marked variant of the recipe; verbatim (si calidum volueris, uvam passam addes).

author: Apicius
provenance: Bibliotheca Augustana (www.hs-augsburg.de/~harsch), text after the Teubner edition (M. E. Milham)
source_text: Salsum sine salso: iecur coques, teres, et mittes piper aut liquamen aut salem. addes oleum. iecur leporis aut haedi aut agni aut pulli, et, si volueris, in formella piscem formabis. oleum viridem supra adicies.
question: In cuius animalis figuram iecur tritum in salso sine salso apud Apicium formatur?
question_en: Into the shape of what animal is the ground liver molded in the 'salt fish without salt fish' of Apicius?
answer_en: Into the shape of a fish.
derivation: Salsum sine salso, the famous Apician counterfeit: seasoned liver of hare, kid, lamb or chicken is pressed in a little mold into the shape of a fish and glossed with green oil. Named trompe-l'oeil dish; verbatim (in formella piscem formabis).

author: Apicius
provenance: Bibliotheca Augustana (www.hs-augsburg.de/~harsch), text after the Teubner edition (M. E. Milham)
source_text: Aliter salsum sine salso: cuminum tantum quantum quinque digitis tollis, piperis ad dimidium eius et unam spicam alei purgatam teres, liquamen superfundes, oleum modice superstillabis. hoc aegrum stomachum valde reficit et digestionem facit.
question: Quid salsum sine salso ex cumino, pipere et aleo apud Apicium valde reficit?
question_en: What does the 'salt fish without salt fish' of cumin, pepper, and garlic greatly restore, according to Apicius?
derivation: The dietetic claim attached to the cumin-pepper-garlic salsum sine salso: it strongly restores a sick stomach and aids digestion — food as medicine, a fixture of Roman table culture. Verbatim (hoc aegrum stomachum valde reficit et digestionem facit).

author: Augustine
source_text: Marcus Regulus, imperator populi Romani, captiuus apud Carthaginienses fuit.
question: Apud quos captiuus fuit Marcus Regulus, imperator populi Romani?
question_en: Among whom was Marcus Regulus, a general of the Roman people, a captive?
derivation: Anchored to Marcus Regulus (named, 'imperator populi Romani'); single answer (the Carthaginians), supported verbatim. Closed-book: Regulus's captivity among the Carthaginians is a famous Roman exemplum.

author: Augustine
source_text: Cato enim numquam Caesarem uicerat, cui uictus dedignatus est subici et, ne subiceretur, a se ipso elegit occidi.
question: Cui uictori se subicere dedignatus Cato mortem sibi consciuit, ut Augustinus scribit?
question_en: To which victor did Cato disdain to submit, choosing instead to take his own life, as Augustine writes?
derivation: Anchored to Cato; single-name answer (dative Caesari), supported verbatim ('cui uictus dedignatus est subici et... a se ipso elegit occidi'). A distinct fact from the place of his death. Closed-book: Cato's refusal to live under Caesar's victory is famous.

author: Augustine
source_text: Egregius Romani nominis Marcus Marcellus, qui Syracusas urbem ornatissimam cepit, refertur eam prius fleuisse ruituram et ante eius sanguinem suas illi lacrimas effudisse.
question: Quam urbem Marcus Marcellus cepit, ut Augustinus refert?
question_en: Which city did Marcus Marcellus capture, as Augustine relates?
derivation: Anchored to Marcus Marcellus; single place-name answer (Syracusas), supported verbatim ('qui Syracusas urbem ornatissimam cepit'). Closed-book: Marcellus's capture of Syracuse (212 BC) is a well-known historical fact. 'ut Augustinus refert' mirrors the text's 'refertur.'

author: Augustine
source_text: Fabius, Tarentinae urbis euersor, a simulacrorum depraedatione se abstinuisse laudatur. Nam cum ei scriba suggessisset quid de signis deorum, quae multa capta fuerant, fieri iuberet, continentiam suam etiam iocando condiuit.
question: Cuius urbis euersor fuit ille Fabius qui se a deorum simulacrorum depraedatione abstinuisse laudatur?
question_en: Of what city was that Fabius the destroyer, who is praised for keeping himself from plundering the statues of the gods?
derivation: Anchored to Fabius via the detail that he abstained from plundering the gods' statues; single place answer (Tarentum), supported verbatim ('Tarentinae urbis euersor'). Closed-book: Fabius Maximus's recapture of Tarentum (209 BC) is historical.

author: Augustine
source_text: et ecce audio vocem de vicina domo cum cantu dicentis et crebro repetentis, quasi pueri an puellae, nescio: 'tolle lege, tolle lege.'
question: Quae verba Augustinus, in horto sedens, a voce quasi pueri vel puellae de vicina domo crebro repeti audivit?
question_en: What words did Augustine, sitting in the garden, hear repeated again and again by a voice as of a boy or girl from a neighboring house?
derivation: The famous chant that prompted Augustine to open the apostle's codex. Anchored to Augustine + the garden scene; the quoted words are supported verbatim by "'tolle lege, tolle lege.'" Closed-book (one of the most famous moments in the Confessions) and translatable ('take up and read').

author: Auctor incertus (Corpus Caesarianum)
source_text: Caesar Aegypto atque Alexandrea potitus reges constituit quos Ptolomaeus testamento scripserat atque obtestatus erat populum Romanum ne mutarentur. Nam maiore ex duobus pueris, rege, amisso minori tradidit regnum maiorique ex duabus filiis, Cleopatrae, quae manserat in fide praesidiisque eius; minorem, Arsinoen, cuius nomine diu regnasse impotenter Ganymeden docuimus, deducere ex regno statuit, ne qua rursus nova dissensio, prius quam diuturnitate confirmarentur regibus imperia, per homines seditiosos nasceretur.
question: Cui Caesar, Aegypto potitus, regnum Aegypti tradidit, quae in fide praesidiisque eius permanserat?
question_en: To whom did Caesar, having taken control of Egypt, hand over the kingdom of Egypt, she who had remained loyal under his protection?
derivation: Name fact anchored to Caesar and Egypt: after winning the war he settled the throne on Cleopatra (with the younger surviving brother), supported verbatim by 'maiorique ex duabus filiis, Cleopatrae, quae manserat in fide praesidiisque eius'. Caesar's establishment of Cleopatra on the Egyptian throne is closed-book.

author: Caesar
source_text: Mittit in Sardiniam cum legione una Valerium legatum, in Siciliam Curionem pro praetore cum legionibus duabus; eundem, cum Siciliam recepisset, protinus in Africam traducere exercitum iubet. Sardiniam obtinebat M. Cotta, Siciliam M. Cato; Africam sorte Tubero obtinere debebat.
question: Quis ex Pompeianis Siciliam obtinebat, quam Caesar Curionem occupare iussit?
question_en: Who held Sicily for the Pompeians, the province Caesar ordered Curio to seize?
derivation: Name fact anchored to Sicily and Curio; single named answer supported verbatim by 'Siciliam M. Cato [obtinebat]', with Curio sent there with two legions. Cato Uticensis abandoning Sicily before Curio is closed-book.

author: Caesar
source_text: Eodemque tempore his rebus subsidio DC Numidae ex oppido peditesque CCCC mittuntur a Varo, quos auxilii causa rex Iuba paucis diebus ante Uticam miserat.
question: Quis rex Numidarum P. Attio Varo apud Uticam auxilia adversus Curionem misit?
question_en: Which king of the Numidians sent auxiliaries to Publius Attius Varus at Utica against Curio?
derivation: Name fact anchored to Varus + Utica + Curio; supported verbatim by 'rex Iuba ... Uticam miserat', the Numidian troops then deployed by Varus ('mittuntur a Varo'). Juba's intervention on the Pompeian side in Africa is closed-book.

author: Caesar
source_text: At Curio numquam se amisso exercitu, quem a Caesare fidei commissum acceperit, in eius conspectum reversurum confirmat atque ita proelians interficitur.
question: Quis Caesaris dux in Africa, amisso exercitu, ad Caesarem reverti recusans proelians interfectus est?
question_en: Which of Caesar's commanders in Africa, having lost his army, refused to return to Caesar and was killed fighting?
derivation: Name/outcome fact anchored to Caesar + Africa; supported verbatim by 'Curio ... in eius conspectum reversurum confirmat atque ita proelians interficitur'. His army was destroyed to the last man ('Milites ad unum omnes interficiuntur', same chapter). Curio's death with his army at the Bagradas is among the most famous episodes of the African campaign; closed-book.

author: Caesar
source_text: Ibi casu rex erat Ptolomaeus, puer aetate, magnis copiis cum sorore Cleopatra bellum gerens, quam paucis ante mensibus per suos propinquos atque amicos regno expulerat.
question: Cum qua sorore, quam regno expulerat, Ptolomaeus rex Aegypti eo tempore bellum gerebat?
question_en: With which sister, whom he had driven from the kingdom, was Ptolemy, king of Egypt, then at war?
derivation: Name fact anchored to Ptolemy, king of Egypt; supported verbatim by 'cum sorore Cleopatra bellum gerens, quam ... regno expulerat'. The war between Ptolemy and his sister Cleopatra is closed-book.

author: Auctor incertus (Corpus Caesarianum)
source_text: Caesar trinis castris potitus occisisque hostium X milibus fugatisque compluribus se recepit L militibus amissis, paucis sauciis in castra, ac statim ex itinere ante oppidum Thapsum constitit elephantosque LXIIII ornatos armatosque cum turribus ornamentisque capit.
question: Ad quod oppidum maritimum Caesar Scipionis Iubaeque copias acie devicit?
question_en: At which coastal town did Caesar defeat in battle the forces of Scipio and Juba?
derivation: Place fact anchored to Caesar against Scipio and Juba. The rout (three camps taken, 10,000 slain) and Caesar's halt 'ante oppidum Thapsum' are supported verbatim; the battle of Thapsus (46 BC) that destroyed the Republican army is among the best-known facts of the civil wars.

author: Auctor incertus (Corpus Caesarianum)
source_text: C. Interim Vergilius postquam terra marique clausus se nihil proficere intellexit suosque interfectos aut fugatos, M. Catonem Uticae sibi ipsum manus attulisse, regem vagum ab suisque desertum ab omnibus aspernari, Saburram eiusque copias ab Sittio esse deletas, Uticae Caesarem sine mora receptum, de tanto exercitu reliquias esse nullas, ipse sibi suisque liberis a C. Caninio proconsule qui eum obsidebat, fide accepta seque et sua omnia et oppidum proconsuli tradit.
question: In quo oppido Africae M. Cato sibi ipse mortem conscivit?
question_en: In which town of Africa did Marcus Cato take his own life?
derivation: Place and name fact anchored to M. Cato; supported verbatim by 'M. Catonem Uticae sibi ipsum manus attulisse'. Cato's suicide at Utica after the Thapsus disaster, the source of his cognomen Uticensis, is closed-book.

author: Caesar
source_text: Apud Helvetios longe nobilissimus fuit et ditissimus Orgetorix.
question: Quis apud Helvetios longe nobilissimus ac ditissimus fuit?
question_en: Who was by far the noblest and richest man among the Helvetii?
derivation: Name fact anchored to the Helvetii; single named answer supported verbatim. Orgetorix is the well-known instigator of the Helvetian migration; closed-book.

author: Caesar
source_text: Remi, qui proximi Galliae ex Belgis sunt, ad eum legatos Iccium et Andebrogium, primos civitatis, miserunt, qui dicerent se suaque omnia in fidem atque potestatem populi Romani permittere, neque se cum reliquis Belgis consensisse neque contra populum Romanum coniurasse.
question: Qui populus Belgarum primus legatos ad Caesarem misit seque in fidem populi Romani permisit?
question_en: Which people of the Belgae was the first to send legates to Caesar and to commit itself to the protection of the Roman people?
derivation: Anchored to the Belgae and Caesar; the Remi alone broke from the coalition and submitted first ('Remi ... ad eum legatos ... miserunt, qui dicerent se ... in fidem atque potestatem populi Romani permittere'). The Remi's early alliance is a staple of BG II; closed-book.

author: Caesar
source_text: Ob easque res ex litteris Caesaris dierum XV supplicatio decreta est, quod ante id tempus accidit nulli.
question: Quot dierum supplicatio ob res a Caesare in Belgis gestas Romae decreta est?
question_en: A thanksgiving of how many days was decreed at Rome for the deeds Caesar accomplished among the Belgae?
derivation: Historical fact anchored to Caesar; a 15-day supplicatio was decreed for these achievements, an unprecedented honour ('dierum XV supplicatio decreta est, quod ante id tempus accidit nulli'). Single number answer supported verbatim; the first 15-day thanksgiving ever voted, closed-book.

author: Caesar
source_text: Exigua parte aestatis reliqua Caesar, etsi in his locis, quod omnis Gallia ad septentriones vergit, maturae sunt hiemes, tamen in Britanniam proficisci contendit, quod omnibus fere Gallicis bellis hostibus nostris inde subministrata auxilia intellegebat.
question: In quam insulam Caesar exigua parte aestatis reliqua proficisci contendit?
question_en: To which island did Caesar hasten to set out when only a small part of the summer remained?
derivation: Place fact marking Caesar's first expedition to Britain, anchored to Caesar and the time of year; answer supported verbatim by 'tamen in Britanniam proficisci contendit'. The first Roman crossing to Britain is a closed-book landmark.

author: Caesar
source_text: summa imperi bellique administrandi communi consilio permissa Cassivellauno, cuius fines a maritimis civitatibus flumen dividit, quod appellatur Tamesis, a mari circiter milia passuum LXXX.
question: Quod flumen, ut Caesar scribit, fines Cassivellauni a maritimis civitatibus dividit?
question_en: Which river, as Caesar writes, divides the territory of Cassivellaunus from the maritime states?
derivation: Geography fact anchored to Cassivellaunus and Caesar; single river answer supported verbatim by 'cuius fines a maritimis civitatibus flumen dividit, quod appellatur Tamesis'. The Thames is closed-book.

author: Caesar
source_text: Alterum vergit ad Hispaniam atque occidentem solem; qua ex parte est Hibernia, dimidio minor, ut aestimatur, quam Britannia, sed pari spatio transmissus atque ex Gallia est in Britanniam. In hoc medio cursu est insula, quae appellatur Mona.
question: Quae insula, ut Caesar tradit, medio in cursu inter Britanniam et Hiberniam sita est?
question_en: Which island, as Caesar reports, lies midway in the passage between Britain and Ireland?
derivation: Geography fact anchored to Britannia and Hibernia; single named answer supported verbatim by 'In hoc medio cursu est insula, quae appellatur Mona'. Caesar's island Mona is closed-book.

author: Auctor incertus (Corpus Caesarianum)
source_text: Erat idem temporis Sex. Pompeius frater qui cum praesidio Cordubam tenebat, quod eius provinciae caput esse existimabatur
question: Quod oppidum, a Sex. Pompeio cum praesidio tentum, caput Hispaniae ulterioris esse existimabatur?
question_en: Which town, held with a garrison by Sextus Pompeius, was considered the capital of Further Spain?
derivation: Place fact anchored to Sextus Pompeius (Pompey the Great's younger son) and the province. Supported verbatim by 'Cordubam tenebat, quod eius provinciae caput esse existimabatur'. That Corduba was the capital of Hispania Ulterior, garrisoned by Sextus, is closed-book.

author: Cato
source_text: Et virum bonum quom laudabant, ita laudabant: bonum agricolam bonumque colonum; amplissime laudari existimabatur qui ita laudabatur.
question: Quibus verbis maiores, ut Cato scribit, virum bonum amplissime laudabant?
question_en: With what words, as Cato writes, did the ancestors most highly praise a good man?
answer_en: A good farmer and a good husbandman.
derivation: The famous claim of the praefatio: the highest praise for a man was to call him 'bonum agricolam bonumque colonum.' Anchored to Cato + the maiores; the answer is the exact predicate phrase, supported verbatim. Closed-book: one of the most-quoted lines of Cato. Imperfect 'laudabant' kept indicative; 'ut Cato scribit' is a parenthetical author-frame.

author: Cato
source_text: Praedium quod primum siet, si me rogabis, sic dicam: de omnibus agris optimoque loco iugera agri centum, vinea est prima, vel si vino multo est; secundo loco hortus irriguus; tertio salictum; quarto oletum; quinto pratum; sexto campus frumentarius; septimo silva caedua; octavo arbustum; nono glandaria silva.
question: Quod agri genus Cato inter omnia primo loco numerat?
question_en: Which kind of farmland does Cato rank first among all?
derivation: Cato's well-known ranking of the nine kinds of farmland, with the vineyard (vinea) first. Anchored to Cato; single answer 'vineam,' supported verbatim by 'vinea est prima.' Closed-book: a standard datum in discussions of Roman agronomy. Only the first place is asked (the full list would fail short-answer).

author: Cato
source_text: Brassica est quae omnibus holeribus antistat.
question: Quod holus Cato omnibus holeribus antistare scribit?
question_en: Which vegetable does Cato write surpasses all other vegetables?
derivation: Cato's famous superlative praise of the cabbage as the best of all vegetables, opening his cabbage-chapter. Anchored to Cato; single answer 'brassicam,' supported verbatim. Closed-book: Cato's enthusiasm for cabbage is well-known trivia (discussed e.g. by Pliny). 'antistare' + dative; acc. subject 'brassicam' under 'scribit.'

author: Catullus
source_text: CVI dono lepidum nouum libellum arida modo pumice expolitum? Corneli, tibi: namque tu solebas meas esse aliquid putare nugas iam tum, cum ausus es unus Italorum omne aeuum tribus explicare cartis doctis, Iuppiter, et laboriosis.
question: Cui Catullus lepidum novum libellum suum dedicavit?
question_en: To whom did Catullus dedicate his charming new little book?
derivation: The dedication of the libellus, named in the poem ('Corneli, tibi') — one of the most famous dedications in Latin poetry; the addressee is canonically Cornelius Nepos. Entity-anchored to Catullus + his libellus; single named answer.

author: Catullus
source_text: PASSER, deliciae meae puellae, quicum ludere, quem in sinu tenere, cui primum digitum dare appetenti et acris solet incitare morsus
question: Quod animal in deliciis habuit puella Catulli?
question_en: What animal did Catullus' girl keep as her darling pet?
derivation: Lesbia's pet sparrow — the most famous pet in Latin literature, and evidence of Roman pet-keeping. Anchored to Catullus' puella (Lesbia); one-word answer stated verbatim ('passer, deliciae meae puellae').

author: Catullus
source_text: TAM gratum est mihi quam ferunt puellae pernici aureolum fuisse malum, quod zonam soluit diu ligatam.
question: Quid zonam Atalantae, puellae pernicis, diu ligatam solvisse ferunt?
question_en: What is said to have loosed the long-tied girdle of Atalanta, the swift girl?
derivation: The golden apple that ended Atalanta's race and virginity — myth as shared story; the text's 'puella pernix' is the canonical Atalanta. 'ferunt' keeps the traditional frame; the apple and girdle are verbatim.

author: Catullus
source_text: Amastri Pontica et Cytore buxifer, tibi haec fuisse et esse cognitissima ait phaselus
question: Qua arbore mons Cytorus in Ponto abundat, ut Catullus testatur?
question_en: In what tree does Mount Cytorus in Pontus abound, as Catullus attests?
derivation: Cytorus 'buxifer' — box-bearing Cytorus was proverbial for its boxwood, a standing geographic epithet. Anchored to the named mountain; one-word answer supported by the epithet.

author: Catullus
source_text: nam tui Catulli plenus sacculus est aranearum.
question: Quo plenus est sacculus Catulli, cum Fabullum ad cenam vocat?
question_en: What is Catullus' purse full of when he invites Fabullus to dinner?
derivation: The purse full of cobwebs — the proverbial image of an empty wallet, quoted ever since. Anchored to Catullus + the invitation to Fabullus; one-word answer verbatim.

author: Catullus
source_text: di magni, horribilem et sacrum libellum! quem tu scilicet ad tuum Catullum misti, continuo ut die periret, Saturnalibus, optimo dierum!
question: Quo festo die Calvus poeta Catullo libellum pessimorum poetarum dono misit?
question_en: On what festival day did the poet Calvus send Catullus a booklet of dreadful poets as a present?
derivation: Gift-exchange at the Saturnalia — Calvus' joke-gift of bad poetry arrives 'Saturnalibus'. Festival custom anchored to Calvus + Catullus; one-word answer verbatim.

author: Catullus
source_text: MINISTER uetuli puer Falerni inger mi calices amariores, ut lex Postumiae iubet magistrae ebrioso acino ebriosioris.
question: Cuius vini calices puer minister apud Catullum ingerere iubetur?
question_en: Cups of what wine is the serving-boy in Catullus ordered to pour?
derivation: Falernian, the most celebrated Roman wine, served old and unmixed ('uetuli Falerni') — named-wine food culture. Anchored to Catullus' drinking poem; one-name answer verbatim.

author: Catullus
source_text: nam sanctae Veneri Cupidinique uouit, si sibi restitutus essem desissemque truces uibrare iambos, electissima pessimi poetae scripta tardipedi deo daturam infelicibus ustulanda lignis.
question: Quis deus apud Catullum 'tardipes' vocatur, cui scripta pessimi poetae ustulanda dantur?
question_en: Which god is called 'slow-footed' in Catullus, to whom the worst poet's writings are given to burn?
derivation: The lame fire-god: 'tardipedi deo' is the canonical periphrasis for Vulcan, to whose flames the vowed writings go. The lameness of Vulcan is shared myth; one-name answer.

author: Catullus
source_text: nunc o caeruleo creata ponto, quae sanctum Idalium Vriosque apertos quaeque Ancona Cnidumque harundinosam colis quaeque Amathunta quaeque Golgos quaeque Durrachium Hadriae tabernam
question: Quae dea, caeruleo ponto creata, Idalium, Amathunta Golgosque colit apud Catullum?
question_en: Which goddess, born of the blue sea, dwells in Idalium, Amathus, and Golgi according to Catullus?
derivation: Venus' sea-birth and her canonical Cypriot cult seats (Idalium, Amathus, Golgi, plus Cnidus and Ancona) — ambient religious geography. Anchored by the named shrines; one-name answer.

author: Catullus
source_text: SALAX taberna uosque contubernales, a pilleatis nona fratribus pila
question: Qui fratres gemini apud Catullum 'pilleati' dicuntur?
question_en: Which twin brothers are called 'felt-capped' in Catullus?
derivation: The pilleus (the egg-half felt cap) is the canonical attribute of the Dioscuri; Catullus locates the tavern nine pillars from 'the felt-capped brothers' (their temple in the Forum). Shared iconographic knowledge; two-name answer.

author: Catullus
source_text: caue despuas, ocelle, ne poenas Nemesis reposcat a te. est uehemens dea: laedere hanc caueto.
question: Quae dea vehemens poenas a superbis reposcit, ut Catullus Licinium monet?
question_en: Which vehement goddess exacts penalties from the scornful, as Catullus warns Licinius?
derivation: Nemesis as the punisher of pride and scorn — 'est uehemens dea: laedere hanc caueto' — shared religious knowledge. One-name answer verbatim.

author: Catullus
source_text: NON custos si fingar ille Cretum, non Ladas ego pinnipesue Perseus, non si Pegaseo ferar uolatu
question: Quis heros apud Catullum 'pinnipes' vocatur?
question_en: Which hero is called 'wing-footed' in Catullus?
derivation: Perseus' winged sandals — his canonical attribute, fixed in the epithet 'pinnipes'. Listed with Ladas, Pegasus, and the guardian of Crete (Talos) as bywords for speed; one-name answer verbatim.

author: Catullus
source_text: namque Iunia Manlio, qualis Idalium colens uenit ad Phrygium Venus iudicem, bona cum bona nubet alite uirgo
question: Quis erat 'Phrygius iudex', ad quem Venus Idalium colens venisse dicitur apud Catullum?
question_en: Who was the 'Phrygian judge' to whom Venus of Idalium is said to have come in Catullus?
derivation: The Judgment of Paris — 'Phrygius iudex' is the canonical periphrasis for Paris judging the goddesses; the bride is as fair as Venus before him. Shared myth; one-name answer.

author: Catullus
source_text: talis illius a bona matre laus genus approbet, qualis unica ab optima matre Telemacho manet fama Penelopeo.
question: A qua matre optima Telemacho unica fama manet, ut Catullus canit?
question_en: From what best of mothers does Telemachus' unmatched good name endure, as Catullus sings?
derivation: Penelope as the canonical chaste mother whose virtue guarantees her son's fame ('Telemacho... Penelopeo'). Shared Homeric knowledge; one-name answer verbatim.

author: Catullus
source_text: at si forte eadem est ulmo coniuncta marito, multi illam agricolae, multi coluere iuuenci
question: Cui arbori 'marito' vitis coniungi solet, ut in carmine nuptiali Catulli canitur?
question_en: To what tree as its 'husband' is the vine customarily wedded, as sung in Catullus' wedding poem?
derivation: The vine trained on the elm — the standard Italian husbandry practice, proverbially the 'marriage' of vine and elm, and the poem's simile for the bride. One-word answer verbatim.

author: Catullus
source_text: cum lecti iuuenes, Argiuae robora pubis, auratam optantes Colchis auertere pellem ausi sunt uada salsa cita decurrere puppi
question: Quam pellem lecti iuvenes Argivi Colchis avertere ausi sunt, ut Catullus canit?
question_en: What fleece did the chosen Argive youths dare to carry off from the Colchians, as Catullus sings?
derivation: The Golden Fleece as the object of the Argonauts' voyage ('auratam... Colchis auertere pellem') — myth as shared story; short answer verbatim.

author: Catullus
source_text: quare facta uirum multantes uindice poena Eumenides, quibus anguino redimita capillo frons exspirantis praeportat pectoris iras, huc huc aduentate
question: Quo capillo frons Eumenidum redimita est, ut Catullus describit?
question_en: With what hair is the brow of the Eumenides wreathed, as Catullus describes?
derivation: The canonical iconography of the Furies: snake-wreathed brows ('anguino redimita capillo frons'), avengers of men's deeds. Anchored to the Eumenides; one-word answer verbatim.

author: Catullus
source_text: quod tibi si sancti concesserit incola Itoni... annuit, ut tauri respergas sanguine dextram, tum uero facito ut memori tibi condita corde haec uigeant mandata... funestam antennae deponant undique uestem, candidaque intorti sustollant uela rudentes
question: Qualia vela Theseus victor tollere debebat, ut patri Aegeo salutem suam significaret?
question_en: What kind of sails was the victorious Theseus to hoist to signal his safety to his father Aegeus?
derivation: Aegeus' charge: put off the mourning canvas and raise white sails if Theseus lives — the sail-signal he then forgot. Canonical myth stated verbatim ('candidaque... sustollant uela'); anchored to Theseus + Aegeus.

author: Catullus
source_text: cum interea infirmo quatientes corpora motu ueridicos Parcae coeperunt edere cantus... currite ducentes subtegmina, currite, fusi.
question: Quae deae in nuptiis Pelei veridicum carmen cecinerunt, fila fusis ducentes?
question_en: Which goddesses sang the truth-telling song at Peleus' wedding while drawing the threads on their spindles?
derivation: The Parcae spinning as they prophesy — distaff, thread and spindle ('currite ducentes subtegmina, currite, fusi') are their canonical apparatus. Anchored to the wedding of Peleus; one-name answer verbatim.

author: Catullus
source_text: nascetur uobis expers terroris Achilles, hostibus haud tergo, sed forti pectore notus, qui persaepe uago uictor certamine cursus flammea praeuertet celeris uestigia ceruae.
question: Quis filius Peleo et Thetidi nasciturus a Parcis canitur?
question_en: What son do the Fates sing will be born to Peleus and Thetis?
derivation: The prophecy of Achilles' birth, fearless and swifter than the deer ('flammea praeuertet celeris uestigia ceruae'). The central genealogical fact of the myth; one-name answer verbatim.

author: Catullus
source_text: non illi quisquam bello se conferet heros, cum Phrygii Teucro manabunt sanguine Troicaque obsidens longinquo moenia bello, periuri Pelopis uastabit tertius heres.
question: Quis 'periuri Pelopis tertius heres' apud Catullum Troiae moenia longinquo bello vastabit?
question_en: Who is the 'third heir of perjured Pelops' who in Catullus will lay waste the walls of Troy in a long war?
derivation: The genealogical riddle assumes the shared line Pelops - Atreus - Agamemnon: the third heir who besieged Troy. Pelops 'periurus' for his betrayal of Myrtilus. Canonical; one-name answer.

author: Catullus
source_text: testis erit magnis uirtutibus unda Scamandri, quae passim rapido diffunditur Hellesponto
question: In quod fretum Scamander amnis diffunditur, ut Catullus canit?
question_en: Into what strait does the river Scamander pour, as Catullus sings?
derivation: Trojan geography: the Scamander empties into the Hellespont — stated verbatim, and choked with corpses by Achilles in the prophecy. One-name answer.

author: Catullus
source_text: nam tum Helenae raptu primores Argiuorum coeperat ad sese Troia ciere uiros
question: Cuius feminae raptu Troia primores Argivorum ad sese civit, ut Catullus scribit?
question_en: By the abduction of what woman did Troy begin to summon the chiefs of the Argives against herself, as Catullus writes?
derivation: The rape of Helen as the cause of the Trojan War — the most shared of Greek myth-facts, stated verbatim ('Helenae raptu'). One-name answer.

author: Catullus
source_text: hic, uelut in nigro iactatis turbine nautis lenius aspirans aura secunda uenit iam prece Pollucis, iam Castoris implorata
question: Quibus deis precibus imploratis nautis turbine iactatis aura secunda venit, ut Catullus scribit?
question_en: To which gods do sailors tossed in the storm address the prayers that bring the favoring breeze, as Catullus writes?
derivation: The Dioscuri as rescuers of storm-tossed sailors, invoked by name at sea — the practice itself (distinct from the votive dedication in c.4). Two-name answer verbatim.

author: Catullus
source_text: CHOMMODA dicebat, si quando commoda uellet dicere, et insidias Arrius hinsidias... Ionios fluctus, postquam illuc Arrius isset, iam non Ionios esse sed Hionios.
question: Quid Arrius verbis perperam addebat, cum 'chommoda' pro 'commoda' et 'hinsidias' pro 'insidias' diceret?
question_en: What did Arrius wrongly add to his words when he said 'chommoda' for 'commoda' and 'hinsidias' for 'insidias'?
derivation: Misplaced aspiration as a social marker of speech: Arrius' hypercorrect h's turned even the Ionian sea 'Hionian'. The fact — that aspiration betrayed one's class and schooling — is cultural and survives translation; the quoted examples carry the point.

author: Catullus
source_text: ODI et amo. quare id faciam, fortasse requiris. nescio, sed fieri sentio et excrucior.
question: Quid Catullus simul se facere sentit, nescius quare, in celeberrimo suo disticho?
question_en: What does Catullus feel himself doing at once, not knowing why, in his most famous couplet?
derivation: 'Odi et amo' — the most famous distich in Latin, proverbial for the torment of contradictory passion. Anchored to Catullus; two-word answer verbatim.

author: Catullus
source_text: atque in perpetuum, frater, aue atque uale.
question: Quibus verbis Catullus fratrem mortuum in perpetuum salutat?
question_en: With what words does Catullus salute his dead brother forever?
derivation: 'Ave atque vale' — the canonical Roman farewell to the dead, closing c.101 'in perpetuum'; the phrase became the epitome of Latin funerary address. Short answer verbatim.

author: Catullus
source_text: cur non diuitiis Croesum superare potis sit, uno qui in saltu tot bona possideat
question: Quis rex apud Catullum, ut in proverbio, divitiarum summarum exemplum est?
question_en: Which king stands in Catullus, proverbially, as the exemplar of supreme wealth?
derivation: Croesus of Lydia as the byword for riches ('diuitiis Croesum superare') — the shared proverb of wealth. One-name answer verbatim.

author: Anonymi (tituli sepulcrales)
source_text: Hospes, quod deico paullum est, asta ac pellege.
question: Quo vocabulo celeberrimum Claudiae elogium sepulcrale eum qui praeterit statim compellat?
question_en: With what word of address does the most famous epitaph of Claudia immediately hail the passer-by?
derivation: Opening word of the most famous Roman epitaph, the elogium of Claudia (CLE 52 = CIL 1.1211), anthologized in every Latin reader. 'Hospes' is the classic epigraphic address to the passer-by (so too B 53, 838, 1532). Anchored to the named celebrated text; single verifiable answer (the poem's first word). Criterion 8 holds because the famous poem's content, not an obscure person, carries the fact.

author: Anonymi (tituli sepulcrales)
source_text: Debita libertas iuveni mihi lege negata morte immatura reddita perpetua est.
question: Quid mors, ut in titulis sepulcralibus servorum Romanorum legitur, servis tandem perpetuum dedit?
question_en: What, as one reads in the epitaphs of Roman slaves, did death at last give slaves in perpetuity?
derivation: The distinctively Roman slave-epitaph topos: death confers the freedom life (and law) denied — 'debita libertas ... morte ... reddita perpetua est', corroborated by B 1331 ('nunc mors perpetua libertatem dedit'). Rooted in the Roman institutions of slavery and manumission, so culturally salient at the level of shared custom, not of the anonymous individual; single short answer supported verbatim.

author: Anonymi (tituli sepulcrales)
source_text: quisque huic tumulo possuit ardente lucernam, illius cineres aurea terra tegat.
question: Quod munus ardens ad tumulos mortuorum ponere Romani pii solebant?
question_en: What burning offering did dutiful Romans customarily place at the tombs of the dead?
derivation: The custom of placing a lit lamp (lucerna) at the tomb, attested by this epitaph's reciprocal blessing on whoever sets one there ('quisque huic tumulo possuit ardente lucernam'). Grave lamps are a staple of Roman funerary cult and archaeology — ambient cultural knowledge; the stone's obscure Septima is not the subject. Single-word answer supported verbatim.

author: Anonymi (tituli sepulcrales)
source_text: Dis Manibus sacrum. memoriae aeternae C. Valeri Saturnini, qui vixit annis noviens denis, prope convenientibus annis.
question: Quibus numinibus tituli sepulcrales Romani, litteris D M notati, dedicari solent?
question_en: To which divinities are Roman tombstones, marked with the letters D M, customarily dedicated?
answer_en: To the Di Manes, the spirits of the dead.
derivation: The universal Roman dedication formula D(is) M(anibus): tombs are consecrated to the deified spirits of the dead, the Di Manes. Attested verbatim here ('Dis Manibus sacrum') and in B 439; cf. B 1269 'sacri sunt Manes'. The single most recognizable convention of Roman epigraphy — flagship criterion-8 material; fixed two-word answer.

author: Gaius
source_text: unde olim patricii dicebant plebiscitis se non teneri, quia sine auctoritate eorum facta essent; sed postea lex Hortensia lata est, qua cautum est, ut plebiscita universum populum tenerent.
question: Qua lege cautum est ut plebiscita universum populum tenerent, ut Gaius tradit?
question_en: By what law was it provided that plebiscites should bind the whole people, as Gaius reports?
derivation: Gaius records the lex Hortensia, which made plebiscites binding on the entire people (patricians included). Closed-book famous legal-history fact, anchored to the named law, single named-entity answer verbatim ('lex Hortensia lata est, qua cautum est...').

author: Anonymi (tituli parietarii)
source_text: venimus hoc cupidi, multo magis hire cupjimus ut liceat nostros visere, Roma, Lares
question: Quos deos suos visere cupiunt viatores in celebri disticho parietario Pompeiano, quod incipit 'venimus huc cupidi'?
question_en: Which gods of their own do the travelers in the famous Pompeian wall distich beginning 'venimus huc cupidi' long to go and see?
derivation: The anthologized homesickness distich: the writers came eagerly but long far more to go back, 'ut liceat nostros visere, Roma, Lares.' The cultural fact is the Lares as the household gods whose sight means home; anchored by the famous incipit and the address to Roma; single-name answer supported verbatim ('nostros ... Lares'; vulgar spellings hoc = huc, hire = ire kept in the source).

author: Anonymi (tituli parietarii)
source_text: calos Paris isse, Septentrio.
question: Quo vocabulo, e lingua Graeca sumpto, fautores Pompeiani histriones suos in parietibus acclamabant?
question_en: With what word, borrowed from Greek, did Pompeian fans acclaim their actors on the walls?
derivation: The theatrical acclamation calos (Greek kalos, 'beautifully!, bravo!'), scratched for the star performer: 'calos Paris isse' (= calos Paris ipse — very likely the celebrated pantomimus Paris). The acclamation formula, not the fan, is the fact; the Greek loan survives translation as 'the cheer used for actors'; supported verbatim.

author: Anonymi (tituli parietarii)
source_text: Idibus Iulis inaures postas ad Faustilla. pro X II usura deduxit aeris assem ex summa XXX.
question: Cuius metalli nummus erat as, quo usurae pretiaque minuta in titulis Pompeianis numerantur?
question_en: Of what metal was the as, the coin in which petty interest and small prices are reckoned in Pompeian graffiti?
derivation: The as as the small bronze coin of everyday reckoning: in this pawnbroking record (earrings deposited with the moneylender, 'inaures postas ad Faustilla') the interest deducted is 'aeris assem' — an as of bronze. The coin and its metal are ambient Roman money-culture; the private transaction is only the anchor's setting; supported verbatim.

author: Anonymi (tituli parietarii)
source_text: imperatore Antonino et Alessanro, Grato et Seleuco cos. Kalendis Iunis Celius Saturninus sebaciaria fecit
question: Quorum magistratuum nominibus Romani annos in titulis designare solebant?
question_en: By the names of which magistrates did Romans customarily designate the year in inscriptions?
derivation: Eponymous consular dating — the year named by its two consuls — attested in this graffito of a Roman vigilis: 'Grato et Seleuco cos. Kalendis Iunis' (the consuls of AD 221). One of the most basic institutions of Roman civic time-reckoning, ambient for any reader of Roman documents; single-word answer; 'Se(leuco)' expanded per normalization.

author: Justinian (Corpus Iuris Civilis)
source_text: Placuit publica auctoritate decem constitui viros, per quos peterentur leges a graecis civitatibus et civitas fundaretur legibus: quas in tabulas eboreas perscriptas pro rostris composuerunt, ut possint leges apertius percipi. qui ipsi animadverterunt aliquid deesse istis primis legibus ideoque sequenti anno alias duas ad easdem tabulas adiecerunt: et ita ex accedenti appellatae sunt leges duodecim tabularum.
question: Quot viri publica auctoritate constituti sunt, ut leges duodecim tabularum conderentur, secundum Pomponium?
question_en: How many men were appointed by public authority to establish the law of the Twelve Tables, according to Pomponius?
derivation: Pomponius: ten men (decemviri) were appointed and composed the Twelve Tables (two more tables added the following year giving the name). Closed-book, anchored to the Twelve Tables + decemviri, number answer (decem) verbatim from 'decem constitui viros'.

author: Cicero; Vergil (pilot)
work: Latin-specific pilot: prose rhythm (Cicero, Orator) and scansion (Vergil)
source_text: senarios vero et Hipponacteos effugere vix possumus; magnam enim partem ex iambis nostra constat oratio.
question: Cuius pedis magna ex parte orationem cotidianam constare Cicero adfirmat, eo quod sermoni proximus sit?
question_en: Of which foot does Cicero affirm that ordinary speech largely consists, as nearest to conversation?
derivation: Cicero notes that a great part of ordinary speech falls into iambs, which is why iambic verses slip in unawares. Latin-specific: it concerns the quantitative make-up of Latin speech. Closed-book for a reader of the Orator.

author: Cicero; Vergil (pilot)
work: Latin-specific pilot: prose rhythm (Cicero, Orator) and scansion (Vergil)
source_text: Dochmius autem e quinque syllabis, brevi, duabus longis, brevi, longa, ut est hoc: amicos tenes.
question: Ex quot syllabis constat dochmius ille, cuius exemplum Cicero 'amicos tenes' adfert?
question_en: Of how many syllables is the dochmius composed, for which Cicero gives the example 'amicos tenes'?
derivation: The dochmius is a five-syllable metrical unit (short, two longs, short, long). Latin-specific: a quantitative pattern anchored to Cicero's own example. Short-answer and verifiable from the quoted text.

author: Cicero; Vergil (pilot)
work: Latin-specific pilot: prose rhythm (Cicero, Orator) and scansion (Vergil)
source_text: quadripedante putrem sonitu quatit ungula campum.
question: In illo Vergilii versu 'quadripedante putrem sonitu quatit ungula campum', quem sonum numerus dactylicus imitatur?
question_en: In Vergil's line 'quadripedante putrem sonitu quatit ungula campum', what sound does the dactylic rhythm imitate?
answer_en: The beat of a galloping horse's hooves.
derivation: The rushing dactyls of the line enact the sound of galloping hooves (onomatopoeia). Latin-specific: the imitation lives in the Latin metrical rhythm and is lost in any prose or non-quantitative rendering. One of the most celebrated sound-effects in Latin verse.

author: Macrobius
source_text: Aedem vero Saturni aerarium Romani esse voluerunt, quod tempore quo incoluit Italiam fertur nullum in eius finibus furtum esse commissum.
question: Quem usum publicum aedi Saturni Romani tribuerunt, ut apud Macrobium refertur?
question_en: What public use did the Romans give to the temple of Saturn, as reported in Macrobius?
derivation: The temple of Saturn housed the Roman public treasury (aerarium), because under Saturn no theft occurred and all was held in common. Anchored to the temple; single answer, verbatim. Well-known institution.

author: Macrobius
source_text: in ditione autem Iunonis sunt omnes Kalendae, unde et Varro libro quinto Rerum divinarum scribit Iano duodecim aras pro totidem mensibus dedicatas.
question: Quot aras Iano dedicatas esse, pro totidem mensibus, Varro apud Macrobium scribit?
question_en: How many altars does Varro, cited in Macrobius, write were dedicated to Janus, one for each of the months?
derivation: Varro records twelve altars to Janus, one per month. Anchored to Janus and Varro; number answer, verbatim. Calendar-cult fact framed as Varro's claim.

author: Macrobius
source_text: Augustus deinde est qui Sextilis antea vocabatur, donec honori Augusti daretur ex senatusconsulto.
question: Quo nomine mensis Sextilis, ex senatusconsulto, in honorem principis appellatus est?
question_en: By what name was the month Sextilis renamed by decree of the senate, in honor of the emperor?
derivation: Sextilis became Augustus by senatorial decree. Anchored to the month and the emperor; single-name answer, verbatim. Core calendar-naming fact.

author: Macrobius
source_text: Omni autem intercalationi mensis Februarius deputatus est, quoniam is ultimus anni erat.
question: Cui mensi omnis intercalatio apud Romanos deputata est, ut apud Macrobium refertur?
question_en: To which month was all intercalation assigned among the Romans, as reported in Macrobius?
derivation: Intercalation was placed in February (then the year's last month, after the Terminalia on the 23rd). Anchored to the practice; single-name answer, verbatim. Core calendar mechanism.

author: Macrobius
source_text: Hinc est quod simulachris et Aesculapii et Salutis draco subiungitur.
question: Quod animal simulacris Aesculapii et Salutis subiungitur, ut apud Macrobium refertur?
question_en: What creature is placed beside the statues of Aesculapius and Salus, as reported in Macrobius?
derivation: A serpent accompanies the statues of Aesculapius and Salus (the snake sloughs its skin, like renewal of health). Anchored to the iconography; single-creature answer, verbatim. Canonical Aesculapian attribute.

author: Macrobius
source_text: Qui enim moriens poema suum legavit igni quid nisi famae suae posteritati subtrahendo curavit?
question: Cui rei Vergilius moriens poema suum (Aeneida) legavit, ut Evangelus apud Macrobium refert?
question_en: To what did Vergil, dying, bequeath his poem (the Aeneid), as Evangelus reports in Macrobius?
derivation: The famous tradition that the dying Vergil left orders for the Aeneid to be burned. Anchored to Vergil and his poem; short answer, verbatim. Celebrated literary anecdote.

author: Macrobius
source_text: ut hoc est ex epistola ad C. Cassium dictatoris violatorem: Vellem Idibus Martiis me ad coenam invitasses, profecto reliquiarum nihil fuisset.
question: Quibus Idibus, secundum Ciceronis epistolam ad Cassium apud Macrobium relatam, dictator Caesar occisus est?
question_en: On which Ides, according to Cicero's letter to Cassius reported in Macrobius, was the dictator Caesar slain?
derivation: Cicero's letter to Cassius ('the dictator's violator') alludes to the Ides of March killing and wishes Antony too had died ('no leftovers'). Anchored to Cassius and Caesar; date answer, supported verbatim. The most salient date in Roman history.

author: Macrobius
source_text: Nam et Salios Herculi dedit, quos tantum Marti dicavit antiquitas.
question: Cui deo soli antiquitas Salios sacerdotes dicaverat, ut apud Macrobium refertur?
question_en: To which god alone had antiquity dedicated the Salii priests, as reported in Macrobius?
derivation: The Salii were the priesthood of Mars. Anchored to the priesthood; single-name answer, supported verbatim. Well-known Roman priestly institution.

author: Macrobius
source_text: porcum Troianum mensis inferant, quem illi ideo sic vocabant, quasi aliis inclusis animalibus gravidum, ut ille Troianus equus gravidus armatis fuit.
question: Quo nomine appellabatur porcus aliis animalibus intus inclusis fartus, ad similitudinem equi Troiani, ut apud Macrobium refertur?
question_en: By what name was a pig stuffed with other animals inside called, on the analogy of the Trojan horse, as reported in Macrobius?
derivation: The 'porcus Troianus' was a pig stuffed with other animals, named for the Trojan horse full of armed men. Anchored to the dish and the analogy; short name answer, supported verbatim. Salient luxury dish.

author: Martial
source_text: Alea parva nuces et non damnosa videtur; Saepe tamen pueris abstulit illa natis.
question: Quae alea parva nec damnosa pueris esse videtur apud Martialem?
question_en: What is regarded as a small and harmless gamble for boys in Martial?
derivation: Nuts were the proverbial small-stakes gambling of children, especially at the Saturnalia (cf. the proem's 'Lude nucibus'). Anchored to the named stake; one-word answer supported verbatim (Alea parva nuces).

author: Martial
source_text: Sortitus thecam calamis armare memento: Cetera nos dedimus, tu leviora para.
question: Quibus instrumentis thecam librariam armare debet qui eam sortitus est, ut monet Martialis?
question_en: With what implements must the man who has drawn a writing-case arm it, as Martial advises?
derivation: The theca libraria was the case for one's reed pens — the winner of the lot must furnish the calami himself. A named object of Roman writing culture; one-word answer supported verbatim.

author: Martial
source_text: Haec tibi erunt armata suo graphiaria ferro: Si puero dones, non leve munus erit.
question: Quo armatum est graphiarium apud Martialem?
question_en: With what is the stylus-case (graphiarium) armed in Martial?
derivation: The graphiarium held the iron styli for writing on wax — Martial adds it makes no slight gift for a schoolboy. A named object of writing culture; answer supported verbatim (armata suo ferro).

author: Martial
source_text: Pax me certa ducis placidos curvavit in usus. Agricolae nunc sum, militis ante fui.
question: Cuius fuit ante falx illa quae nunc agricolae est, ut loquitur ipsa apud Martialem?
question_en: Whose was the sickle before, which now belongs to the farmer, as it says of itself in Martial?
derivation: The famous sword-beaten-into-sickle couplet: the emperor's assured peace bent the soldier's blade to the farmer's peaceful use. Anchored to the falx (the lemma) speaking of itself; one-word answer supported verbatim (militis ante fui).

author: Martial
source_text: Ebria nos madidis rumpit tibicina buccis: Saepe duas pariter, saepe monaulon habet.
question: Quot tibias pariter tibicina saepe inflat apud Martialem?
question_en: How many pipes does the flute-girl often blow at once, in Martial?
derivation: The tibicina of the banquet played the double pipe — two tibiae at once — or sometimes the single monaulos. A fact of Roman musical culture anchored to the named player and instrument; number answer supported verbatim.

author: Martial
source_text: Si vis esse satur, nostrum potes esse Priapum: Ipsa licet rodas inguina, purus eris.
question: Cuius dei imago e siligine ficta inter dona Saturnalicia editur apud Martialem?
question_en: The image of what god, shaped from fine wheat flour, is eaten among the Saturnalian gifts in Martial?
derivation: The Priapus siligineus (the lemma): pastry-work in the shape of the god Priapus, of fine siligo flour, which one may eat entire and stay 'pure.' A named festive confection; answer supported by lemma + couplet (nostrum potes esse Priapum).

author: Martial
source_text: Psittacus a vobis aliorum nomina discam: Hoc didici per me dicere CAESAR HAVE.
question: Quam salutationem psittacus ille per se dicere didicit apud Martialem?
question_en: What greeting did the parrot in Martial learn to say all by itself?
derivation: Talking parrots were taught greetings as luxury pets; this one learned unprompted to hail the emperor — a famous piece of imperial-age bird lore (cf. the raven of the Ara). Anchored to the parrot gift; short quoted answer supported verbatim.

author: Martial
source_text: Si tibi talis erit, qualem dilecta Catullo Lesbia plorabat, hic habitare potest.
question: Quae puella, Catullo dilecta, avem suam mortuam plorabat, ut memorat Martialis?
question_en: What girl, beloved of Catullus, wept for her dead bird, as Martial recalls?
derivation: The most famous pet bird of Latin literature — Lesbia's passer, mourned in Catullus's poems — invoked to size the ivory cage. Two named literary figures; one-word answer supported verbatim (dilecta Catullo Lesbia plorabat).

author: Martial
source_text: Invisae nimium pueris grataeque magistris, Clara Prometheo munere ligna sumus.
question: Cuius munere clara sunt ligna ferularum, ut ait Martialis?
question_en: By whose gift is the wood of the fennel-stalks (ferulae) famous, as Martial says?
answer_en: By Prometheus's (he carried the stolen fire in a fennel stalk).
derivation: The myth that Prometheus brought fire to men hidden in a fennel stalk (ferula) — 'famous for Prometheus's gift.' Named mythic figure + named plant; one-word answer supported verbatim (Clara Prometheo munere ligna).

author: Martial
source_text: In pretio scopas testatur palma fuisse. Otia sed scopis nunc analecta dedit.
question: Ex qua arbore scopae Romanae fieri solebant, ut testatur Martialis?
question_en: From what tree were Roman brooms usually made, as Martial attests?
derivation: Brooms (scopae) were made of palm fronds; the couplet adds that the crumb-collector (analecta) has now given brooms a rest. Named object + named material; short answer supported verbatim (scopas... palma).

author: Martial
source_text: Nos Satyri, nos Bacchus amat, nos ebria tigris, Perfusos domini lambere docta pedes.
question: Qui deus cum Satyris suis calathos amare dicitur apud Martialem?
question_en: What god, along with his Satyrs, is said to love the calathus cups, in Martial?
derivation: The calathus as the Bacchic drinking-cup, loved by Bacchus, the Satyrs, and the god's drunken tigress taught to lick her master's wine-drenched feet. Named god + named cup; one-word answer supported verbatim.

author: Martial
source_text: Reddidit Eurydicen vati: sed perdidit ipse, Dum sibi non credit nec patienter amat.
question: Quam uxorem cithara vati Orpheo reddidit, quam ipse mox iterum perdidit?
question_en: What wife did the lyre restore to the bard Orpheus, whom he himself soon lost again?
derivation: The Orpheus myth on the gift of a cithara: the lyre won Eurydice back from the underworld, but the bard lost her by not trusting himself and looking back. Canonical shared story; one-word answer supported verbatim (Reddidit Eurydicen vati... perdidit ipse).

author: Martial
source_text: Mutari melius tauro, pater optime divum, Tunc poteras, Io cum tibi vacca fuit.
question: In quod animal Iuppiter propter Europam mutatus est, ut pingitur apud Martialem?
question_en: Into what animal did Jupiter change for Europa, as painted in Martial?
derivation: On the painted Europa (the lemma): Jupiter became a bull to carry her off — the joke adds he should have done it when Io was his cow. Named god + named girl; short answer supported by lemma + couplet (mutari... tauro).

author: Martial
source_text: Barbara pyramidum sileat miracula Memphis, Assyrius iactet nec Babylona labor;
question: Cuius urbis Aegyptiae miracula sunt pyramides apud Martialem?
question_en: To which Egyptian city do the marvels of the pyramids belong, according to Martial?
derivation: Martial assigns the pyramids to Memphis, the standard Roman association of the pyramids with that city. Entity-anchored (pyramids, Egypt, Martial); one-word verifiable answer; shared geographic knowledge of the ancient wonder list.

author: Martial
source_text: Prostratum uasta Nemees in ualle leonem nobile et Herculeum fama canebat opus.
question: Quis heros leonem in valle Nemees prostravisse fama canebatur?
question_en: Which hero was famed in story to have laid low the lion in the valley of Nemea?
derivation: The Nemean lion as Hercules' celebrated labor - canonical shared myth, evidenced verbatim ('Herculeum... opus'). Anchored to Nemea; one-name answer.

author: Martial
source_text: Ne tibi pallentes moveant fastidia caules, nitrata viridis brassica fiat aqua.
question: Qua aqua brassica coquenda est, ut viridis maneat, teste Martiale?
question_en: In what water should cabbage be cooked so that it stays green, on Martial's testimony?
derivation: Insider kitchen technique: nitrum (soda) in the cooking water keeps greens green — the same trick prescribed by Apicius. Anchored to cabbage + Martial; brief-phrase answer supported verbatim.

author: Martial
source_text: Miraris, quotiens gemmantis explicat alas, et potes hunc saevo tradere, dure, coco?
question: Quae avis, quamquam gemmantes alas mirantibus explicat, tamen saevo coco tradi solet, ut queritur Martialis?
question_en: Which bird, though it spreads its jeweled wings for admirers, is nonetheless handed over to the cruel cook, as Martial protests?
derivation: The peacock (the epigram's lemma), admired for its 'jeweled' train yet served at luxury tables — Martial's reproach presupposes the shared custom of eating peafowl. Named-bird answer.

author: Martial
source_text: Sanguine de nostro tinctas, ingrate, lacernas induis, et non est hoc satis, esca sumus.
question: Cuius animalis sanguine lacernae purpureae tinguntur, ut queritur ipsa concha apud Martialem?
question_en: With the blood of which creature are purple cloaks dyed, as the shellfish itself complains in Martial?
derivation: The murex furnished both the purple dye of Roman dress and a dish — 'you wear cloaks dyed in our blood, and, not content with that, we are food.' The double use is the checkable cultural fact.

author: Ovid
source_text: Este procul, vittae tenues, insigne pudoris, Quaeque tegis medios, instita longa, pedes.
question: Cuius rei insigne erant vittae tenues feminarum Romanarum?
question_en: Of what were the thin headbands (vittae) of Roman women the badge?
derivation: Dress-code fact: the vitta was the mark of the respectable (chaste) woman, which is why Ovid banishes it from his poem. Stated verbatim ('insigne pudoris'). Culturally salient Roman costume knowledge.

author: Ovid
source_text: Este procul, vittae tenues, insigne pudoris, Quaeque tegis medios, instita longa, pedes.
question: Quae pars vestis matronarum Romanarum pedes medios tegebat?
question_en: What part of the Roman matron's dress covered the middle of her feet?
derivation: The instita, the flounce sewn to the matron's stola reaching the feet, emblem of the married woman. Stated verbatim; canonical Roman dress fact.

author: Ovid
source_text: Nec te praetereat Veneri ploratus Adonis, Cultaque Iudaeo septima sacra Syro.
question: Quoto quoque die Iudaei sacra sua colunt, ut Ovidius significat?
question_en: Every how many days do the Jews keep their rites, as Ovid indicates?
derivation: The Jewish sabbath ('septima sacra' of the 'Syrian Jew') observed at Rome, listed among the regular gathering-days. Ethnographic-religious fact, culturally salient in Augustan Rome; 'septima sacra' verbatim.

author: Ovid
source_text: Et bene, quod cogit, si nolis, linea iungi, Quod tibi tangenda est lege puella loci.
question: Quae res in sedilibus Circi vicinos, etiam si nolint, iungi cogebat?
question_en: What on the Circus benches forced neighbors together, even unwilling?
derivation: The linea, the marked divisions of the narrow Circus seating, pressed spectators against each other 'by the law of the place'. Realia of Circus seating, stated verbatim ('cogit... linea iungi').

author: Ovid
source_text: At cum pompa frequens caelestibus ibit eburnis, Tu Veneri dominae plaude favente manu;
question: Quales deorum effigies in pompa Circensi ferebantur?
question_en: Of what material were the images of the gods carried in the Circus procession?
derivation: The pompa circensis opened the races with ivory statues of the gods borne in procession ('caelestibus... eburnis'). Canonical rite of the games; short material answer, verbatim.

author: Ovid
source_text: Tergaque Parthorum Romanaque pectora dicam, Telaque, ab averso quae iacit hostis equo. Qui fugis ut vincas, quid victo, Parthe, relinquis?
question: Quo more Parthi equites tela in hostes iaciunt?
question_en: In what manner do Parthian horsemen hurl their missiles at the enemy?
answer_en: While fleeing, from a turned-away horse.
derivation: The famous 'Parthian shot': the Parthians fight by feigned flight, shooting backwards from the retreating horse ('ab averso quae iacit hostis equo... qui fugis ut vincas'). Ethnographic fact every Roman knew.

author: Ovid
source_text: Luce deas caeloque Paris spectavit aperto, Cum dixit Veneri 'vincis utramque, Venus.'
question: Quae dea iudicio Paridis ambas aemulas formae vicit?
question_en: Which goddess, by the judgment of Paris, defeated both her rivals in beauty?
derivation: The judgment of Paris: Venus victorious over the other two goddesses ('vincis utramque, Venus'). Canonical myth, verbatim support; Ovid's point that Paris judged in daylight is the frame.

author: Ovid
source_text: Tum, cum tristis erat, defensa est Ilios armis: Militibus gravidum laeta recepit equum.
question: Quibus gravidus erat equus ligneus quem Ilios laeta recepit?
question_en: With what was the wooden horse pregnant which Troy joyfully received?
derivation: The Trojan horse 'pregnant with soldiers' ('militibus gravidum... equum'), received by rejoicing Troy. Canonical shared story; verbatim support.

author: Ovid
source_text: Cera vadum temptet, rasis infusa tabellis: Cera tuae primum conscia mentis eat.
question: Qua materia, rasis tabellis infusa, litterae amatoriae Romae scribebantur?
question_en: On what material, spread over smoothed tablets, were love-letters written at Rome?
derivation: Letter-writing realia: wax poured on planed wooden tabellae, the standard medium for (love-)letters. 'Cera... rasis infusa tabellis' verbatim.

author: Ovid
source_text: Hectora donavit Priamo prece motus Achilles; Flectitur iratus voce rogante deus.
question: Cui Achilles corpus Hectoris prece motus donavit?
question_en: To whom did Achilles, moved by prayer, give back the body of Hector?
derivation: The ransom of Hector: Achilles yields the body to Priam's supplication (Iliad 24), cited as shared story. All three names in the verbatim line.

author: Ovid
source_text: Interea, sive illa toro resupina feretur, Lecticam dominae dissimulanter adi,
question: Quo vehiculo dominae Romanae toro resupinae per urbem ferebantur?
question_en: In what conveyance were Roman ladies carried through the city, reclining on a couch?
derivation: The lectica, the curtained litter in which women were borne reclining — daily-life realia named verbatim ('toro resupina feretur, lecticam dominae').

author: Ovid
source_text: Huic, si sorte bibes, sortem concede priorem: Huic detur capiti missa corona tuo.
question: Quid capiti convivarum in conviviis Romanis imponi solebat?
question_en: What was customarily placed on the heads of guests at Roman banquets?
derivation: The banquet garland, passed along and set on the head ('detur capiti missa corona'), with drinking-turns settled by lot ('si sorte bibes') — table realia of the convivium.

author: Ovid
source_text: Turpe, nisi hoc matris precibus tribuisset, Achilles Veste virum longa dissimulatus erat.
question: Qua veste Achilles, matris precibus obsecutus, virum dissimulavit?
question_en: In what garment did Achilles, yielding to his mother's prayers, disguise his manhood?
derivation: Achilles hidden on Scyros in women's dress at Thetis' entreaty — canonical episode ('matris precibus... veste virum longa dissimulatus'). Anchored to Achilles; short answer verbatim.

author: Ovid
source_text: At non Actorides lectum temeravit Achillis: Quantum ad Pirithoum, Phaedra pudica fuit.
question: Quis heros, Actorides dictus, fidus Achilli sodalis fuit?
question_en: Which hero, called 'Actorides' (descendant of Actor), was Achilles' faithful companion?
derivation: Actorides = Patroclus (grandson of Actor through Menoetius), the loyal-friend exemplum who 'did not defile Achilles' bed'. Canonical patronymic identification; anchored to Achilles.

author: Ovid
source_text: Utque leves Proteus modo se tenuabit in undas, Nunc leo, nunc arbor, nunc erit hirtus aper.
question: Quis deus marinus modo in undas, modo in leonem arboremve aprumve se mutare fingitur?
question_en: Which sea god is imagined turning himself now into water, now into a lion, a tree, or a boar?
derivation: Proteus the shape-shifter, with the canonical list of his transformations. Verbatim support; single-name answer.

author: Ovid
source_text: Nunc mihi, siquando, puer et Cytherea, favete, Nunc Erato, nam tu nomen amoris habes.
question: Quae Musa nomen amoris habet, ut Ovidius eam invocans ait?
question_en: Which Muse bears the name of love, as Ovid says in invoking her?
derivation: Erato, the Muse whose name contains Eros/amor, invoked for love-poetry ('nam tu nomen amoris habes'). Shared literary-mythological knowledge; name answer verbatim.

author: Ovid
source_text: Daedalus ut clausit conceptum crimine matris Semibovemque virum semivirumque bovem,
question: Quod monstrum, crimine matris conceptum, Daedalus inclusit?
question_en: What monster, conceived by its mother's crime, did Daedalus shut in?
answer_en: The Minotaur, half-bull man and half-man bull.
derivation: Daedalus builder of the Minotaur's enclosure (the labyrinth); the proverb-famous line 'semibovemque virum semivirumque bovem' defines the monster of Pasiphae's crime. Canonical; verbatim.

author: Ovid
source_text: Ille levi virga (virgam nam forte tenebat) Quod rogat, in spisso litore pingit opus. 'Haec' inquit 'Troia est' (muros in litore fecit): 'Hic tibi sit Simois; haec mea castra puta.
question: Cui deae Ulixes Troiam Simoentaque virga in litore depinxit?
question_en: For which goddess did Ulysses draw Troy and the Simois with a staff on the beach?
derivation: The Calypso inset: she begs the tale of Troy again and again, and Ulysses sketches Troy, the Simois, and the camps in the sand ('in spisso litore pingit'). Calypso is named just above ('illic quoque pulchra Calypso exigit Odrysii fata cruenta ducis'); both entities canonical.

author: Ovid
source_text: Rure suburbano poteris tibi dicere missa, Illa vel in Sacra sint licet empta via.
question: In qua via Romae dona rustica emi poterant, quae e rure suburbano missa esse fingeres?
question_en: On what street in Rome could one buy 'country' gifts and pass them off as sent from a suburban farm?
derivation: The Sacra Via as a market street where produce and fancy goods were sold — Roman shopping topography ('vel in Sacra... empta via'); the deception-advice dropped, the venue-fact kept.

author: Ovid
source_text: Haec tamen audierat: Priameida viderat ipsa: Victor erat praedae praeda pudenda suae.
question: Quam Priami filiam Agamemnon victor praedam domum advexit?
question_en: Which daughter of Priam did the victorious Agamemnon bring home as his prize?
derivation: The 'Priameis' seen by Clytemnestra with her own eyes is Cassandra, Agamemnon's captive — canonical identification of the periphrasis; 'victor... praedae praeda' verbatim for the relationship.

author: Ovid
source_text: Duc, age, discipulos ad mea templa tuos, Est ubi diversum fama celebrata per orbem Littera, cognosci quae sibi quemque iubet.
question: Quid inscriptio illa, toto orbe celebrata, in templo Apollinis Delphici quemque facere iubet?
question_en: What does the world-famous inscription at Apollo's Delphic temple bid each person do?
derivation: The Delphic maxim 'know thyself' ('littera, cognosci quae sibi quemque iubet') at Apollo's temple — Apollo himself is the speaker ('mea templa'), and the Delphic setting is the canonical referent. Proverb of proverbs, verbatim in substance.

author: Ovid
source_text: Vix precibus, Neptune, tuis captiva resolvit Corpora: Mars Thracen occupat, illa Paphon.
question: Cuius dei precibus Vulcanus corpora Martis et Veneris captiva resolvit?
question_en: At which god's entreaties did Vulcan release the captive bodies of Mars and Venus?
derivation: Neptune's intercession freeing the trapped lovers — the Odyssey 8 detail kept by Ovid, verbatim ('precibus, Neptune, tuis').

author: Ovid
source_text: O bene, quod frustra captatis arbore pomis Garrulus in media Tantalus aret aqua!
question: Qua poena Tantalus apud inferos adficitur?
answer: In media aqua sitit et poma frustra captat.
question_en: With what punishment is Tantalus afflicted in the underworld?
answer_en: He thirsts in the midst of water and snatches in vain at the fruit.
derivation: The canonical torment of Tantalus — water and fruit forever out of reach — which Ovid moralizes as the punishment of the 'garrulus' who betrayed divine secrets. Verbatim.

author: Ovid
source_text: Nec suus Andromedae color est obiectus ab illo, Mobilis in gemino cui pede pinna fuit.
question: Quis heros, cui pinna mobilis in gemino pede fuit, Andromedam uxorem habuit?
question_en: Which hero, who had a swift wing on each foot, had Andromeda as his wife?
derivation: Perseus identified by his canonical attribute, the winged sandals ('in gemino... pede pinna'), as Andromeda's husband who never reproached her dark color. Periphrasis with one referent.

author: Ovid
source_text: Qui properant, nova musta bibant: mihi fundat avitum Consulibus priscis condita testa merum.
question: Quorum nominibus Romani vina condita notabant, ut vetustas constaret?
question_en: By whose names did the Romans mark their stored wines, so that the vintage's age was known?
derivation: Wine-jars dated by the consuls of the vintage year ('consulibus priscis condita testa') — the standard Roman vintage-dating custom, verbatim.

author: Ovid
source_text: Arma dedi vobis: dederat Vulcanus Achilli; Vincite muneribus, vicit ut ille, datis.
question: Quis deus Achilli arma dederat?
question_en: Which god had given Achilles his arms?
derivation: Vulcan the maker of Achilles' divine armor (Iliad 18), the comparison Ovid draws for his own 'arms'. Both names verbatim; canonical fact.

author: Ovid
source_text: Et famam pietatis habet, tamen hospes et ensem Praebuit et causam mortis, Elissa, tuae.
question: Quis hospes, pietatis fama notus, Elissae Didoni ensem causamque mortis praebuit?
question_en: Which guest, famed for his piety, furnished Elissa (Dido) with the sword and the cause of her death?
derivation: Dido ('Elissa', her Phoenician name, verbatim) dying by the sword of the guest 'famed for pietas' — the periphrasis can only be pius Aeneas. Canonical Aeneid fact seen from Ovid's angle.

author: Ovid
source_text: Dixit, et e myrto (myrto nam vincta capillos Constiterat) folium granaque pauca dedit;
question: Qua fronde Venus capillos vincire solet?
question_en: With what foliage does Venus customarily bind her hair?
derivation: The myrtle as Venus' sacred plant — she appears to Ovid with hair bound in myrtle and gives him a myrtle leaf and berries. Canonical attribute, verbatim.

author: Ovid
source_text: Quid de veste loquar? Nec vos, segmenta, requiro Nec te, quae Tyrio murice, lana, rubes.
question: Quo animali marino lana Tyria rubebat?
question_en: From what sea-creature did Tyrian wool get its red?
derivation: Tyrian purple dyed with the murex shellfish — the canonical luxury-dye fact ('Tyrio murice, lana, rubes'), dismissed by Ovid in favor of cheaper colors.

author: Ovid
source_text: Ille crocum simulat: croceo velatur amictu, Roscida luciferos cum dea iungit equos:
question: Quae dea, croceo amictu velata, luciferos equos iungit?
question_en: Which goddess, veiled in a saffron cloak, yokes the light-bringing horses?
derivation: The dawn-goddess in her canonical saffron robe ('croceo... amictu') yoking the horses of the light — the epic epithet crocea Aurora, here explaining the saffron dress-color. Periphrasis with one referent.

author: Ovid
source_text: Monstra maris Sirenes erant, quae voce canora Quamlibet admissas detinuere rates.
question: Qua re Sirenes, monstra maris, rates transeuntes detinebant?
question_en: By what did the Sirens, monsters of the sea, detain the passing ships?
derivation: The Sirens as sea-monsters whose song stopped any ship — canonical Odyssey lore stated as a definition. Verbatim.

author: Ovid
source_text: His sua Sisyphides auditis paene resolvit Corpora, nam sociis inlita cera fuit.
question: Qua re aures sociorum Ulixis contra cantum Sirenum munitae erant?
question_en: With what were the ears of Ulysses' companions sealed against the Sirens' song?
derivation: The wax in the comrades' ears while bound Ulysses ('Sisyphides' — the taunt that Sisyphus begot him) nearly broke free — canonical episode, verbatim ('sociis inlita cera').

author: Ovid
source_text: Nota sit et Sappho (quid enim lascivius illa?), Cuive pater vafri luditur arte Getae.
question: Quae poetria in indice legendorum Ovidii nota esse debet, qua nihil lascivius esse ait?
question_en: Which poetess must be known, in Ovid's reading list, than whom he says nothing is more wanton?
derivation: Sappho in the canon of love-reading, with Ovid's famous characterization 'quid enim lascivius illa?'. Name and judgment verbatim; literary-canon fact.

author: Ovid
source_text: Spectentur tepido maculosae sanguine harenae, Metaque ferventi circueunda rota.
question: Quid aurigae in Circo rota ferventi circueundum erat?
question_en: What did the charioteer in the Circus have to round with his glowing wheel?
derivation: The meta, the turning-post skimmed by the 'burning wheel' — the central hazard of the chariot race, verbatim; listed with the blood-stained arena among sights to see.

author: Ovid
source_text: Ad multas lupa tendit oves, praedetur ut unam, Et Iovis in multas devolat ales aves.
question: Quae avis 'Iovis ales' apud poetas Romanos dicitur?
question_en: Which bird is called 'the bird of Jove' by the Roman poets?
derivation: The eagle as Jupiter's bird — here the predator swooping on many birds; the periphrasis 'Iovis ales' presupposes the canonical identification asked. Shared attribute-lore.

author: Ovid
source_text: Vix mihi credetis, sed credite: Troia maneret, Praeceptis Priamo si foret usa satae.
question: Quae Priamo sata vera de Troia monuit, cuius praeceptis si usa esset, Troia maneret?
question_en: Which daughter of Priam gave true warnings about Troy, by whose counsels, had they been heeded, Troy would still stand?
derivation: Cassandra the unheeded prophetess — 'Troy would remain, had it used the counsels of Priam's daughter'. The periphrasis 'satae Priamo' has the one canonical referent; the unbelieved-prophecy fact is verbatim.

author: Ovid
source_text: Tempora digereret cum conditor Urbis, in anno constituit menses quinque bis esse suo.
question: Quot menses Romulus, conditor Urbis, in anno suo esse constituit, ut Ovidius in Fastis narrat?
question_en: How many months did Romulus, the founder of the City, establish in his year, as Ovid relates in the Fasti?
derivation: The famous calendar fact that the original Romulean year had ten months (quinque bis). Anchored to Romulus and the Roman calendar; single number answer supported verbatim. Ambient Roman calendar lore, the starting point of the whole poem.

author: Ovid
source_text: Martis erat primus mensis, Venerisque secundus; haec generis princeps, ipsius ille pater:
question: Cuius dei primus mensis in anno Romuli fuit?
question_en: To which god did the first month of Romulus' year belong?
