derivation: In Romulus' ten-month year the first month was March, named for Mars his father (the second for Venus, ancestress of the race). Anchored to Romulus' year; single divine name, stated verbatim. Core calendar lore.

author: Ovid
source_text: at Numa nec Ianum nec avitas praeterit umbras, mensibus antiquis praeposuitque duos.
question: Quis rex duos menses, Iano et umbris avitis sacros, mensibus antiquis Romanorum praeposuit?
question_en: Which king placed two months, sacred to Janus and to the ancestral shades, before the old Roman months?
derivation: Numa added January (for Janus) and February (for the dead) at the head of the ten old months. Anchored by the named months' gods; one royal name, supported verbatim. Standard Roman calendar history.

author: Ovid
source_text: vindicat Ausonias Iunonis cura Kalendas;
question: Cuius deae curae Kalendae omnium mensium apud Romanos vindicantur?
question_en: To the care of which goddess are the Kalends of every month claimed at Rome?
derivation: The Kalends of each month were sacred to Juno. Anchored to the Roman Kalends; one divine name, verbatim. Fundamental sacred-calendar lore.

author: Ovid
source_text: Iane biceps, anni tacite labentis origo, solus de superis qui tua terga vides,
question: Quis deus solus de superis sua terga videre dicitur?
question_en: Which god alone of the gods above is said to see his own back?
derivation: Janus' two faces mean he alone of the gods sees his own back. Anchored by the god's canonical iconography; single name answer, verbatim. Shared image of Roman religion.

author: Ovid
source_text: arx mea collis erat, quem volgo nomine nostro nuncupat haec aetas Ianiculumque vocat.
question: Qui collis Romanus a Iano deo nomen accepit?
question_en: Which Roman hill took its name from the god Janus?
derivation: The Janiculum was Janus' citadel and bears his name — the god says so himself. Anchored to Janus and Roman topography; one-name answer verbatim. Shared knowledge of the city's hills.

author: Ovid
source_text: verba fides sequitur: noxae tibi deditus hostis spargitur adfuso cornua, Bacche, mero.
question: Quo liquore cornua capri ad aram Bacchi sparguntur?
question_en: With what liquid are the goat's horns sprinkled at Bacchus' altar?
derivation: The rite fulfils the curse: wine is poured over the goat's horns at Bacchus' altar. Anchored to the same named sacrifice; one-word answer verbatim.

author: Ovid
source_text: at ruber, hortorum decus et tutela, Priapus omnibus ex illis Lotide captus erat:
question: Cuius rei decus et tutela Priapus deus habetur?
question_en: Of what is the god Priapus held to be the ornament and guardian?
derivation: Priapus' canonical office: guardian of gardens (his red statues stood in every Roman garden). Anchored to Priapus; one-word answer verbatim. Ambient daily-life religion.

author: Ovid
source_text: nec defensa iuvant Capitolia, quo minus anser det iecur in lances, Inachioti, tuas.
question: Quae avis Capitolia defendisse dicitur, ut Ovidius commemorat?
question_en: Which bird is said to have defended the Capitol, as Ovid recalls?
derivation: The celebrated legend of the geese that saved the Capitol from the Gauls, alluded to as common knowledge ('defensa Capitolia'). Anchored to the Capitol; one-word answer supported verbatim.

author: Ovid
source_text: sancte pater patriae, tibi plebs, tibi curia nomen hoc dedit, hoc dedimus nos tibi nomen, eques.
question: Quod nomen Nonis Februariis plebs, curia, equites Augusto dederunt, ut Ovidius in Fastis canit?
question_en: What title did the plebs, the senate, and the knights confer on Augustus on the Nones of February, as Ovid sings in the Fasti?
derivation: Ovid celebrates the Nones of February (5 Feb.) as the day Augustus received the title pater patriae from all three orders. Anchored to Augustus and the named day; title answer verbatim. Prime imperial-calendar fact.

author: Ovid
source_text: inde deum colimus devectaque sacra Pelasgis: flamen ad haec prisco more Dialis erat.
question: Qui flamen prisco more sacris Lupercalibus intererat, ut Ovidius refert?
question_en: Which flamen took part in the rites of the Lupercalia by ancient custom, as Ovid reports?
derivation: By old custom the flamen Dialis attended the Lupercalia — a specific, checkable cult detail. Anchored to the named festival and priesthood; one-word answer verbatim.

author: Ovid
source_text: venit ad expositos, mirum, lupa feta gemellos: quis credat pueris non nocuisse feram? non nocuisse parum est, prodest quoque. quos lupa nutrit, perdere cognatae sustinuere manus. constitit et cauda teneris blanditur alumnis, et fingit lingua corpora bina sua.
question: Quod animal geminos Romulum et Remum expositos nutrivit?
question_en: What animal nursed the exposed twins Romulus and Remus?
derivation: The she-wolf, newly whelped, suckled and licked the exposed twins — the most shared of all Roman images. Anchored to the twins; one-word answer verbatim.

author: Ovid
source_text: ultima Tarquinius Romanae gentis habebat regna, vir iniustus, fortis ad arma tamen.
question: Quis ultimus regum Romanorum fuit?
question_en: Who was the last of the Roman kings?
derivation: Tarquinius held the last kingship of the Roman race — unjust, though strong in war. Anchored to Rome's kings; one-name answer verbatim. Bedrock shared history.

author: Ovid
source_text: Tarquinius cum prole fugit: capit annua consul iura: dies regnis illa suprema fuit.
question: Quis magistratus, Tarquinio cum prole fugato, annua iura Romae cepit?
question_en: Which magistrate, once Tarquin and his offspring had fled, took up annual power at Rome?
derivation: The end of the monarchy: Tarquin flees with his brood, the consul takes annual office, and that day is the last of the kings — the fact the Regifugium commemorates. Anchored to the named king; office answer verbatim.

author: Ovid
source_text: Iamque duae restant noctes de mense secundo, Marsque citos iunctis curribus urget equos; ex vero positum permansit Equirria nomen, quae deus in campo prospicit ipse suo.
question: Cui deo Equirria, certamina equorum in campo eius acta, sacra sunt?
question_en: To which god are the Equirria sacred, the horse-races held on his own field?
derivation: The Equirria (27 Feb.): chariot-horse races that Mars himself beholds on his own field, the Campus Martius — the name 'truly given' from the races. Anchored to the named festival; one-name answer verbatim.

author: Ovid
source_text: neu dubites primae fuerint quin ante Kalendae Martis, ad haec animum signa referre potes. laurea flaminibus quae toto perstitit anno tollitur, et frondes sunt in honore novae; ianua tum regis posita viret arbore Phoebi; ante tuas fit idem, Curia prisca, fores.
question: Quo die laurea vetus a foribus regis flaminumque et Curiae priscae tollitur et frondes novae ponuntur?
question_en: On what day is the old laurel removed from the doors of the rex, the flamens, and the old Curia, and fresh boughs put up?
derivation: The annual renewal of the laurels on 1 March — Ovid's proof that March once opened the year ('primae... ante Kalendae Martis'). Anchored to the named doors and day; date answer supported verbatim.

author: Ovid
source_text: Vesta quoque ut folio niteat velata recenti, cedit ab Iliacis laurea cana focis. adde quod arcana fieri novus ignis in aede dicitur, et vires flamma refecta capit.
question: Quo die ignis novus in arcana Vestae aede fieri dicitur?
question_en: On what day is the new fire said to be kindled in the inner shrine of Vesta?
derivation: On 1 March Vesta's hearth receives fresh laurel and the sacred fire is renewed — another of Ovid's proofs that the year once began with March. Anchored to Vesta's shrine; date answer. Rite-fact of the state cult.

author: Ovid
source_text: is decies senos ter centum et quinque diebus iunxit et a pleno tempora quinta die.
question: Quot dies Caesar in anno esse constituit, ut Ovidius numerat?
question_en: How many days did Caesar fix in the year, as Ovid reckons?
derivation: Ovid's riddling arithmetic — ten times six (60) plus three hundred and five — gives the Julian year of 365 days (plus the part of a full day; the transmitted 'quinta' for the quarter-day is a known crux, so only the whole number is asked). Anchored to Caesar; number answer supported verbatim.

author: Ovid
source_text: dicite 'tu nobis lucem, Lucina, dedisti': dicite 'tu voto parturientis ades.'
question: Quae dea voto parturientis Romanae adesse invocatur?
question_en: Which goddess is invoked to attend the vow of a Roman woman in labor?
derivation: Juno Lucina, goddess of childbirth, invoked at the Matronalia ('tu voto parturientis ades'). Anchored by the birth-vow context; one-name answer verbatim. Ambient religion of every Roman household.

author: Ovid
source_text: Quis mihi nunc dicet quare caelestia Martis arma ferant Salii Mamuriumque canant?
question: Qui sacerdotes caelestia Martis arma per Urbem ferunt?
question_en: Which priests carry the heavenly arms of Mars through the City?
derivation: The Salii carry the ancilia, the 'heavenly arms' of Mars, in March. Anchored to Mars and his arms; one-name answer verbatim. Prime priesthood fact of the Roman year.

author: Ovid
source_text: 'reddita Saturno sors haec erat: "optime regum, a nato sceptris excutiere tuis." ille suam metuens, ut quaeque erat edita, prolem devorat, immersam visceribusque tenet.'
question: Quis deus, sortem timens qua a nato sceptris excuti debebat, prolem suam devorabat?
question_en: Which god, fearing the oracle that he would be cast from his scepter by a son, devoured his own offspring?
derivation: Saturn swallowed each child as it was born, because of the oracle that his son would dethrone him. Anchored to Saturn and the oracle; one-name answer verbatim. Canonical myth, the frame of the Curetes aition.

author: Ovid
source_text: veste latens saxum caelesti gutture sedit: sic genitor fatis decipiendus erat.
question: Quid Saturno pro Iove infante devorandum datum est?
question_en: What was given to Saturn to swallow in place of the infant Jupiter?
answer_en: A stone hidden in swaddling clothes.
derivation: Rhea's trick: a stone wrapped in cloth settled in the god's celestial gullet, and so the father was cheated of his fate. Anchored to Saturn and Jupiter; short answer verbatim. Canonical myth.

author: Ovid
source_text: ille precabatur, tonitru dedit omina laevo Iuppiter, et laevo fulmina missa polo.
question: Qua caeli parte Iuppiter Romulo urbem condenti tonitru et fulmina dedit?
question_en: From which side of the sky did Jupiter give thunder and lightning to Romulus as he founded the city?
derivation: Jupiter answered Romulus' foundation prayer with omens on the left — thunder and bolts from the left of the sky, the favorable side of Roman augury. Anchored to Romulus and Jupiter; one-word answer verbatim.

author: Ovid
source_text: stabat, ut ante patrem, lacrimis perfusus Achilles: sic flendus Peleus, si moreretur, erat. saepe manus aegras manibus fingebat amicis: morum, quos fecit, praemia doctor habet. oscula saepe dedit, dixit quoque saepe iacenti 'vive, precor, nec me, care, relinque, pater.'
question: Quis puer Chironem morientem tamquam patrem flevit, ab eo doctus?
question_en: Which boy wept for the dying Chiron as for a father, having been taught by him?
derivation: Achilles at Chiron's deathbed, calling his teacher 'father' - Chiron as the tutor of Achilles is shared myth (morum... doctor). Single-name answer verbatim.

author: Ovid
source_text: ex Ope Iunonem memorant Cereremque creatas semine Saturni; tertia Vesta fuit. utraque nupserunt, ambae peperisse feruntur; de tribus impatiens restitit una viri.
question: Quae de tribus Saturni filiabus sola, impatiens viri, virgo restitit?
question_en: Which of Saturn's three daughters alone remained a virgin, refusing a husband?
derivation: Of the three sisters, the other two married and bore children; Vesta alone withstood a husband - why virgins serve her. Single-name answer supported verbatim (tertia Vesta... restitit una).

author: Ovid
source_text: ignis inexstinctus templo celatur in illo: effigiem nullam Vesta nec ignis habet.
question: Quid in templo Vestae pro effigie celatur?
question_en: What is kept hidden in the temple of Vesta in place of any image?
derivation: The undying fire concealed within Vesta's temple, itself without effigy - the hearth as the goddess. Answer verbatim.

author: Ovid
source_text: nullaque dicetur vittas temerasse sacerdos hoc duce, nec viva defodietur humo: sic incesta perit, quia, quam violavit, in illam conditur: est Tellus Vestaque numen idem.
question: Quo supplicio sacerdos Vestae incesta perire solet?
question_en: By what punishment does an unchaste priestess of Vesta die?
answer_en: She is buried alive in the earth.
derivation: The famous penalty of the unchaste Vestal: burial alive, because she is laid into the very deity she violated - Tellus and Vesta being one. Answer verbatim (viva defodietur humo... in illam conditur).

author: Ovid
source_text: Ante mare et terras et quod tegit omnia caelum unus erat toto naturae vultus in orbe, quem dixere chaos: rudis indigestaque moles nec quicquam nisi pondus iners congestaque eodem non bene iunctarum discordia semina rerum.
question: Quo nomine, ut narrat Ovidius in primo Metamorphoseon libro, appellabatur ille unus naturae vultus, rudis indigestaque moles, ante mare et terras et caelum?
question_en: By what name, as Ovid tells in the first book of the Metamorphoses, was that single face of nature called — a rough and unordered mass — before sea and lands and sky existed?
derivation: The opening cosmogonic fact of the Metamorphoses: the primordial state was named Chaos (quem dixere chaos). Anchored to Ovid + Metamorphoses book 1; one-name answer supported verbatim; canonical shared myth every Latin reader carries.

author: Ovid
source_text: Nec caelo contenta suo est Iovis ira, sed illum caeruleus frater iuvat auxiliaribus undis.
question: Quis deus, frater Iovis, iram eius in diluvio auxiliaribus undis iuvit?
question_en: Which god, Jupiter's brother, aided his wrath in the flood with auxiliary waters?
derivation: Neptune ('caeruleus frater', the rector pelagi of the following lines) joins the flood with his waters — the standard identification of Jove's sea-god brother. Anchored to Jupiter + the flood; one-name answer.

author: Ovid
source_text: Ipse tridente suo terram percussit, at illa intremuit motuque vias patefecit aquarum.
question: Quo telo Neptunus terram percussit, ut vias aquarum diluvio patefaceret?
question_en: With what weapon did Neptune strike the earth, to open the ways of the waters for the flood?
derivation: Neptune strikes the earth with his trident and the waters break out — the god's canonical attribute in action. Anchored to Neptune + the flood; one-word answer verbatim (tridente suo).

author: Ovid
source_text: eque sagittifera prompsit duo tela pharetra diversorum operum: fugat hoc, facit illud amorem; quod facit, auratum est et cuspide fulget acuta, quod fugat, obtusum est et habet sub harundine plumbum.
question: Ex quo metallo factum erat telum Cupidinis quod amorem facit?
question_en: Of what metal was Cupid's arrow made that causes love?
derivation: Cupid's two arrows of opposite powers: the love-making one is golden and sharp. One of the most famous images in Latin poetry. Anchored to Cupid's arrows; one-word metal answer verbatim (quod facit, auratum est).

author: Ovid
source_text: eque sagittifera prompsit duo tela pharetra diversorum operum: fugat hoc, facit illud amorem; quod facit, auratum est et cuspide fulget acuta, quod fugat, obtusum est et habet sub harundine plumbum.
question: Quod metallum habet sub harundine telum Cupidinis quod amorem fugat?
question_en: What metal does Cupid's arrow that puts love to flight carry beneath its shaft?
derivation: The counterpart arrow: blunt and leaden, it repels love. Anchored to Cupid's arrows; one-word metal answer verbatim (obtusum est et habet sub harundine plumbum).

author: Ovid
source_text: Excipit hos volucrisque suae Saturnia pennis collocat et gemmis caudam stellantibus inplet.
question: In cuius avis pennis Iuno centum oculos Argi occisi collocavit?
question_en: On the feathers of what bird did Juno place the hundred eyes of the slain Argus?
answer_en: On the feathers of the peacock, her own bird.
derivation: The aetiology of the peacock's starry tail: Juno sets Argus's eyes on the feathers of 'her bird' — the peacock, Juno's canonical bird. Anchored to Juno + Argus; the identification volucris sua = pavo is the shared knowledge the question tests.

author: Petronius
source_text: Trimalchio, lautissimus homo. Horologium in triclinio et bucinatorem habet subornatum, ut subinde sciat quantum de vita perdiderit!
question: Quae duo instrumenta Trimalchio in triclinio suo habebat, ut quantum de vita perdidisset subinde sciret?
question_en: What two devices did Trimalchio keep in his dining room so that he might constantly know how much of his life he had lost?
derivation: One of the most famous introductory details of the Cena Trimalchionis: the clock and the liveried trumpeter in the triclinium. Anchored to the named Trimalchio; two-item answer supported verbatim. The Cena is canonical ambient knowledge for the well-read (criterion 8).

author: Petronius
source_text: Ad sinistram enim intrantibus non longe ab ostiarii cella canis ingens, catena vinctus, in pariete erat pictus superque quadrata littera scriptum CAVE CANEM.
question: Quae verba supra canem pictum in pariete domus Trimalchionis quadrata littera scripta erant?
question_en: What words were written in square capitals above the painted dog on the wall of Trimalchio's house?
derivation: The most famous single detail of the Satyricon: the painted chained dog with the warning CAVE CANEM at Trimalchio's entrance, matching the real mosaic from Pompeii. Anchored to Trimalchio's house; the two-word answer is quoted verbatim. Quintessential shared Roman daily-life knowledge.

author: Petronius
source_text: 'Munus tamen, inquit, tibi dedi — et ego tibi plodo. Computa, et tibi plus do quam accepi. Manus manum lavat.'
question: Quod proverbium de mutuis officiis Echion apud Petronium de munerario et populo profert?
question_en: What proverb about mutual services does Echion quote in Petronius concerning the giver of games and the people?
answer_en: 'One hand washes the other' (manus manum lavat).
derivation: The proverb manus manum lavat, preserved verbatim in Echion's speech — one of the most famous Latin sayings, here in its locus classicus. Anchored to Petronius as the attesting text; the three-word answer is quoted verbatim and its point survives translation.

author: Plautus
source_text: sive adeo aediles perfidiose cui duint, sirempse legem iussit esse Iuppiter, quasi magistratum sibi alterive ambiverit.
question: Qui magistratus Romani, ut prologus Amphitruonis innuit, palmam histrionibus in ludis dabant?
question_en: Which Roman magistrates, as the prologue of the Amphitruo implies, awarded the palm to actors at the games?
derivation: Roman theatrical institution poking through the Greek dress: the aediles ran the ludi and judged the prize (palma) for actors. Anchored to the Amphitruo prologue; one-office answer.

author: Plautus
source_text: regique Thebano Creoni regnum stabilivit suom.
question: Quis Thebis regnabat, cum Amphitruo contra Teloboas pugnaret, ut Plautus tradit?
question_en: Who was reigning at Thebes when Amphitruo fought the Teloboians, as Plautus records?
derivation: Creon as king of Thebes in the Amphitruo/Hercules saga — canonical myth-figure. Anchored to Thebes + the Teloboan war; one-name answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: Ecastor te experior quanti facias uxorem tuam.
question: Quod iusiurandum, quo solae mulieres Romanae utebantur, Alcumena matrona in Amphitruone Plauti profert?
question_en: What oath, used only by Roman women, does the matron Alcumena utter in Plautus' Amphitruo?
derivation: Gendered Roman oath usage evidenced in the text: the matrona swears 'ecastor' (by Castor), the women-only oath, while the men swear edepol/hercle. Roman speech-custom through the Greek mask; one-word answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: virtus praemium est optimum; virtus omnibus rebus anteit profecto: libertas salus vita res et parentes, patria et prognati tutantur, servantur: virtus omnia in sese habet, omnia adsunt bona quem penest virtus.
question: Quid Alcumena in Amphitruone Plauti praemium optimum esse et rebus omnibus anteire canit?
question_en: What does Alcumena in Plautus' Amphitruo sing is the best reward and surpasses all things?
derivation: Alcumena's celebrated canticum in praise of virtus — one of the most quoted moral tags in Plautus ('virtus praemium est optimum'). Anchored to Alcumena + the play; one-word answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: postquam in cunas conditust, devolant angues iubati deorsum in impluvium duo maximi: continuo extollunt ambo capita.
question: In quam partem aedium duo angues iubati in Amphitruone Plauti devolaverunt?
question_en: Into what part of the house did the two crested serpents fly down in Plautus' Amphitruo?
answer_en: Into the impluvium (the rain-basin of the atrium).
derivation: Roman realia through the Greek mask: the snakes descend into the impluvium — the rain-catching basin of the Roman atrium house, anachronistically placed in 'Thebes'. Also fixes the number (duo) and epithet (iubati). One-word answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: Iace, pater, talos, ut porro nos iaciamus. DEM. Maxime. te, Philaenium, mihi atque uxoris mortem. hoc Venerium est.
question: Quo nomine Demaenetus optimum talorum iactum appellat, cum in Asinaria Plauti talos iacit?
question_en: By what name does Demaenetus call the best throw of the knucklebones when he casts the dice in Plautus' Asinaria?
derivation: Roman gaming realia: the highest cast of the tali was the 'Venus' throw. Demaenetus names his winning cast 'Venerium.' Anchored to Demaenetus + Asinaria; one-word answer verbatim (hoc Venerium est).

author: Plautus
source_text: Post mediam aetatem qui media ducit uxorem domum, si eam senex anum praegnatem fortuito fecerit, quid dubitas, quin sit paratum nomen puero Postumus?
question: Quod nomen puero paratum esse Megadorus in Aulularia iocatur, quem senex ex anu uxore genuerit?
question_en: What name does Megadorus in the Aulularia joke is ready-made for a boy begotten by an old man on an aged wife?
derivation: Roman naming custom: Postumus, the cognomen for the late-born (or after-born) child, deployed as the punchline of Megadorus' joke about old men marrying. Anchored to Megadorus; one-name answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: Quid nunc? etiam mihi despondes filiam? Illis legibus, cum illa dote quam tibi dixi. Sponden ergo? Spondeo.
question: Quo verbo sollemni Euclio filiam suam Megadoro in Aulularia Plauti despondet?
question_en: With what solemn word does Euclio betroth his daughter to Megadorus in Plautus' Aulularia?
derivation: The Roman betrothal by sponsio — the formal question-and-answer 'sponden? / spondeo' — enacted on stage. Roman law of engagement through the Greek mask; one-word answer verbatim. Speaker tags stripped per normalization.

author: Plautus
source_text: Fiam, ut ego opinor, Hercules, tu autem Linus.
question: Quem musicae magistrum Hercules interfecit, quo mytho Pistoclerus paedagogo Lydo minatur apud Plautum in Bacchidibus?
question_en: Which music-teacher did Hercules kill, the myth by which Pistoclerus threatens his tutor Lydus in Plautus' Bacchides?
derivation: Myth as shared story: Hercules slew his lyre-teacher Linus; Pistoclerus warns Lydus he will play Hercules to Lydus' Linus. Anchored to the named characters + play; one-name answer supported by the source.

author: Plautus
source_text: Vlixem audivi fuisse aerumnosissimum, qui annis viginti errans a patria afuit.
question: Quot annos Vlixem errantem a patria afuisse Bacchidum versus memorat?
question_en: For how many years does a verse of the Bacchides recall that Ulysses wandered away from his homeland?
derivation: Myth as shared story: Ulysses' twenty-year absence from Ithaca, invoked as the type of the toil-worn wanderer. Anchored via the named hero; single-number answer supported verbatim (annis viginti).

author: Plautus
source_text: nam ego has tabellas obsignatas consignatas quas fero non sunt tabellae, sed equos quem misere Achivi ligneum.
question: Cui rei Troianae Chrysalus tabellas obsignatas comparat, quas ad Nicobulum fert, in cantico Troiano apud Plautum in Bacchidibus?
question_en: To what Trojan device does Chrysalus liken the sealed tablets he carries to Nicobulus, in the Trojan canticum of Plautus' Bacchides?
derivation: The central equation of the canticum: the sealed letter is the wooden horse the Achaeans sent, its written words the armed soldiers hidden inside. Myth as shared story and the play's celebrated set-piece; anchored to Chrysalus + the play; short answer supported verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: Epiust Pistoclerus: ab eo haec sumptae; Mnesilochus Sino est relictus.
question: Quis equum ligneum Troianum fabricatus est, cui Chrysalus Pistoclerum in cantico comparat apud Plautum in Bacchidibus?
question_en: Who built the Trojan wooden horse, the figure to whom Chrysalus likens Pistoclerus in the canticum of Plautus' Bacchides?
derivation: Myth as shared story: Epeus was the craftsman who built the wooden horse; Chrysalus equates Pistoclerus (from whom the tablets came) with Epeus. Anchored to the play's canticum; one-name answer supported by the text (Epiust Pistoclerus).

author: Plautus
source_text: o Troia, o patria, o Pergamum, o Priame periisti senex, qui misere male mulcabere quadringentis Philippis aureis.
question: Cui regi Troiano Chrysalus Nicobulum senem in cantico Troiano comparat apud Plautum in Bacchidibus?
question_en: To which Trojan king does Chrysalus liken the old Nicobulus in the Trojan canticum of Plautus' Bacchides?
derivation: The canticum's equation: the old man to be despoiled is Priam, his house Troy/Pergamum. Myth and the play's set-piece; anchored to the named characters + play; one-name answer supported verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: Mnesilochust Alexander, qui erit exitio rei patriae suae; is Helenam avexit, cuia causa nunc facio obsidium Ilio.
question: Quam mulierem Alexander avexisse dicitur, cuius causa obsidium Ilio fieri Chrysalus in cantico Troiano dicit, apud Plautum in Bacchidibus?
question_en: Which woman did Alexander (Paris) carry off, for whose sake Chrysalus says the siege of Ilium is waged, in the Trojan canticum of Plautus' Bacchides?
derivation: Myth as shared story: Paris (Alexander) abducted Helen, the cause of the Trojan war; Chrysalus casts Mnesilochus as Paris. Anchored to the play's canticum; one-name answer supported verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: Atridae duo fratres cluent fecisse facinus maxumum, quom Priami patriam Pergamum divina moenitum manu armis, equis, exercitu atque eximiis bellatoribus mille cum numero navium decumo anno post subegerunt.
question: Quoto anno Atridae Troiam (Pergamum) cepisse dicuntur, ut Chrysalus in cantico Troiano memorat apud Plautum in Bacchidibus?
question_en: In which year are the sons of Atreus said to have taken Troy (Pergamum), as Chrysalus recalls in the Trojan canticum of Plautus' Bacchides?
derivation: Myth as shared story: Troy fell to the Atridae in the tenth year of the war. Anchored to the play's canticum; number-answer supported verbatim (decumo anno).

author: Plautus
source_text: miles Menelaust, ego Agamemno, idem Vlixes Lartius.
question: Qui duo fratres Atridae Troiam ceperunt, quorum nomina Chrysalus militi et sibi in cantico attribuit, apud Plautum in Bacchidibus?
question_en: Which two brother sons of Atreus took Troy, whose names Chrysalus assigns to the soldier and to himself in the canticum of Plautus' Bacchides?
derivation: Myth as shared story: Agamemnon and Menelaus, the two Atridae who led the Greeks against Troy. Anchored to the play's canticum; two-name answer supported verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: Mnesilochus Sino est relictus, ellum non in busto Achilli, sed in lecto accubat.
question: Quem Graecum apud Troiam relictum, qui hostes falleret, Chrysalus Mnesilocho in cantico comparat apud Plautum in Bacchidibus?
question_en: Which Greek left behind at Troy to deceive the enemy does Chrysalus compare with Mnesilochus in the canticum of Plautus' Bacchides?
derivation: Myth as shared story: Sinon, the Greek left behind to persuade the Trojans to take the wooden horse; Chrysalus casts Mnesilochus as Sinon. Anchored to the play's canticum; one-name answer supported verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: ornamenta absunt: Aiacem, hunc cum vides, ipsum vides.
question: Quem heroem furentem, ornamentis tantum absentibus, Aristophontem ipsum esse Tyndarus apud Plautum in Captivis ait?
question_en: Which raving hero does Tyndarus in Plautus' Captivi say Aristophontes is in person, only the costume lacking?
derivation: Ajax as the proverbial stage madman of tragedy: seeing this man, you see Ajax himself, minus the theatrical costume (ornamenta). Myth + theater convention in one line; anchored to the named characters; one-name answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: Credo ecastor: nam uicinam neminem amo merito magis quam te.
question: Per quem deum mulieres apud Plautum iurare solent, ut Cleostrata et Myrrhina in Casina 'ecastor' et 'mecastor' usurpant?
question_en: By which god do women customarily swear in Plautus, as Cleostrata and Myrrhina use 'ecastor' and 'mecastor' in the Casina?
derivation: Mores/sociolinguistic realia: in Roman usage women swore by Castor (ecastor/mecastor), a gendered oath; here the matrons Cleostrata and Myrrhina use it. Anchored to the named play + characters; one-name answer supported (ecastor).

author: Plautus
source_text: Venus, de paulo paululum hoc tibi dabo haud lubenter. nam tibi amantes propitiantes vinum potantes danunt omnes, mihi haud saepe evenunt tales hereditates.
question: Cui deae amantes, cum vinum potant, propitiantes de eo dare solent, ut Leaena anus apud Plautum ait?
question_en: To which goddess do lovers, when they drink wine, customarily give a propitiating share, as the old woman Leaena says in Plautus?
derivation: Cult custom of lovers: a libation-share of the wine to Venus to win her favor — Leaena grudges the goddess even a drop. Religio of everyday love-cult, with the altar of Venus standing before the leno's door; one-name answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: Mulciber, credo, arma fecit quae habuit Stratippocles: travolaverunt ad hostis. Tum ille prognatus Theti sine perdat: alia apportabunt ei Nerei filiae.
question: Cuius deae marinae filius erat Achilles, cui, armis amissis, Nereides nova apportare poterant, ut Epidicus apud Plautum in Epidico iocatur?
question_en: Of which sea-goddess was Achilles the son, to whom the Nereids could bring new arms when his were lost, as Epidicus jokes in Plautus' Epidicus?
derivation: Myth as shared story: Achilles, son of the Nereid Thetis, had his arms forged by Mulciber (Vulcan); the Nereids his kin could resupply him. Epidicus applies the joke to Stratippocles. Anchored to the named myth + play; one-name answer supported by source (prognatus Theti).

author: Plautus
source_text: MED. Elleborum potabis faxo aliquos viginti dies.
question: Quod medicamentum medicus in Menaechmis Menaechmo, pro insano habito, per viginti fere dies potandum minatur?
question_en: What drug does the doctor in the Menaechmi threaten that Menaechmus, taken for a madman, will drink for some twenty days?
derivation: Hellebore, the proverbial cure for madness in antiquity, here prescribed for some twenty days. Ambient medical culture (elleborum as the madman's drink); anchored to the medicus + Menaechmus; one-word answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: Achillem orabo, aurum ut mihi det, Hector qui expensus fuit.
question: Cuius Troiani corpus auro expensum (id est redemptum) esse Charinus apud Plautum in Mercatore memorat?
question_en: Whose Trojan body does Charinus in Plautus' Mercator recall as having been ransomed for gold?
derivation: Myth as shared story: Hector's corpse was ransomed from Achilles for its weight in gold (Hector qui expensus fuit). Anchored to the named heroes + play; one-name answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: di penates meum parentum, familiai Lar pater, vobis mando, meum parentum rem bene ut tutemini.
question: Quibus dis domesticis Charinus, patria excedere parans, rem parentum suorum tutandam mandat apud Plautum in Mercatore?
question_en: To which household gods does Charinus, about to leave his homeland, entrust the safekeeping of his parents' estate in Plautus' Mercator?
answer_en: To the Penates and the household Lar.
derivation: Domestic-cult realia: the Penates and the Lar familiaris as the guardians of the household and its property. Anchored to Charinus + play; answer supported verbatim (di penates... Lar).

author: Plautus
source_text: nam isti quidem hercle orationi Oedipo opust coniectore, qui Sphingi interpres fuit.
question: Cuius monstri aenigma Oedipus solvit, ut Milphio in Poenulo Plauti memorat?
question_en: Whose riddle did Oedipus solve, as Milphio recalls in Plautus' Poenulus?
derivation: A myth-as-shared-story reference: Oedipus was the interpreter of the Sphinx's riddle. Anchored to Oedipus + the play; one-name answer supported verbatim (Oedipo... qui Sphingi interpres fuit). Canonical Greek myth carried by any well-read reader.

author: Plautus
source_text: Adibo hosce atque appellabo Punice. si respondebunt, Punice pergam loqui; si non, tum ad horum mores linguam vertero.
question: Qua lingua Hanno Poenus in Poenulo Plauti loqui incipit, cum in scaenam venit et homines alloquitur?
question_en: In what language does the Carthaginian Hanno begin to speak in Plautus' Poenulus, when he comes on stage and addresses the men?
derivation: The famous fact that Plautus put real Punic on the Roman stage: Hanno enters and speaks Punic (the longest surviving Punic text in literature). Anchored to Hanno + the play; one-word answer supported verbatim (appellabo Punice... Punice pergam loqui). Translatable as a fact about which language, not about the Punic words themselves.

author: Plautus
source_text: omnes ordine sub signis ducam legiones meas, avi sinistra, auspicio liquido atque ex mea sententia.
question: Qua avi, dextra an sinistra, auspicium prosperum esse Pseudolus, legiones suas ducturus, significat?
question_en: With the bird on which side, right or left, does Pseudolus, about to lead out his 'legions,' indicate that the auspices are favorable?
answer_en: With the bird on the left.
derivation: Roman augural realia in the slave's mock-triumphal language: in Roman practice the bird on the left (avis sinistra) is the favorable sign, paired here with auspicio liquido, 'a clear auspice.' Anchored to Pseudolus; short answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: Cererem te meliust quam Venerem sectarier: amori haec curat; tritico curat Ceres.
question: Cui rei Ceres dea curat, ut Sceparnio in Rudente Plauti ait, cum Venus amori curet?
question_en: What does the goddess Ceres look after, as Sceparnio says in Plautus' Rudens, while Venus looks after love?
derivation: The canonical division of divine provinces — Venus over love, Ceres over grain — stated as folk wisdom (the same pairing behind 'sine Cerere et Libero friget Venus'). Shared religious knowledge; anchored to the two named goddesses; one-word answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: spectatores, vos quoque ad cenam vocem, ni daturus nil sim neque sit quicquam pollucti domi, nive adeo vocatos credam vos esse ad cenam foras. verum si voletis plausum fabulae huic clarum dare, comissatum omnes venitote ad me ad annos sedecim.
question: Post quot annos Daemones spectatores comissatum ad se invitat in extremo Rudente Plauti?
question_en: After how many years does Daemones, at the very end of Plautus' Rudens, invite the spectators to come revel at his house?
answer_en: In sixteen years ('ad annos sedecim,' as he himself puts it).
derivation: The closing joke to the audience: applaud, and you are all invited to a party — sixteen years from now. A quotable epilogue-fact of the play's last lines; anchored to the play + speaker; one-number answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: adeunt, perquirunt quid sit causae ilico: alienum aes cogat an pararit praedium, uxorin sit reddenda dos divortio.
question: Quid uxori divortio facto reddendum esse apud Plautum in Sticho memoratur?
question_en: What is mentioned in Plautus' Stichus as having to be given back to a wife when a divorce takes place?
derivation: Legal realia embedded in Gelasimus' list of stock reasons for holding an auction: debts to be paid, an estate bought, or a dowry to be returned upon divorce — the actio rei uxoriae in everyday form. Anchored to the auction scene; one-word answer verbatim.

author: Plautus
source_text: simulque ad cursuram meditabor me ad ludos Olympios.
question: Ad quos ludos cursuram se meditari Pinacium puer citus iocatur?
question_en: For what games does the swift boy Pinacium joke that he is training himself in running?
derivation: The Olympic games and their footrace as shared Greek athletic culture, invoked by the running slave-boy. Anchored to Pinacium; short answer verbatim.

author: Pliny the Younger
source_text: C. Plinius Traiano imperatori. Tua quidem pietas, imperator sanctissime, optaverat, ut quam tardissime succederes patri; sed di immortales festinaverunt virtutes tuas ad gubernacula rei publicae quam susceperas admovere.
question: Ad quem imperatorem Plinius minor epistulas decimi libri suas direxit, a quo vicissim responsa accepit?
question_en: To which emperor did Pliny the Younger address his letters of the tenth book, and from whom he received replies in turn?
derivation: Addressee fact: the whole of Book X is the official correspondence between Pliny and the emperor Trajan; the salutations read 'C. Plinius Traiano imperatori' / 'Traianus Plinio', and 10.1 addresses Trajan as the new emperor who succeeded his (adoptive) father Nerva. Closed-book famous; entity-anchored to Pliny + Book X; single-name answer.

author: Pliny the Younger
source_text: Rursus, cum transissem in orarias nauculas, contrariis ventis retentus aliquanto tardius quam speraveram, id est XV Kal. Octobres, Bithyniam intravi.
question: In quam provinciam, a Traiano legatus missus, Plinius minor ante diem quintum decimum Kalendas Octobres ingressus est?
question_en: Into which province, sent as Trajan's legate, did Pliny the Younger enter on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of October (17 September)?
derivation: Province fact: Pliny governed the province of Bithynia (and Pontus) as Trajan's special legate; he records 'Bithyniam intravi' on a.d. XV Kal. Oct. Answer supported verbatim. Closed-book famous (Pliny's governorship of Bithynia). The full province was Bithynia et Pontus (cf. 10.108 'Bithynas et Ponticas civitates', 10.112 'Bithyni et Pontici').

author: Pliny the Younger
source_text: Cognitionibus de Christianis interfui numquam: ideo nescio quid et quatenus aut puniri soleat aut quaeri.
question: Cuius generis hominum cognitionibus se numquam interfuisse Plinius minor Traiano scribens fatetur?
question_en: At the trials of what kind of people does Pliny the Younger, writing to Trajan, confess he had never been present?
derivation: The famous letter 10.96, in which Pliny consults Trajan on how to handle Christians, opens by admitting he had never attended cognitiones de Christianis. Entity-anchored (Pliny + Christians), short answer supported verbatim, closed-book famous.

author: Pliny the Younger
source_text: Nubes — incertum procul intuentibus ex quo monte; Vesuvium fuisse postea cognitum est — oriebatur, cuius similitudinem et formam non alia magis arbor quam pinus expresserit.
question: Ex quo monte nubem illam ortam esse postea cognitum esse Plinius tradit?
question_en: From which mountain does Pliny report it was afterwards recognized that the cloud had risen?
derivation: The eruption mountain: 'Vesuvium fuisse postea cognitum est.' Closed-book famous; entity-anchored, single place answer; the canonical fact of the letter.

author: Pliny the Younger
source_text: Nubes — incertum procul intuentibus ex quo monte; Vesuvium fuisse postea cognitum est — oriebatur, cuius similitudinem et formam non alia magis arbor quam pinus expresserit. Nam longissimo velut trunco elata in altum quibusdam ramis diffundebatur.
question: Cui arbori potissimum similem fuisse nubem e Vesuvio ortam Plinius scribit?
question_en: To what tree above all does Pliny say the cloud that rose from Vesuvius was most similar?
derivation: Famous simile: the eruption column shaped 'non alia magis arbor quam pinus' — a long trunk spreading into branches at the top (umbrella pine). Translatable (a tree, not wordplay), entity-anchored, short answer; one of the best-known images in Latin literature.

author: Pliny the Elder
source_text: orbem certe dicimus terrae globumque verticibus includi fatemur.
question: Quam figuram terrae ipsius esse Plinius adfirmat?
question_en: What shape does Pliny affirm the earth itself to have?
answer_en: The shape of a globe (a sphere).
derivation: The roundness of the earth: Pliny says we call it the orb of the earth and admit it is a globe enclosed by poles, and elsewhere argues it from ships vanishing over the horizon (2.164) and the rounding of water. Entity-anchored to the earth; short answer (a sphere) supported verbatim by orbem... terrae globumque. Indirect statement governed by adfirmat. Closed-book: the sphericity of the earth is a textbook tenet of ancient cosmology.

author: Pliny the Elder
source_text: Hanc ergo formam eius aeterno et inrequieto ambitu, inenarrabili celeritate, viginti quattuor horarum spatio circumagi solis exortus et occasus haut dubium reliquere.
question: Quot horarum spatio totum mundum semel circumagi Plinius tradit?
question_en: In how many hours does Pliny say the whole world turns around once?
answer_en: In the space of twenty-four hours.
derivation: Number fact: the heaven/world completes one rotation in 24 hours (sunrise to sunrise). Entity-anchored to the mundus; single numeric answer supported verbatim by viginti quattuor horarum spatio circumagi. Indirect statement (mundum circumagi) governed by tradit. Closed-book: the daily rotation of the celestial sphere is a commonplace of ancient (geocentric) astronomy.

author: Pliny the Elder
source_text: apud Graecos autem investigavit primus omnium Thales Milesius Olympiadis XLVIII anno quarto praedicto solis defectu, qui Alyatte rege factus est urbis conditae anno CLXX.
question: Quis Graecorum primus solis defectum praedixisse a Plinio traditur?
question_en: Which of the Greeks is recorded by Pliny as the first to have predicted a solar eclipse?
derivation: The famous prediction of a solar eclipse by Thales of Miletus (in the reign of Alyattes). Entity-anchored to the Greeks; single named answer supported verbatim by investigavit primus omnium Thales Milesius... praedicto solis defectu. Nominativus cum infinitivo (Thales praedixisse traditur). Closed-book and iconic in the history of science.

author: Pliny the Elder
source_text: Pyrenaei montes Hispanias Galliasque disterminant promunturiis in duo diversa maria proiectis.
question: Qui montes Hispanias Galliasque inter se disterminant secundum Plinium?
question_en: Which mountains separate the Spains from the Gauls, according to Pliny?
derivation: Boundary fact: the Pyrenees divide Spain from Gaul. Two named regions, one mountain-range answer supported verbatim. Closed-book, textbook geography.

author: Pliny the Elder
source_text: fluvius Rubico, quondam finis Italiae.
question: Qui fluvius quondam finis Italiae fuisse a Plinio dicitur?
question_en: Which river does Pliny say was once the boundary of Italy?
derivation: The Rubicon as the former boundary of Italy (proper). Single named-river answer supported verbatim by Rubico, quondam finis Italiae. Closed-book and iconic (Caesar's crossing).

author: Pliny the Elder
source_text: a quo VII p. introrsus liberum oppidum Delphi sub monte Parnaso, clarissimi in terris oraculi Apollinis.
question: Sub quo monte oppidum Delphi, cum clarissimo Apollinis oraculo, situm esse Plinius tradit?
question_en: Under which mountain does Pliny say the town of Delphi, with its most famous oracle of Apollo, is situated?
derivation: The location of Delphi, seat of the most famous oracle of Apollo, beneath Mount Parnassus. Anchored to Delphi plus Apollo's oracle; single named-mountain answer supported verbatim by Delphi sub monte Parnaso. Closed-book, iconic. Indirect statement oppidum situm esse governed by tradit.

author: Pliny the Elder
source_text: Sed iure laudetur in litore Aegyptii maris Alexandria, a Magno Alexandro condita in Africae parte ab ostio Canopico XII p. iuxta Mareotim lacum, qui locus antea Rhacotes nominabatur.
question: A quo Alexandria in Aegypto condita esse a Plinio traditur?
question_en: By whom does Pliny say Alexandria in Egypt was founded?
derivation: Founder fact: Alexander the Great founded Alexandria. Anchored to the city; single named-founder answer (ablative of agent) supported verbatim by Alexandria, a Magno Alexandro condita. Nominativus cum infinitivo governed by traditur; closed-book and iconic.

author: Pliny the Elder
source_text: ac magis etiamnum meridiana Babylonia, eadem Mesopotamia inter Euphraten et Tigrin.
question: Inter quae duo flumina regionem Mesopotamiam sitam esse Plinius tradit?
question_en: Between which two rivers does Pliny say the region of Mesopotamia lies?
answer_en: Between the Euphrates and the Tigris.
derivation: Mesopotamia lies between the Euphrates and the Tigris. Anchored to the named region; two-river answer supported verbatim by Mesopotamia inter Euphraten et Tigrin. Indirect statement (Mesopotamiam sitam esse) governed by tradit; closed-book (the very meaning of 'Mesopotamia').

derivation: Augustus countermanded Vergil's testamentary wish that his poems (the Aeneid) be burned. Single named answer supported verbatim (Divus Augustus carmina Vergili cremari ... vetuit); closed-book and iconic in literary history.

question: Quem unum Marcellus, captis Syracusis, violari vetuit, ut Plinius tradit?
question_en: Whom alone did Marcellus forbid to be harmed when Syracuse was captured, according to Pliny?
derivation: When Syracuse fell, Marcellus ordered that Archimedes alone be spared (he was nonetheless killed through a soldier's ignorance). Two recognizable entities, single named answer (Archimedes) supported verbatim by ne violarentur unus. Closed-book and famous.

question: Cuius artificis opus est Iuppiter Olympius, ut Plinius tradit?
question_en: Whose work is the Olympian Jupiter (Zeus), according to Pliny?
derivation: The chryselephantine Olympian Zeus (one of the Seven Wonders) is the work of Phidias; Pliny says it bears daily witness to his skill. Single named answer supported verbatim (Phidiae Iuppiter Olympius cotidie testimonium perhibet); closed-book and iconic.

author: Suetonius
source_text: Patris patriae cognomen universi repentino maximoque consensu detulerunt ei.
question: Quod cognomen Augusto universi consensu detulerunt?
question_en: What title did all by consensus confer on Augustus?
derivation: Supported by 'Patris patriae cognomen universi ... detulerunt ei' (conferred 2 BC, through Valerius Messala). Iconic title, entity-anchored, single answer.

author: Suetonius
source_text: Incitato equo, cuius causa pridie circenses, ne inquietaretur, uiciniae silentium per milites indicere solebat, praeter equile marmoreum et praesaepe eburneum praeterque purpurea tegumenta ac monilia e gemmis domum etiam et familiam et supellectilem dedit, quo lautius nomine eius inuitati acciperentur; consulatum quoque traditur destinasse.
question: Quem honorem C. Caesar equo suo Incitato destinasse traditur?
question_en: What office is Gaius Caesar said to have intended for his horse Incitatus?
derivation: Iconic story: his horse Incitatus, lavished with a marble stable and ivory manger, whom he is said to have meant to make consul. Supported verbatim ('consulatum quoque traditur destinasse'). Indirect statement (destinasse) under traditur; entity-anchored to Caligula and Incitatus; single-office answer; closed-book.

author: Suetonius
source_text: Cum decretis sibi a senatu ornamentis triumphalibus leviorem maiestati principali titulum arbitraretur velletque iusti triumphi decus, unde adquireret Britanniam potissimum elegit, neque temptatam ulli post Diuum Iulium et tunc tumultuantem ob non redditos transfugas.
question: Quam insulam Claudius, post Diuum Iulium a nullo temptatam, expeditione sua in deditionem recepit?
question_en: Which island, untried by anyone since the deified Julius, did Claudius receive in surrender by his expedition?
derivation: Claudius's annexation of Britain, his sole military expedition, supported by 'unde adquireret Britanniam potissimum elegit, neque temptatam ulli post Diuum Iulium.' Place answer, anchored to Claudius and Julius Caesar; iconic closed-book fact.

author: Suetonius
source_text: Contra senatus adeo laetatus est, ut repleta certatim curia non temperaret, quin mortuum contumeliosissimo atque acerbissimo adclamationum genere laceraret, scalas etiam inferri clipeosque et imagines eius coram detrahi et ibidem solo affligi iuberet, novissime eradendos ubique titulos abolendamque omnes memoriam decerneret.
question: Quid senatus de Domitiano occiso decrevit, titulos eius ubique eradi iubens?
question_en: What did the senate decree about the slain Domitian, ordering his inscriptions to be erased everywhere?
answer_en: That all memory of him be abolished (the damnatio memoriae).
derivation: Historical fact: the senate rejoiced at Domitian's death and decreed his inscriptions erased and all memory of him abolished (damnatio memoriae). Supported verbatim by 'novissime eradendos ubique titulos abolendamque omnes memoriam decerneret.' Entity-anchored to the senate + Domitian; short noun-phrase answer; closed-book.

author: Suetonius
source_text: Progenies Caesarum in Nerone defecit; quod futurum, compluribus quidem signis, sed vel evidentissimis duobus apparuit.
question: In quo principe progeniem Caesarum defecisse Suetonius initio Vitae Galbae tradit?
question_en: In which emperor does Suetonius, at the start of the Life of Galba, report that the line of the Caesars came to an end?
derivation: The famous opening sentence of the Life. Entity-anchored to the Caesars and Nero; single-name answer supported verbatim by 'Progenies Caesarum in Nerone defecit.' Indirect statement (progeniem ... defecisse) governed by tradit. Closed-book: the Julio-Claudian line ended with Nero (AD 68), one of the most-quoted lines of this Life.

author: Suetonius (Vita Horati)
source_text: Scripta quidem eius usque adeo probavit mansuraque perpetuo opinatus est, ut non modo Saeculare carmen componendum iniunxerit sed et Vindelicam victoriam Tiberii Drusique, privignorum suorum, eumque coegerit propter hoc tribus Carminum libris ex longo intervallo quartum addere;
question: Quod carmen Augustus Horatio componendum iniunxit?
question_en: What poem did Augustus charge Horace with composing?
derivation: Commission fact, supported verbatim ('Saeculare carmen componendum iniunxerit'); the subject of 'iniunxerit' is Augustus, established in the preceding context. Anchored to Augustus and Horace; that Augustus commissioned the Carmen Saeculare for the Secular Games is a canonical, closed-book fact.

author: Suetonius
source_text: et in amitae quidem laudatione de eius ac patris sui utraque origine sic refert: 'Amitae meae Iuliae maternum genus ab regibus ortum, paternum cum diis inmortalibus coniunctum est. nam ab Anco Marcio sunt Marcii Reges, quo nomine fuit mater; a Venere Iulii, cuius gentis familia est nostra.'
question: A qua dea gentem Iuliam ortam esse Caesar in laudatione amitae suae Iuliae adfirmavit?
question_en: From which goddess did Caesar declare the gens Iulia descended, in the eulogy of his aunt Iulia?
derivation: From Caesar's funeral oration for his aunt Iulia (covers the aunt-Iulia ask). Indirect statement (gentem...ortam esse) under adfirmavit. Anchored to gens Iulia + Venus; single named answer, supported verbatim. Iconic (Venus Genetrix).

author: Suetonius
source_text: Deposita prouinciae spe pontificatum maximum petit non sine profusissima largitione; in qua reputans magnitudinem aeris alieni, cum mane ad comitia descenderet, praedixisse matri osculanti fertur domum se nisi pontificem non reuersurum. atque ita potentissimos duos competitores multumque et aetate et dignitate antecedentes superauit, ut plura ipse in eorum tribubus suffragia quam uterque in omnibus tulerit.
question: Quod sacerdotium amplissimum Caesar, duobus potentioribus competitoribus superatis, adeptus est?
question_en: Which supreme priesthood did Caesar obtain, defeating two more powerful competitors?
derivation: Office fact, anchored to Caesar; he won the pontificatus maximus over two older, more distinguished rivals. Single named answer supported verbatim. Closed-book.

author: Suetonius
source_text: Igitur cum Bibulo consul creatur.
question: Quo collega Caesar primum consulatum gessit?
question_en: With which colleague did Caesar hold his first consulship?
derivation: Colleague fact: Caesar's first consulship was shared with Bibulus (praenomen Marcus given earlier in the same chapter, 'Marcoque Bibulo'). Anchored to Caesar + consulship; iconic ('Iulius and Caesar' joke that follows). Single named answer.

author: Suetonius
source_text: consecutusque cohortis ad Rubiconem flumen, qui prouinciae eius finis erat, paulum constitit, ac reputans quantum moliretur, conuersus ad proximos: 'etiam nunc,' inquit, 'regredi possumus; quod si ponticulum transierimus, omnia armis agenda erunt.'
question: Quod flumen prouinciae Caesaris finis erat, quo transito ille bellum ciuile incohavit?
question_en: Which river was the boundary of Caesar's province, by crossing which he began the civil war?
derivation: Geography/event fact: the Rubicon was the boundary of Caesar's province and the river of the civil war's start. Anchored to Caesar + province boundary; single named answer supported verbatim. Iconic.

author: Suetonius
source_text: tunc Caesar: 'eatur,' inquit, 'quo deorum ostenta et inimicorum iniquitas uocat. Iacta alea est,' inquit. atque ita traiecto exercitu, adhibitis tribunis plebis, qui pulsi superuenerant, pro contione fidem militum flens ac ueste a pectore discissa inuocauit.
question: Quod dictum Caesari tribuitur, cum exercitum trans Rubiconem traiceret?
question_en: What saying is attributed to Caesar as he led his army across the Rubicon?
derivation: Famous saying, anchored to Caesar + Rubicon crossing. Fact-seeking 'what did he say'; translatable ('the die is cast'); verbatim in source. Closed-book and iconic.

author: Suetonius
source_text: Pontico triumpho inter pompae fercula trium uerborum praetulit titulum veni : vidi : vici non acta belli significantem sicut ceteris, sed celeriter confecti notam.
question: Quem titulum trium uerborum Caesar in triumpho Pontico inter pompae fercula praetulit?
question_en: What three-word placard did Caesar display among the floats at his Pontic triumph?
answer_en: 'I came, I saw, I conquered' (veni, vidi, vici).
derivation: The Pharnaces-victory dispatch, anchored to Caesar + Pontic triumph. Verbatim three-word answer; translatable; iconic. Closed-book.

author: Suetonius
source_text: Conuersus hinc ad ordinandum rei publicae statum fastos correxit iam pridem uitio pontificum per intercalandi licentiam adeo turbatos, ut neque messium feriae aestate neque uindemiarum autumno conpeterent; annumque ad cursum solis accommodauit, ut trecentorum sexaginta quinque dierum esset et intercalario mense sublato unus dies quarto quoque anno intercalaretur.
question: Quot dierum annum Caesar, fastos corrigens, ad cursum solis accommodavit?
question_en: To how many days did Caesar set the year when, reforming the calendar, he adjusted it to the course of the sun?
derivation: Calendar-reform fact (the Julian calendar), anchored to Caesar. Single number answer (365 days; intercalary day every fourth year) supported verbatim. Closed-book, iconic.

author: Suetonius
source_text: atque ita tribus et uiginti plagis confossus est uno modo ad primum ictum gemitu sine uoce edito, etsi tradiderunt quidam Marco Bruto irruenti dixisse: kai su teknon
question: Quid Caesar Marco Bruto irruenti dixisse a quibusdam traditur?
question_en: What do some report Caesar said to Marcus Brutus as he rushed at him?
answer_en: 'Kai su, teknon' ('You too, child', in Greek).
derivation: Reported last words to Brutus, in Greek, attributed ('tradiderunt quidam'), anchored to Caesar + Marcus Brutus. Verbatim quote; fact-seeking 'what did he say'. Closed-book, iconic.

author: Suetonius
source_text: Gadisque uenisset, animaduersa apud Herculis templum Magni Alexandri imagine ingemuit et quasi pertaesus ignauiam suam, quod nihil dum a se memorabile actum esset in aetate, qua iam Alexander orbem terrarum subegisset.
question: Cuius imagine apud Herculis templum Gadibus conspecta Caesar ingemuit?
question_en: At whose statue, seen in the temple of Hercules at Gades, did Caesar sigh?
derivation: Iconic episode, anchored to Caesar + Gades + temple of Hercules; he sighed before Alexander's statue. Single named answer supported verbatim. Closed-book.

author: Suetonius
source_text: Pompeioque Marcum Crassum reconciliauit ueterem inimicum ex consulatu, quem summa discordia simul gesserant; ac societatem cum utroque iniit, ne quid ageretur in re publica, quod displicuisset ulli e tribus.
question: Cum quibus duobus uiris Caesar societatem iniit, ne quid in re publica ageretur ulli e tribus displicens?
question_en: With which two men did Caesar form an alliance, so that nothing should be done in the state displeasing to any of the three?
derivation: The First Triumvirate, anchored to Caesar; he reconciled Pompey and Crassus and joined both in a pact. Named answer supported verbatim. Closed-book, iconic.

author: Suetonius
source_text: sed maxime Cleopatram ... quam denique accitam in urbem non nisi maximis honoribus praemiisque auctam remisit filiumque natum appellare nomine suo passus est.
question: Cuius reginae filium Caesar nomine suo appellari passus est?
question_en: Whose son did Caesar allow to be called by his own name?
derivation: Relation fact, anchored to Caesar + Cleopatra; he allowed her son to bear his name (Caesarion). Single named answer supported verbatim. Closed-book.

author: Suetonius
source_text: quae si qui inuestigare et persequi uelit, quartam elementorum litteram, id est D pro A et perinde reliquas commutet.
question: Quam litteram Caesar in notis suis pro A scribebat?
question_en: Which letter did Caesar write in place of A in his cipher?
derivation: The 'Caesar cipher' fact, anchored to Caesar; in his secret letters he substituted the fourth letter, D, for A. Single answer supported verbatim; translatable (a shift cipher). Closed-book, iconic.

author: Suetonius
source_text: continuum consulatum, perpetuam dictaturam praefecturamque morum, insuper praenomen Imperatoris.
question: Cuius generis dictaturam Caesar recepit?
question_en: What kind of dictatorship did Caesar receive?
derivation: Office fact, anchored to Caesar; he was made dictator in perpetuity (perpetua dictatura). Single answer supported verbatim. Closed-book, iconic.

author: Suetonius
source_text: Non in alia re tamen damnosior quam in aedificando domum a Palatio Esquilias usque fecit, quam primo transitoriam, mox incendio absumptam restitutamque auream nominavit.
question: Quo nomine Nero domum suam ingentem a Palatio ad Esquilias porrectam appellavit?
question_en: By what name did Nero call his huge house stretching from the Palatine to the Esquiline?
derivation: Supported by 'auream nominavit'. The Domus Aurea, his palace from the Palatine to the Esquiline. Entity-anchored to Nero, short name answer, closed-book famous.

author: Suetonius
source_text: Senecam praeceptorem ad necem compulit, quamvis saepe commeatum petenti bonisque cedenti persancte iurasset suspectum se frustra periturumque potius quam nociturum ei.
question: Quem praeceptorem suum Nero ad necem compulit?
question_en: Which of his teachers did Nero force to his death?
derivation: Supported by 'Senecam praeceptorem ad necem compulit', which names Seneca both as Nero's teacher (praeceptor) and as forced to suicide. Entity-anchored, single-name answer, closed-book famous.

author: Suetonius
source_text: Capreas se contulit, praecipue delectatus insula, quod uno paruoque litore adiretur, saepta undique praeruptis immensae altitudinis rupibus et profundo mari.
question: In quam insulam Tiberius se contulit, ubi reliquam uitam in secessu egit?
question_en: To which island did Tiberius betake himself, where he spent the rest of his life in seclusion?
derivation: Tiberius's later withdrawal to Capri, supported by 'Capreas se contulit, praecipue delectatus insula.' Entity-anchored, single place answer, closed-book and iconic.

author: Suetonius
source_text: Cuius brevi compos, et ad perdomandam Iudaeam relictus, novissima Hierosolymorum oppugnatione duodecim propugnatores totidem sagittarum confecit ictibus, cepitque ea natali filiae suae tanto militum gaudio ac favore, ut in gratulatione imperatorem eum consalutaverint.
question: Quam urbem Titus, ad perdomandam Iudaeam relictus, novissima oppugnatione cepit?
question_en: Which city did Titus, left to subdue Judaea, capture in the final assault?
derivation: The famous conquest: Titus took Jerusalem in the final assault of the Jewish war (AD 70). Supported by 'novissima Hierosolymorum oppugnatione ... cepitque ea.' Entity-anchored to Titus + Jerusalem; single-place answer; closed-book.

author: Suetonius
source_text: Et tamen nemine ante se munificentia minor, amphitheatro dedicato thermisque iuxta celeriter exstructis, munus edidit apparatissimum largissimusque; dedit et navale proelium in veteri naumachia, ibidem et gladiatores atque uno die quinque milia omne genus ferarum.
question: Quod opus Titus dedicavit, thermis iuxta celeriter exstructis, cum munus apparatissimum ederet?
question_en: What structure did Titus dedicate, with baths quickly built nearby, when he gave a most lavish show?
answer_en: The amphitheatre (the Flavian Amphitheatre, the Colosseum).
derivation: Building fact: Titus dedicated the amphitheatre (the Colosseum) and built adjacent baths. Supported verbatim by 'amphitheatro dedicato thermisque iuxta celeriter exstructis.' Entity-anchored to Titus; single-answer; the most famous act of his reign.

author: Suetonius
source_text: Quaedam sub eo fortuita ac tristia acciderunt, ut conflagratio Vesevi montis in Campania, et incendium Romae per triduum totidemque noctes, item pestilentia quanta non temere alias.
question: Qui mons in Campania sub Tito principe conflagravit?
question_en: Which mountain in Campania erupted during the reign of Titus?
derivation: The eruption of Vesuvius (AD 79), the great disaster of Titus's reign. Supported verbatim by 'conflagratio Vesevi montis in Campania.' Entity-anchored to Titus's reign + Campania; single-place answer; closed-book. (source_text keeps the Latin Library spelling 'Vesevi' for 'Vesuvii'.)

author: Suetonius (Vita Vergilii)
source_text: Deinde scripsit 'Georgica' in honorem Maecenatis, qui sibi mediocriter adhuc noto opem tulisset adversus veterani cuiusdam violentiam.
question: In cuius honorem Vergilius Georgica scripsit?
question_en: In whose honor did Vergil write the Georgics?
derivation: Dedicatee fact, supported verbatim ('Georgica in honorem Maecenatis'). Anchored to Vergil and the Georgica, single-name answer, closed-book.

author: Suetonius (Vita Vergilii)
source_text: 'Aeneida' prosa prius oratione formatam digestamque in XII libros particulatim componere instituit.
question: In quot libros Vergilius Aeneida digessit?
question_en: Into how many books did Vergil arrange the Aeneid?
derivation: Number fact, supported verbatim ('digestam ... in XII libros'). Anchored to Vergil and the Aeneid, single number answer, closed-book.

author: Suetonius (Vita Vergilii)
source_text: Mantua me genuit, Calabri rapuere, tenet nunc Parthenope; cecini pascua rura duces.
question: Quae tria se cecinisse Vergilius in epitaphio suo dicit?
question_en: What three things does Vergil say in his epitaph that he sang?
answer_en: Pastures, fields, and leaders (the Eclogues, Georgics, and Aeneid).
derivation: The famous epitaph ('Mantua me genuit ...') names his three works as 'pascua rura duces.' Supported verbatim, short list answer; the line is iconic and closed-book, the answer translatable (the three subjects = his three poems).

author: Tacitus
source_text: Urbem Romam a principio reges habuere; libertatem et consulatum L. Brutus instituit.
question: Quis Romae libertatem et consulatum instituisse a Tacito traditur?
question_en: Who, according to Tacitus, is said to have established liberty and the consulship at Rome?
derivation: From the same opening sentence. Anchored to Rome + the founding of the Republic; single named person, supported verbatim by 'libertatem et consulatum L. Brutus instituit'. Nominative-and-infinitive (instituisse ... traditur). Closed-book: L. Brutus as founder of liberty and the consulship is a stock fact.

author: Tacitus
source_text: auctor nominis eius Christus Tibero imperitante per procuratorem Pontium Pilatum supplicio adfectus erat
question: Quo principe imperante et per quem procuratorem Christum supplicio adfectum esse Tacitus tradit?
question_en: Under which emperor and by which procurator does Tacitus report that Christ was executed?
derivation: Anchored to Christus; two named entities (the emperor Tiberius, the procurator Pontius Pilatus), both supported verbatim by 'Tibero imperitante per procuratorem Pontium Pilatum supplicio adfectus erat' (the text reads 'Tibero'). Indirect statement (Christum ... adfectum esse) governed by tradit. Closed-book: the execution of Christ by Pilate under Tiberius is among the most famous facts derivable from Tacitus.

author: Tacitus
source_text: nam Augustus inter alia dominationis arcana, vetitis nisi permissu ingredi senatoribus aut equitibus Romanis inlustribus, seposuit Aegyptum ne fame urgeret Italiam quisquis eam provinciam claustraque terrae ac maris quamvis levi praesidio adversum ingentis exercitus insedisset.
question: Quam provinciam Augustus seposuit, vetans ne senatores aut inlustres equites Romani sine permissu eo ingrederentur?
question_en: Which province did Augustus set apart, forbidding senators or distinguished Roman knights to enter it without permission?
derivation: Augustus's reservation of Egypt as an imperial preserve (the context of Germanicus's unauthorized entry into Alexandria). Anchored to Augustus + Egypt + the ban on senators; single named province, supported verbatim by 'vetitis nisi permissu ingredi senatoribus aut equitibus Romanis inlustribus, seposuit Aegyptum'. Closed-book stock fact of Roman administration.

author: Tacitus
source_text: Pulso Tarquinio adversum patrum factiones multa populus paravit tuendae libertatis et firmandae concordiae, creatique decemviri et accitis quae usquam egregia compositae duodecim tabulae, finis aequi iuris.
question: Quis magistratus duodecim tabulas, ut apud Tacitum legitur, composuit?
question_en: Which magistracy composed the Twelve Tables, as recorded by Tacitus?
derivation: Same sentence of the law excursus, distinct fact. Anchored to the Twelve Tables; single named office, supported verbatim by 'creatique decemviri et ... compositae duodecim tabulae'. Closed-book: the decemviri who drew up the Twelve Tables (451-450 BC).

author: Tacitus
source_text: Septimo die otium placuisse ferunt, quia is finem laborum tulerit; dein blandiente inertia septimum quoque annum ignaviae datum.
question: Quoto quoque die Iudaeos otium agere Tacitus tradit?
question_en: On every which day does Tacitus report that the Jews keep rest?
derivation: The Sabbath. Anchored to the Jews + Tacitus; single ordinal-number answer, supported verbatim by 'Septimo die otium placuisse'. Indirect statement (Iudaeos otium agere) governed by tradit. Closed-book: the Jewish seventh-day rest is a stock fact; Tacitus's reported reason ('quia is finem laborum tulerit') is not asked, only the day.

author: Tacitus
source_text: Sue abstinent memoria cladis, quod ipsos scabies quondam turpaverat, cui id animal obnoxium.
question: Quo animali Iudaeos abstinere Tacitus tradit?
question_en: From which animal does Tacitus report that the Jews abstain?
derivation: Jewish abstention from pork. Anchored to the Jews + Tacitus; single named animal in the ablative (abstinere + abl.), supported verbatim by 'Sue abstinent'. Closed-book: abstaining from pork is a defining, widely known Jewish custom.

author: Tacitus
source_text: Aegyptii pleraque animalia effigiesque compositas venerantur, Iudaei mente sola unumque numen intellegunt: profanos qui deum imagines mortalibus materiis in species hominum effingant; summum illud et aeternum neque imitabile neque interiturum.
question: Quot numina Iudaeos mente sola intellegere Tacitus tradit?
question_en: How many deities does Tacitus report the Jews conceive with the mind alone?
derivation: Jewish monotheism. Anchored to the Jews (contrasted with the Egyptians) + Tacitus; single-number answer, supported verbatim by 'Iudaei mente sola unumque numen intellegunt'. Indirect statement (Iudaeos intellegere) governed by tradit. Closed-book: that the Jews worship one God is a stock fact.

author: Tacitus
source_text: Igitur nulla simulacra urbibus suis, nedum templis sistunt; non regibus haec adulatio, non Caesaribus honor.
question: Quot simulacra Iudaei in urbibus suis, nedum templis, statuunt, ut Tacitus tradit?
question_en: How many images do the Jews set up in their cities, let alone their temples, according to Tacitus?
derivation: Jewish aniconism. Anchored to the Jews + Tacitus; single answer 'nulla', supported verbatim by 'nulla simulacra urbibus suis, nedum templis sistunt'. Closed-book ethnographic fact (parallels the Germania 'Nullas ... urbes' structure).

author: Tacitus
source_text: Magna pars Iudaeae vicis dispergitur, habent et oppida; Hierosolyma genti caput. Illic immensae opulentiae templum, et primis munimentis urbs, dein regia, templum intimis clausum.
question: Quae urbs Iudaeae genti caput est, ut Tacitus tradit?
question_en: Which city is the capital of the Jewish people, according to Tacitus?
derivation: Anchored to the Jewish people + Tacitus; single named city, supported verbatim by 'Hierosolyma genti caput'. Closed-book: Jerusalem as the Jews' chief city and temple-city is universally known.
